News.title: ‘Sporty’ girl, 14, who collapsed and died at cricket club is pictured as tributes flood in for ‘deeply loved twin’
News.content:
unimaginable void ‘Sporty’ girl, 14, who collapsed and died at cricket club is pictured as tributes flood in for ‘deeply loved twin’

A TEENAGE girl who sadly died after collapsing at a cricket club has been pictured as tributes pour in.

Emergency services rushed to the scene after 14-year-old Amélia Jones collapsed at the club in Cornwall.



The sporty teen, who loved netball and cricket, collapsed at Grampound Road Cricket Club on August 20.

She died after being rushed to hospital in a medical incident.



Her family has paid tribute to the “deeply loved daughter, sister, friend, and cherished twin”.

A fundraiser set up by her uncle read: “There are no words that can truly express the heartbreak of losing a child.

“She had the most beautiful smile and brought so much happiness to the people around her.

“She had so many interests and little things that made her wonderfully and uniquely Amélia.

“Her love of sport was a huge part of her life. Just last week, Amélia captained the Cornwall Girls Under-14s against Glamorgan — an achievement that reflected her talent, confidence and determination.

“She was also exceptionally talented and academically gifted.



“Her passing has left an unimaginable void in the lives of everyone who knew and loved her.

“We are raising funds to help with Amélia’s funeral expenses and to ease some of the family’s immediate financial burden in the weeks and months ahead.”

A cricket club spokesperson said: “It is with profound sadness that Grampound Road Cricket Club can confirm a tragic incident took place on Thursday evening.

“A teenage girl collapsed and was taken to hospital, but has now sadly died. This is believed to be a medical incident not connected to cricket.”

The Club Chair Lewis Sanders said: “Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with her family, friends and everyone who knew and loved her at this unimaginably difficult time.



“We would also like to thank all those who responded on Thursday evening, particularly those who provided immediate first aid and the emergency services including the Cornwall Air Ambulance.”

News.title: Birmingham to become England’s first 20mph city with speed limit on nearly ALL roads in ‘anti-motorist’ plan
News.content:
BIRMINGHAM is set to become England’s first 20mph city under controversial plans to cut speed limits across almost all of its roads.

The city’s council, led by a coalition of Liberal Democrats, Greens and independents, has pushed for every route except major A-roads to cap speeds despite critics blasting the plans as “anti-motorist”.



Town hall leaders insisted the move would ensure private vehicles “no longer dominate street life”, while actively encouraging residents to walk or cycle instead.

The controversial plan also promises to reallocate space on the tarmac to build a public transport network they believe is more fitting for a major city.



But critics have branded the initiative an “anti-motorist policy” that will hamper travel and snarl up transit across the West Midlands.

Richard Holden, the shadow transport secretary, said that left-wing councils had turned 20mph into the “national speed of bureaucracy”.



Meanwhile, Reform UK’s Jex Parkin, the leader of Birmingham’s opposition, said of the latest proposal: “This is another anti-motorist policy from a council that seems determined to make getting around Birmingham harder.

“People already have enough congestion, restrictions and disruption to deal with without another blanket measure being imposed on them.”

The shift marks a stark turning point for a city once celebrated as Britain’s motoring capital due to its heritage of mass vehicle manufacturing and pioneering road engineering.

In its plan, which was put out for public consultation last week, Birmingham City Council said: “A limit of 20mph will be standard on all local roads.



“Residential neighbourhoods and local centres will be places where people are put first.

“Cars will no longer dominate street life around homes and schools.”

The authority has been discussing the measure for several years, after it declared a road safety emergency in July 2024, but plans would need to go through consultation before being adopted.

The move echoes a contentious nationwide scheme introduced in Wales by the Labour government in 2023.

That default 20mph limit sparked immediate backlash, forcing ministers to water down the rules a year later as local councils began restoring 30mph zones.



The debate comes as Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham pushes for further regional devolution.

Greater local control could soon grant authorities across the country the powers to enforce similar measures on their own road networks.

England has had a 30mph speed limit in residential areas since 1935, but almost a third of roads now have a 20mph restriction.

The number of drivers caught breaking 20mph speed limits has increased dramatically, from 37,219 drivers in 2023 to 125,133 in 2025.

Bristol currently holds the highest proportion of reduced-speed routes in England, with 86 per cent of its roads set to 20mph.



However, unlike Birmingham, officials in Bristol have stopped short of adopting a total blanket approach.

The Department for Transport said in June that 20mph limits “should only be used where they are appropriate and supported by evidence”.

A Birmingham City Council spokesman said: “Evidence from around the world on slower speed limits is very clear: it reduces collisions, saves lives and reduces injuries – so our message is simple: slower is safer.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Slower speeds are less intimidating towards those who walk or cycle, activities that we need to encourage more of if we are to reduce the number of harmful emissions and traffic levels in the city.”

The spokesman added that the city’s 20mph rollout had so far been done on a “targeted basis in response to local road safety concerns or near to schools”.

News.title: At least 14 newborn babies killed as fire engulfs hospital’s maternity ward after ‘air conditioning unit explosion’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BABY TRAGEDY At least 14 newborn babies killed as fire engulfs hospital’s maternity ward after ‘air conditioning unit explosion’

AT LEAST 14 newborn babies have been killed after a horror fire tore through a hospital’s maternity ward.

An air conditioning unit reportedly exploded sparking the deadly blaze and trapping several people inside with just one baby being rescued alive.



Nineteen people were saved in total from inside the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital after the fire broke out.

These included the newborn tot, six other children, 10 women and two men.



All survivors were reportedly rushed to intensive care units for further treatment.

Pakistani officials believe the fire broke out on the hospital’s third floor at around 6.45am this morning.



Six fire trucks, four ambulances and dozens of emergency responders rushed to the scene to carry out rescue operation around PIMS.

The compressor of an air-conditioning unit exploded inside the gynaecology unit of the nursery, according to local reports.

Pictures from the scene show glass windows close to where the fire broke out shattered under the intense heat.

Health Minister Mustafa Kamal told Geo News: “The fire spread very quickly, and the hospital’s electricity also went out immediately with the explosion.”



The infants in the ward were in incubators or connected to oxygen equipment at the time of the fire, Kamal added.

Newborns who died will have to be identified using DNA tests, local police said.

Heartbroken parents have been unable to say their goodbyes as the bodies of the babies remain with medical examiners.

Rescuers said no doctors, ward boys or other staff were in the incubation centre when the fire broke out.



Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an “immediate investigation” into the cause of the fire.

He said in a statement that he has “deep sorrow and heartfelt regret” over the hospital tragedy.

Sharif added: “Such a situation with children is irreparable.”

An eight-member inquiry committee has been set up to investigate the fire.

News.title: Moment police officer borrows bike from passerby then races after ‘thief’ and tackles him to ground
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a police officer borrows a bike from a cyclist and uses it to chase down a suspected thief.

After commandeering the bicycle, bodycam footage shows the cop tackling the man to the ground and shouting: “You’re f****** nicked!”.



The chase began with the officer driving through the streets of Twickenham, south-west London in pursuit of an alleged thief.

Realising he needs to carry on the chase on foot, the Metropolitan Police officer exits his car and starts running.



But he soon passes a member of the public with a bike – who says: “Do you guys want to chase him on this?”.

The grateful officer replies “would you mind?” and tells the cyclist he only needs it for “five minutes”.



He races off, eventually reaching the suspect on a towpath near to the Twickenham Stoop stadium.

He then tackles the man to the ground and shouts: “Get over, get on the ground”.



“You’re f****** nicked!” he adds.

The officer then contacts his team, saying: “Additional officers coming to join me.

“I’m going to have to repatriate this bike to my hero member of the public.”

Insp Jon McLoughlin said of the incident: “The video below shows a recent arrest after a bike was stolen on Whitton High Street and is a great example of the public and police working together.

“In this case, a quick-thinking cyclist lent an officer their bike so they could continue their pursuit of a suspect.



“It’s a brilliant example of how a small act can make a big difference.”

This isn’t the first time an officer has used a member of the public to help catch a suspect.

In June, one armed police officer was helped by a van driver in the middle of a police chase before they catch the suspect fleeing on foot.



The officer clutching a firearm can be seen approaching a mini-roundabout after the suspect evaded attempts to arrest him.

Standing in the middle of the road, he then turns to a passing motorist in a van who stops and urges the officer to “get in the back, get in the back”.

The officer climbs in shouting “go, go, go” and tells the driver to follow the other officers.

In another amusing clip an out of breath bobby is picked up by a driver as he is chasing down two thieving boys.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The woman who filmed the incident said she and her friend were driving home when they saw the chase unfold.



“He opened the door and told us to follow the suspect,” she said.

News.title: Horror moment soapbox cart ploughs into crowd during race when it loses control after jump and injures eight
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a soapbox cart loses control and ploughs into a crowd of spectators during a traditional race, injuring eight.

Horrifying footage shows the cart whizz down a steep street in Ecuador before losing control after a jump and veering into bystanders.



The racer immediately smashes through fences and tyres used as safety barriers sending the cart driver flying into spectators on the pavement.

Horrified witnesses rush to help the wounded as one of the drivers writhes in agony from the impact.



A huge crowd immediately starts pulling the barricades off the injured spectators.

The crash unfolded as 51 teams competed in celebrations marking the 128th anniversary of the San Roque parish, in Imbabura, Ecuador, on August 23.

A cart racing in the “Fuerza Libre” (Open) category was the one to lose control on the two-mile course.

These makeshift vehicles can go faster than 60mph on the dangerous route, which features bumpy hills.



The eight injured in the chaos were rushed to hospitals in Atuntaqui and Ibarra for treatment.

Event organiser Steven Terán said safety measures had been put in place for the race but acknowledged that competitions of this type carry inherent risks.

Fortunately, there were no fatalities.



Soapbox cart racing is very popular in hilly, rally-crazed Ecuador.

The phenomenon, which is dubbed Carrera Coches de Madera – or “wooden car race”, dates back to the 1940s, according to Quito Informa.

Certain events, like the one involving the crash, have carts crewed by two riders.

One is responsible for steering, while others push with their feet in the slower sections.

Riders throw their bodies around to make sharp turns, akin to bobsleigh races.



These high-speed gravity-fuelled street races often draw large crowds of keen spectators.

News.title: PM must find the courage to stop taxing families and small businesses to the hilt to fund freebies for Benefits Street
News.content:
It’s the Taxman

THE next time Andy Burnham gets his guitar out he might as well treat voters to a version of The Beatles classic Taxman.

Because be in no doubt, our Prime Minister is preparing to launch yet another massive Labour cash grab.

Economists reckon the Autumn Budget could swipe another £25billion.



That would be on a par with the pain former Chancellor Rachel Reeves dished out last November which was on TOP of her £40billion of tax rises in 2024. The reason for this doom loop?



Keir Starmer ducked ALL the tough choices while his successor doesn’t seem to have much of a plan either. There are STILL no concrete proposals to slash eye-watering welfare payments.

In just a few weeks this summer, Burnham has already spent billions on small-change help for families such as £45 off their energy bills and two quid bus fares. The PM also has big plans to deliver radical change in social care — but no clue how to pay for it.

Chancellor John Healey rightly wants to ramp up defence spending. But there are already billions missing from Starmer and Reeves’s Defence Investment Plan which fell way short of what military chiefs were demanding.



Meanwhile, backbench Labour MPs refuse to consider any spending cuts.

It means only one thing: massive tax rises. Unless Burnham finds the courage to stop taxing families and small businesses to the hilt to fund freebies for Benefits Street, nothing will change.

He’ll be back for more of your money NEXT year. And the year after, too.

A bitter taste

A CLASSIC example of the consequences of Labour’s addiction to tax and spending is the perilous state of our pubs.



When he was trying to get elected as an MP, Andy Burnham raised hopes that he would halve VAT for boozers.

But as with so many pledges that dripped casually off his tongue, the reality inside No10 is very different.

Treasury ministers now bleakly warn such a move would “cost a lot of money.”

But what’s the cost to our communities when their local pub closes down?

Goodbye Dolly

VERY few people have used their success to help others quite like Dolly Parton.



One of the greatest country stars, it was the way she shared her hard-earned fortune that made her so unique.

More than 150million books have been given to kids thanks to the Dollywood Foundation, inspired by the struggles of her dad who couldn’t read or write.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Famed for her blonde wigs and big boobs, Dolly quipped: “It takes a lot of money to look this cheap.”

But the truth is that nothing about Dolly was cheap. She was solid gold from 9 to 5 — and in every other hour too.

News.title: Kemi Badenoch set to reshuffle her top team ahead of Tory conference after the summer break
News.content:
FRESH FACES Kemi Badenoch set to reshuffle her top team ahead of Tory conference after the summer break

TORY leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to make changes to her top team after the summer break.

She is said to be preparing a reshuffle ahead of the Conservative conference in October.



Energy’s Claire Coutinho is expected to step away from the front bench before maternity leave.

Shadow Solicitor General Helen Grant has asked to stand down.



Julia Lopez could also be moved after PM Andy Burnham scrapped the Science, Innovation and Technology department covered by her brief.

Restless MPs from the 2024 intake are said to be pushing for promotion, , with Katie Lam, Harriet Cross and Aphra Brandreth among those tipped for bigger jobs.

A Tory source said: “A lot of the new intake want jobs because they think the shadow cabinet are lazy and they have to pick up the slack.”

There has also been speculation over the futures of shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Dame Priti Patel but neither is currently expected to be replaced.

Tory sources last night played down suggestions a major overhaul is being planned and stressed some changes would simply be needed because of Labour’s machinery-of-government shake-up, Ms Coutinho’s maternity leave and Ms Grant’s decision to step down.

News.title: Dolly Parton dies after brief battle with cancer as Taylor Swift leads tributes
News.content:
Dolly Parton's life in her own songs

Many of Dolly Parton's songs reveal details of her life, whether that's through the lyrics themselves or the hidden true story behind them.

Coat of Many Colours (1971)

Dolly's single 'Coat of Many Colours' is an autobiographical song, about how her mother had made her a coat out of rags when she was younger. In the lyrics, Dolly recounted how her family struggled to afford clothes and her mother's ingenuity with a needle and thread left her daughter at the mercy of classmates' ridicule.

She sang: “I know we had no money, but I was rich as I could be, in my coat of many colors my mama made for me.”

My Tennessee Mountain Home (1973)

Dolly really did grow up in a Tennessee Mountain Home. She spent her childhood in a two-room log cabin in Locust Ridge, with her parents and all her siblings.

Though they didn't have electricity or running water, the lyrics point towards everything Dolly loved about her childhood home, including: "Sittin' on the front porch on a summer afternoon, in a straight back chair on two legs leaned against the wall, as I watch the kids a-playin' with their June bugs on a string and chase the glowin' fireflies when evenin' shadows fall."

Jolene (1973)

Jolene was a red-headed bank clerk who had flirted with Dolly's husband, Carl Dean, early in their marriage. Though Carl was deeply devoted to Dolly, she had feared losing him to the glamourous clerk and penned the song to get through her jealousy.

I Will Always Love You (1974)

Dolly's career kicked off when she formed a partnership with Porter Wagoner. But there came a point where she felt the need to move on and the only way she could explain it was through song.

Thus, I Will Always Love You was born. The song, which is one of the most loved break-up tracks ever, was origianlly written to tell Porter that though Dolly would always love him, their time together was over.

News.title: Raheem Sterling charged with dangerous driving and laughing gas possession after motorway crash
News.content:
Raheem Sterling charged with dangerous driving and laughing gas possession after motorway crash

Raheem Sterling is due in court next month to face charges of dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen

View 2 Images Raheem Sterling is without a club after playing for Feyenoord last season (Image: Gabriel Calvino Alonso/Getty Images)

Former England star Raheem Sterling has been charged following a crash on the motorway in May.

The 31-year-old, who is currently without a club, was arrested on May 28 following a collision on the M3 involving his black 4x4 Lamborghini. He is now due at Basingstoke magistrates court on September 15 to face three charges.

A Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary spokesman said: “A driver will appear in court next month to face charges following a collision on the M3.

“Raheem Sterling, 31, from Berkshire, has been charged for the following offences: dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, failing to provide a specimen.

“The charges come following a single vehicle collision, involving a Lamborghini, on the M3 southbound, close to the Minley Interchange, on 28 May, 2026.

Article continues below

View 2 Images Raheem Sterling is currently without a club (Image: NurPhoto, NurPhoto via Getty Images)

“No other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported. Mr Sterling is due to appear at Basingstoke magistrates court on 15 September.”

The ex-Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal and Chelsea forward had just finished his stint playing for Feyenoord at the time of the crash. After being frozen out of the first-team set-up, he terminated his contract with Chelsea in January in order to join the Dutch club.

Article continues below

He played under former Premier League striker Robin van Persie, but the short-term move didn't go to plan, with no goals or assists coming in his eight appearances for Feyenoord.

The four-time Premier League winner has spent the summer looking for a new club - a search which has so far proven unsuccessful. He has been keeping busy in the off-season by coaching at his own RS7 Academy.

News.title: 404lb woman on three takeaways a day loses 12st after comment at slimming group
News.content:
404lb woman on three takeaways a day loses 12st after comment at slimming group

Siân Robinson would sometimes eat McDonald's twice a day and then have pizza for dinner

404lb woman on three takeaways a day loses 12st after comment at slimming group

A woman who says she was addicted to food and regularly ate three takeaways a day has shed more than 13 stone. At her heaviest, Siân Robinson weighed 28st 12lbs and wore a size 32.

‌



The 33-year-old would start her day with a McDonald’s breakfast before having Greggs or another McDonald’s for lunch. Dinner could be a large half-and-half Domino’s pizza with wedges, with chocolate, crisps and cookies eaten in between meals.

‌



After years of failed diets, Siân’s weight began taking a devastating toll on her everyday life. She became breathless walking upstairs, avoided public transport because she worried about taking up too much space and needed a mobility scooter to get around Disney World in March 2024.

‌



View 7 Images Siân needed a mobility scooter to get around

“I was scared of flying and fitting in the seat,” said Siân, from Worcester, Worcestershire. “I didn’t like public transport in case I had to sit by someone and make them uncomfortable due to my size. Most physical activity was so hard for me.

‌



“It was affecting my day-to-day life. I had no confidence. I felt I’d lost my spark and was hiding away. I didn’t want to attend any events or meet friends, etc., as I was worried people would look at me because of my size.”

Siân said one cruel comment at a slimming group particularly stuck with her. She said: “People very rarely made comments. They just didn’t want to speak about it. However, something that has stuck with me is that at a local slimming group.

View 7 Images Siân before her weight loss

‌



“I attended for the first time in a while, and the lady weighing there said, ‘Oh my God, Siân, I didn’t recognise you; you’ve got so big’.

“That really upset me I was so upset when I realised I’d need a mobility scooter to get round Disney. It cost $60 a day but was essential because I just couldn’t do it. I was only 30 and already needed a scooter. I wondered how many years I had left with the way it was going.”

‌



Siân says her struggles with her weight began in childhood and food eventually came to dominate her life. She said: “I was always the biggest in my class at school. I noticed this from early years, and looking back in photos, I was always a bigger child.

View 7 Images Siân Robinson weighed 28st 12lbs and wore a size 32

‌



“I went on my first diet at a slimming club at the age of 10, and would always lose a bit, then put more back on. It became more of an addiction for me. All I would think about was food, and my life would revolve around it.”

But after getting engaged to her partner of 13 years, Matt, 32, in August 2024, Siân decided she wanted to transform her health before walking down the aisle. The aesthetics nurse prescriber began taking the weight-loss jab Mounjaro in November 2024 as a final attempt before considering surgery.

She has since lost 13st 10lbs, dropping from a size 32 to a size 16. Siân said: “I wanted to feel amazing on my wedding day and fit into my dream dress. I wanted something that actually worked, as one last try before I would make the decision to have surgery.

‌



View 7 Images Siân after her weight loss

“I followed a lot of people who were on Mounjaro and decided I wanted to give it a go. I chose a company that was CQC registered, and I felt safe with. I ordered the pen whilst I was on a Disney cruise, and it was waiting for me when I got home.

‌



“I felt terrified. I was scared that it wouldn’t work and the only thing left would be surgery. I was also scared I’d have horrific side effects, but I haven’t.”

Siân has also overhauled her diet, ditching her regular takeaways in favour of high-protein, balanced meals. She now starts her day with a protein shake and has salads, sandwiches or eggs with avocado on toast for lunch.

View 7 Images Siân has been using jabs

‌



Dinner might be chicken skewers with a jacket potato and salad. Siân said: “I now focus on the nutrition and fuelling my body rather than just food. I haven’t had Domino’s since December 2024. My likes and dislikes have completely changed.”

Now weighing 15st 2.3lbs and wearing a size 16, Siân says she has regained the confidence she thought she had lost. She hopes to shed another three stone before her wedding next July. She added: “My life is completely different. I have confidence, and I feel like I’ve got my spark back.

‌



View 7 Images Siân used to be addicted to food

“I want to go out, buy new clothes and enjoy myself. I go to the gym regularly; I’m not out of breath, feel physically fitter, and I’m making plans like going on holiday and enjoying life. I could have cried the first time I went clothes shopping for a size 16.

‌



“It was finally working, and I felt good in myself. I’m now wearing clothes I like rather than clothes that just hide me People can’t believe it; sometimes they don’t recognise me.

View 7 Images Siân hasn't had a Domino's in two years

Article continues below

“Everyone is so proud. Matt is so proud and happy for me. I’m going back to Disney next month, and I can’t wait to be able to walk around. It feels amazing, life-changing. To anyone else who is struggling with their weight and doesn’t know where to start, don’t be scared to give it another try.

“I’m so glad I made the decision to try. I feel free.”

News.title: 'I blew £35k on boob job and designer handbags - but cleared £12k in a month with clever debt trick'
News.content:
'I blew £35k on boob job and designer handbags - but cleared £12k in a month with clever debt trick'

Sarah Outtridge, 31, has been in debt since the age of 18 thanks to purchases ranging from an £8,000 breast augmentation and £1,000 a month on clothes

View 4 Images Sarah found herself in debt after blowing cash on impulse buys - including handbags (Image: SWNS)

A midwife who accumulated £35,000 in debt on cosmetic surgery and clothes has already cleared £12,000 in one month by using the snowball method. Sarah Outtridge, 31, says she has been in debt since the age of 18, after buying big ticket items “on impulse” including a £7,500 car on finance in 2020, an £8,000 breast augmentation, and £4,500 courses in property and aesthetics.

‌



She also used Klarna to help pay for new clothes - spending up to £1,000 in just one month on new items. In July 2026, Sarah calculated her total debt - £34,856.67 - and overhauled her lifestyle. She has employed the snowball method - where you pay off your smallest debts first, then roll those payments into larger debts, building momentum until all debts are cleared.

‌



So far, she has wiped off £12,000 including her £3,250 Monzo credit card debt using money she was due to spend on a £7,000 tummy tuck procedure in September 2026 - which she has now cancelled. Working an extra two 12-and-a-half-hour shifts per week, she brings home around £4,000 per month, putting 50% of it to repayments.

‌



She has also paid off her £1,000 Klarna debt and has opted to close her account completely. Sarah has set herself the goal of paying off her debt entirely by the end of 2027, and hopes to then go on and save up an emergency fund of three months' expenses by March 2028.

View 4 Images Sarah used Klarna to help pay for new clothes (Image: SWNS)

Her end goal is to save £50,000 to buy a new home - as she currently lives in supported housing - by December 2029. Sarah, from Hackney, East London, says: “Since I turned 18 it’s been ongoing, I’ve never not been in debt.

‌



“I was completely out of control spending on mostly things I did not need through pure impulse. I was so sick of it. It’s just constantly feeling like I’m working, having no money and I want to save for a house and I was thinking ‘it’s impossible with all this debt’.

“It was a vicious cycle. I would buy big things and cosmetic surgery was one of them. I’d say because it was my first cosmetic surgery, I wouldn’t say I was addicted but especially Botox and filler I got into a routine of having it regularly every two to three months.

“I had a breast augmentation costing £8,000. I got a car on finance before which was really high interest because my credit score was not that great. I couldn’t get a permit to park where I live and I was paying £2,000 per year to park in the borough.

‌



“I ended up selling the car as it was not much use – I was constantly paying for parking, finance and insurance. I lost some of the value of the car after selling it. It would be for clothes, like on Klarna, as well.

“One month I spent £1,000 through Klarna and basically I’d think, ‘Oh yeah, I’ll pay and spread the payments over the next three months’. It would be the same process and I’d buy more and buy more."

After calculating her debts, Sarah has employed a method of paying off her smallest debt first and working through them methodically. Feeling like she was “constantly living” in her overdraft and burnt out from working, Sarah’s hopes of one day affording a house deposit spurred her on to “take accountability” for her finances.

‌



“I thought it was around £20,000 thinking off the top of my head,” she says. “I didn’t sit down and calculate it. When I did finally do that, with all the interest added it was over £30,000.

“I thought ‘this is crazy’ and way more than I thought and something has got to change. I’ve got to reduce my outgoings completely and aggressively get rid of the debt.

“I’ve been doing that, doing extra shifts at work and budgeting every week. I had a tummy tuck booked in Turkey in September this year and I have cancelled that. I paid off my Monzo credit card by cancelling that procedure."

‌



View 4 Images Sarah with her plan for financial freedom (Image: SWNS)

Sarah has been paying off chunks between £500 and £1,000 per week due to her overtime work, and despite not setting a specific weekly budget for herself, has been cost-cutting wherever she can.

“I have cleared out the cupboards of food and have only been getting things it makes sense to buy,” she says. “I’m doing no buys as well so I’m not buying new clothes. I’m walking everywhere – I have completely cut public transport and uber.”

‌



Meal prepping has also kept costs low, as well as cancelling her £40 per month gym membership. Sarah has also switched energy providers from Fuse Energy to Good Energy through U-Switch, which she estimates will save her £37 annually.

View 4 Images Sarah has written her savings goals down in a notebook (Image: SWNS)

“It’s a big weight lifted off my shoulders,” she says. “I feel so motivated every time I pay a bit more towards my loans. There is a light at the end of the tunnel.

‌



“I felt weighed down before and drained like I was living in survival mode. At the moment I’m building a future for myself and it’s freeing. I’m getting my life back."

Sarah began sharing her story on TikTok last month, and has already received “loads” of comments and supportive messages. “People are saying I’m brave for putting it out there,” she says. “Even people at work have been saying ‘Sarah because of you I’ve cleared off my credit card’."

Sarah’s debt breakdown

Before

‌



Monzo credit card (which paid for aesthetics appointments, shopping and clothes): £3,250 – included £247.84 interest

Monzo loan (for composite bonding): £6,000 over five years – included £3,106.25 interest

News.title: Energy bills rise to three-year high as winter Ofgem price cap announced
News.content:
Energy bills rise to three-year high as winter Ofgem price cap announced

The price cap sets a maximum limit on how much you can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity you use, as well as the daily standing charge

View 2 Images Energy bills are rising again this winter (Image: Westend61 via Getty Images)

Energy bills will rise to the highest level in three years for millions of households this winter after Ofgem announced its latest price cap.

‌



The price cap is rising by 4% from this October - just as many households will turn on their heating as temperatures start to fall.

‌



The typical household that pays by direct debit will see their annual bill increase from £1,663 to £1,723 - a £60 increase. Energy bills had already risen by 13% in July as uncertainty around the Iran war continues to drive up gas costs.

‌



The latest increase comes despite a temporary VAT cut on electricity bills that is set to come into effect in October. Ofgem said without the cut, annual energy bills would have been £45 higher.

View 2 Images The new price cap comes into force from October (Image: Getty)

But analysts say prices could rise further in January, when the price cap is updated again, with bills currently forecast to increase by a further 9% in the new year. This would put an average January bill up to £1,872 a year.

‌



Dr Craig Lowrey, Principal Consultant at Cornwall Insight, said: “Where January bills land will depend on whether the situation in the Middle East calms down in the next couple of months.

“However, even if we saw an end to the conflict, lower stocks going into winter as demand increases mean falling bills in January is unlikely.”

Neil Kenward, Ofgem Director General for Markets, said: “High international gas prices are continuing to drive energy costs in the UK. We welcome the Government’s intervention to remove VAT from electricity bills, without which customers would have faced even higher costs this winter.”

‌



What is the Ofgem price cap?

Around 22 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs that are covered by the price cap. It applies to standard variable rate (SVR) tariffs, which is your supplier's default plan if you have not fixed into an energy deal.

The price cap sets a maximum limit on how much you can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity you use, as well as the daily standing charge. The standing charge is a fixed fee you pay to be connected to the grid.

But the price cap does not put a total cap on how much you will pay for energy - so your bill is still based on how much gas and electricity you use. This means your bill can be higher or lower than the price cap figure.

‌



The main price cap figure represents what a typical billpayer who pays by direct debit can expect to pay. Ofgem updated the way it calculates this in July, as it says households are using less energy now to save money.

It previously said the average household uses 2,700 kWh of electricity and 11,500 kWh of gas per year - but now, it says this has fallen to 2,500 kWh of electricity and 9,500 kWh of gas.

Under its old definition of typical use, the July price cap would be £1,862 a year and the October price cap would be £1,935.

‌



Despite its main figure representing an annual bill, the price cap is actually reviewed every three months by Ofgem.

There are different unit rates and standing charges for prepayment customers, or if you pay when you get a bill. If you are on a fixed tariff, you will not be impacted by the price cap change. Ofgem estimates that 11 million are on fixed tariffs.

Get the best deals and tips from Mirror Money WHATSAPP GROUP: Get money news and top deals straight to your phone by joining our Money WhatsApp group here. We also treat our community members to special offers, promotions, and adverts from us and our partners. If you don’t like our community, you can check out any time you like. If you’re curious, you can read our Privacy Notice. NEWSLETTER: Or sign up to the Mirror's Money newsletter here for all the best advice and shopping deals straight to your inbox.

‌



Should I lock into a fixed tariff now?

Sarah Coles, head of personal finance at AJ Bell, said there are fixed deals available that will save you money compared to being on the price cap.

She said: "22 million households are still on a price cap tariff, so if you’re one of them, you could consider fixing. Some deals are charging up to £100 less than the October price cap, so you could save money immediately."

The price cap changes every three months, so whether fixing is right for you depends on how you think energy bills will change over the next year.

‌



If you are considering a fixed tariff, check for any exit fees in case you want to leave your contract early.

Laura Hinton from MoneySuperMarket Energy, added: "For households concerned about what their bills might look like this winter, fixing now could provide certainty, protection from future price cap increases and potentially significant savings."

How to cut your energy bill

There are plenty of simple things you can do around your home to cut your energy bill. Turning appliances off standby can save you around £45 a year, while not overfilling the kettle can save you another £10, according to the Energy Saving Trust.

‌



You can also reduce your bill £26 a year by washing your clothes at 30C and reducing your washing machine use by one run per week for a year.

It could also pay you to get your home ready for winter. You can keep your home insulated on a budget by sealing up draughts, covering bare floors and bleeding your radiators so your heating works as efficiently as possible.

If you are worried about falling behind on your energy bill, speak to your supplier as soon as possible. They should be able to offer you support, such as a payment plan, payment breaks or affordable debt repayments.

Article continues below

Your supplier may also have hardship funds that you could be entitled to. For example, the British Gas Energy Trust offers grants worth up to £1,700 to help people clear their debt - and it is possible to access this help even if you are not a British Gas customer.

There are also Government help schemes. The Warm Home Discount gives you £150 off your electricity bill if you are claiming certain means-tested benefits.

Winter Fuel Payments are worth up to £300 and are paid to pensioners who have a taxable income of less than £35,000.

News.title: Fire rips through Pakistan hospital killing 14 newborn babies as 'air-con unit explodes'
News.content:
Fire rips through Pakistan hospital killing 14 newborn babies as 'air-con unit explodes'

An air conditioner compressor reportedly exploded inside a nursery in Pakistan on Wednesday morning killing at least 14 newborn babies, according to hospital officials

View 3 Images At least 14 families have been torn apart following a devastating fire at a nursery in Pakistan (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

A fire has ripped through a hospital killing 14 newborn babies after an air conditioning unit exploded, hospital officials have confirmed.

‌



The horror incident happened in the early hours of Wednesday August 26 at a major government hospital in Pakistan’s capital. The fire broke out on the third floor of the mother and child unit of PIMS hospital, one of the main state-run hospitals in the city.

‌



The nursery at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences housed at least 15 newborns when the fire broke out, hospital officials said. At least one baby was rescued.

‌



View 3 Images A heartbroken mother at the scene (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Rescue officials said the fire began at about 6:45 a.m., after the compressor of an air-conditioning unit reportedly exploded inside the nursery, which is part of the hospital’s gynaecology ward.

The newborns in the ward hit by the blaze were either on oxygen equipment or in incubators, Health Minister Mustafa Kamal told Geo News. He said: "The fire spread very quickly, and the hospital's electricity also went out immediately with the explosion."

‌



Firefighters quickly responded and extinguished the blaze, and rescue teams were carrying out cooling operations at the site, local media reported.

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has released a statement expressing "deep sorrow and heartfelt regret" over the hospital fire.

Sharif has instructed authorities to "conduct an immediate investigation", according to the statement from his office. "Such a situation with children is irreparable", the statement continues.

‌



Sharif expresses his "heartfelt condolences to the families of the innocent children", adding "his heart is saddened by this tragic incident". Authorities say the blaze has now been extinguished.

Islamabad's District Magistrate setup a fact-finding committee in the aftermath of the deadly fire, which will produce a report on the tragedy "within 24 hours". This will include probing what caused the fire to start.

View 3 Images Security personnel stand next to an ambulance following the fire at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) Hospital (Image: Aamir QURESHI / AFP via Getty Images)

Article continues below

PIMS hospital was in the news last week after Pakistan's former Prime Minister Imran Khan was briefly taken there from prison to be seen by doctors. Khan's lawyers said the 73-year-old suffered from several health conditions, including deteriorating eyesight, but doctors deemed him "medically fit", before he was taken back to jail.

The Mirror has contacted Shehbaz Sharif's press office and the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences for comment.

News.title: Train strike over August Bank Holiday to spark chaos as 3 services to London impacted
News.content:
Train strike over August Bank Holiday to spark chaos as 3 services to London impacted

A number of services will be effected on Sunday and Monday and commuters have been told to travel only if necessary, as union members strike over safety concerns

View 4 Images East Midlands Railway has confirmed plans for a "significantly reduced" timetable for services to and from London (Image: Getty Images)

Commuters have been advised to expect disruptions to train services over the bank holiday weekend as strike action is planned.

‌



A number of services will be affected on Sunday and Monday, including disruptions expected by East Midlands Railway (EMR) as members of the Rail, Maritime and Transport union (RMT) strike over safety concerns.

‌



EMR said it is holding "constructive discussions" with the union.

‌



View 4 Images Commuters have been advised to expect disruptions to train services over the bank holiday weekend (Image: Getty Images)

The rail service has confirmed plans for a "significantly reduced" timetable for services to and from London on both days.

Passengers have been advised to check details before embarking on their journeys and to only travel if necessary.

‌



Philippa Cresswell, customer experience director at EMR, said the company recognise "how frustrating this disruption will be for customers".

"We are very sorry for the impact this will have on August bank holiday plans," she said.

"We strongly advise customers to only travel to or from London if their journey is essential on Sunday, August 30 and Monday, August 31, and to check their full journey, including first and last trains, before setting out."

‌



View 4 Images Passengers have been advised to check details before embarking on their journeys (Image: ADAM VAUGHAN/EPA/Shutterstock)

Sunday, August 30 will experience further disruption.

No LNER trains will run between London King's Cross and Peterborough as digital signalling upgrades are carried out by Network Rail.

‌



EMR services to and from London St Pancras are expected to be busy on Sunday, with the increase in demand coinciding with the reduced services.

Sheffield and Nottingham stations will likely be busy, with queues to board services expected.

EMR shared the following details on the services affected:

‌



Sunday, August 30

Services will start from approximately 8am and finish before 7pm.

EMR Intercity:

‌



One train per hour between Nottingham and London St Pancras

One train per hour between Sheffield and London St Pancras

EMR Connect:

One train per hour between Corby and London St Pancras.

No rail replacement bus services will be provided.

‌



Network Rail is carrying out essential engineering work on the East Coast Main Line, affecting services to and from London King's Cross.

LNER trains will start and terminate at Peterborough and replacement busses will operate to and from Bedford for onward connections with Thameslink to London St Pancras.

View 4 Images Strikes are also expected in September (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Monday, August 31

EMR services will start from approximately 8am and finish before 7pm.

EMR Intercity:

‌



One train per hour between Nottingham and London St Pancras

One train per hour between Sheffield and London St Pancras

EMR Connect:

One train per hour between Corby and London St Pancras

No rail replacement bus services will be provided

Article continues below

Members of the RMT union will also take strike action on Wednesday, September 16 and Thursday, September 17 and EMR is assessing the impact of the industrial action on services.

One shopper said: 'It's honestly the best thing I feel like I've invested in household-wise'

A heated airer offers a more economical alternative, and Lakeland has now cut the price of a range of its heated airers ahead of the colder months. News.title: The life of an iconic country singer
News.content:
Iconic country musician Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80, her family announced on her social media.

"Sadness lies with us, not with Dolly," Parton's nephew Brian Seaver said in a video announcement.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.

Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy."

She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her show business career that spanned more than 60 years.

Follow for live updates and read more about Dolly's life.

News.title: Household energy bills to hit three-year high as Ofgem announces 4% rise from October
News.content:
Energy prices for millions of households will rise to the highest level for three years, under regulator Ofgem's price cap.

The cap reflects the rise in the wholesale cost of gas, paid by suppliers, but will hit household bills just as the colder weather arrives in October.

Ofgem said the price cap will increase by 4% compared with the current level, with a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity paying Â£60 a year more.

More than a third of households are now on fixed tariffs so their prices will not change.

Suppliers say energy debt has rocketed and, with high bills likely to persist, have called for more support for those struggling to pay.

The government says VAT is being cut from electricity bills in October, including for those on fixed deals, with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh saying ministers will "keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills".

But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices may rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households at the coldest time of the year.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said: "High international gas prices are continuing to drive energy costs in the UK. We welcome the government's intervention to remove VAT from electricity bills, without which customers would have faced even higher costs this winter.

"Savings are available by choosing a fixed tariff, which are available at Â£100 or more below the October price cap."

News.title: NHS failing child sex abuse victims in adulthood, say psychiatrists
News.content:
People sexually abused as children who seek help in later life for mental health problems are being failed by the NHS, senior doctors have told the BBC.

The Royal College of Psychiatrists is issuing a public apology for what it says is decades of mismanagement and misdiagnosis in the UK.

For some, it has worsened their traumas, it said.

The college said mental health staff have been too focussed on treating symptoms rather than exploring how past traumatic experiences can still affect patients.

Support is improving, it said, but there must be better training and more investment - something NHS bosses have said is being introduced.

The apology has been included in a report, external by the college and given to the BBC.

Immediate past president of the college, Dr Lade Smith, said she was "sorry" that, too often, victims have suffered "avoidable harm when seeking help".

The report details how treatment has sometimes been inappropriate, while people have been re-traumatised by the experience of repeated assessments and history-taking and not always being believed.

Dr Smith told the BBC it was clear people were not getting the support they needed, and that this was not just a failing of psychiatrists, but the whole mental health system.

"Services are so fragmented. The system is set up to provide short, discreet episodes of care. Psychiatrists do not get the time to build up a relationship with patients so they can be properly supported.

"They are lucky if they get eight sessions of therapy, when it could take eight sessions for a person just to disclose the abuse.

"And these are just the people who get support â many don't even get seen by mental health services because services are so stretched," she said.

News.title: Dad of woman who took her own life says Treasury failed in its duty of care
News.content:
The father of a civil service employee who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers has said the lack of support given to her by the Treasury "beggars belief".

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, David Moffat said he did not feel the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death.

He added that her loss was "devastating", and had "torn such a big hole in our lives".

The Treasury said "it will learn the lessons from this tragedy".

On 19 May 2025, Chloe went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

"Chloe's first comment was, 'Oh, this must be serious, there's two of you here'", David told Today's Emma Barnett. "So that's the first time that she was aware of anything [that] might be a to do."

"And then they worked through and put several allegations to her that she'd shared confidential information."

During the meeting, David said she had asked on several occasions if she would lose her job, and if she could have a friend there - both of which were refused.

A coroner found at an inquest earlier in August that the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy, which would have made clear that if the allegations against Chloe were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

"Even though she asked, they said they could not determine the outcome," David said.

Straight after the meeting, Chloe was locked out of her emails. "That was all part of the shock and awe of it all for Chloe," David said.

The coroner found that the meeting between Chloe and her managers "materially contributed" to her death.

News.title: Why Pride is facing a backlash - from inside and outside the LGBT community
News.content:
Matt left Crewe as soon as he could, aged 18, feeling that he wasn't accepted as a young gay man. The only LGBT scene to mention was a tiny, makeshift bar behind a curtain in the back of an out-of-town pub.

He left in 2015, but this June found himself returning home, for Crewe Pride.

For Matt, it was a significant homecoming. "It really took me back to when I was a kid growing up here, trying to navigate my identity. It felt so important to be there and see how a town that wasn't particularly welcomingâ¦ has changed and flourished."

For many, these small, community Pride events feel a world away from the huge celebrations in the UK's largest cities.

But Matt's happy weekend in Crewe masks a growing culture war over Pride. Over the last few years, a number of councils have withdrawn their support for Pride festivals, while some big brands - perhaps nervous about being seen as too "woke" - have become hesitant to associate themselves with them. On top of all that, there's a long-running complaint from some LGBT campaigners that Pride has become overly commercialised; while the argument over trans issues has also made matters more fraught.

It's leading some to ask: what future do Pride events have?

News.title: Yellow warnings in force as rain and thunderstorms hit parts of UK
News.content:
Downpours and thunderstorms will continue to bring the risk of flooding to parts of the UK on Wednesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms is valid from 03:00 until 22:00 BST, covering much of the Midlands, parts of northern, eastern and southern England, as well as the far east of Wales.

The rain could be heavy enough to bring flash flooding and travel disruption, with lightning and large hail posing additional hazards.

A further Met Office yellow warning has been issued for Thursday with more thunderstorms expected.

For some areas that have seen barely any rain so far this August, the next few days could bring the wettest weather in many weeks.

News.title: As Ukraine hits Russia's refineries, Russia targets Ukraine's petrol pumps
News.content:
"Fill up quickly and move on," Mayor Ihor Terekhov warns drivers in Ukraine's second largest city Kharkiv.

Two petrol stations in the city in Ukraine's north-east were hit by Russian drones on Monday, which local officials say wounded two people. In another attack on a petrol station outside the city of Kryvyi Rih last week, three people were killed.

Russia's campaign of targeting civilian filling stations with drones and missiles began in earnest in April, primarily in regions on the front line, and the attacks are steadily growing more frequent.

At the same time, Russia has endured two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

In total, Russia has hit at least 246 filling stations across Ukraine so far, says Oleksandr Sirenko, an analyst with Ukrainian energy think-tank Nafto Rynok ("Oil Market").

In July alone, the Centre for Information Resilience, an open-source investigation non-profit group, verified 114 Russian strikes on filling stations, compared with 66 the month before.

Given the threat, police have issued special guidance urging motorists to leave petrol stations and, if necessary, to abandon their vehicles whenever air raid alerts sound.

"You can fix your car, but you won't get your life back," says one police force in the Dnipropetrovsk region.

The damage is highly disruptive and puts civilians at considerable risk.

According to Sirenko, initially the attacks were being carried out with smaller, remote-controlled drones, but then Russia started using bigger, more expensive and more destructive Iranian-made Shahed drones.

One Shahed drone is estimated to cost between $20,000 (Â£14,500) and $50,000 (Â£36,000).

"One petrol station took five Shahed hits," Sirenko tells the BBC. "These Shaheds cost more than the petrol station."

News.title: Father's house rammed before son died in A66 crash
News.content:
A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.

Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.

Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.

The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.

There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

News.title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
News.content:
Smokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found.

The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10.

They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine.

And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine, external, which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed.

News.title: Young care leavers dying early a 'national tragedy'
News.content:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today, report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

News.title: Libyan cleared after Lockerbie bombing trial dies aged 70
News.content:
Fhimah worked for the carrier in Malta before the bombing of Pan Am 103.

The charges against Fhimah and Megrahi were first announced by Scotland and the United States in 1991.

Years of sanctions imposed on Libya by the United Nations led to the two men being handed over to stand trial at a Scottish court sitting in the Netherlands.

In 2001, three judges convicted Megrahi of mass murder and jailed him for life, but found Fhimah not guilty.

Megrahi died from cancer in 2012, after being freed on compassionate grounds by the Scottish government.

Fhimah always denied any involvement and was welcomed home to Libya by the country's late dictator Colonel Muammar Gaddafi.

In 2022, the FBI revealed that he had been implicated in the case again, through an alleged confession made by another Libyan who is facing trial in the United States.

Abu Agila Mohammad Masud Kheir Al-Marimi is said to have told a Libyan police officer that he took part in a plot to bomb the plane along with Fhimah and Megrahi, when all three were members of the Libyan intelligence service.

Al-Marimi has denied making the bomb that brought down the jumbo jet and claims the confession is false and was made under duress.

The contents of Al-Marimi's alleged confession and other new evidence which has emerged from Libya has led to speculation that Fhimah could have faced a second trial over the attack on the airliner.

The indictment against Fhimah announced by the US Government in 1991 is still outstanding.

Under the Double Jeopardy (Scotland) Act 2011, external, a suspect can be tried over the same crime a second time, if there is new evidence - which was not available during the original trial - that substantially strengthens the case against them.

The BBC understands Scottish and US prosecutors would have looked at taking fresh action against Fhimah, if Al-Marimi was convicted by the court in Washington.

But pursuing a prosecution in Scotland or the US would have been legally challenging and politically sensitive, given his acquittal by the Scottish court in 2001.

Al Marimi is now due to stand trial in Washington in January, after a federal court judge agreed to postpone the case for a third time.

The delay, requested by the defence, followed the emergence of "newly discovered" evidence on the case.

The postponement was not connected to Fhimah's reported death.

News.title: 'I'm still paying a mortgage for a home destroyed by a fire'
News.content:
Sarah Williams vividly remembers watching her home burn down on the news. On 26 August 2024, she was on holiday when a neighbour texted her to say the Spectrum Building in east London was on fire.

But two years on from the blaze in Dagenham, which left more than 80 people homeless, residents including Williams say they are still "in limbo".

The leaseholder said: "We're still just stuck waiting for other people to make decisions about our future."

She added that in a year's time, the money they were given through insurance to pay for alternative accommodation will run out, and she is still paying her mortgage for a home that does not exist.

At the time of the blaze, from which at least 20 people were rescued, work was under way to remove dangerous cladding. An investigation found the scaffolding around the building at the time had caused the fire to spread, although the exact cause of the blaze is unknown.

The government had provided almost Â£6m through its Building Safety fund to remediate the building - administered by the Greater London Authority (GLA) â with a clause stating that if the work was not completed, the money would have to be repaid.

The Spectrum Building was demolished in December 2024 after surveyor reports deemed it unsafe.

The building's freeholder, Arinium Ltd, has since gone into administration, leaving the administrators, FRP, in control of the company's assets, including the insurance proceeds.

The government says, external the GLA has told the building's administrators that the GLA may be owed money as part of the insolvency process.

The government says this is a standard procedural step and would not affect the money residents are owed, as the GLA would only receive any funds left after residents had been fully compensated.

The GLA said that, as is standard practice in insolvency law, it had informed the administrators of the government's interest as a potential creditor.

News.title: Calls for GPS monitoring of domestic abuse suspects after murder
News.content:
The campaign has been started by Lynne Mackenzie, herself a domestic abuse survivor, who lives a few miles from the isolated cottage where Stacy was killed in July.

Stacy's husband Jim Mair, 43, whose body was found beside her, had been charged with assaulting her but had reportedly been granted bail, external on condition that he did not approach her.

While Mackenzie did not know Stacy personally, she said she was shocked at her murder which happened just six days after the death of another domestic abuse victim, Vikki Soloman, in Edinburgh.

She told BBC Scotland News the killings led her to question whether enough was being done to protect women in Stacy's situation.

"Every time driving in and out of the village I was aware of the police at the end of the road," she said.

"And it really got me thinking what could we have done? What could have been put in place beforehand? What else do we need?"

She has been in contact with Stacy's family who have agreed for her name to be associated with the campaign.

News.title: 'We just want to get home' - dozens stranded in Tunisia after cancelled Belfast flight
News.content:
Dozens of people from Northern Ireland have been left stranded in Tunisia after their EasyJet flight home was cancelled, with the airline telling them it had no other flights available for another 10 days.

One man told BBC News NI he has spent Â£4,000 on travel home for his family-of-five, while another woman, Georgina Doherty, said she and her six children were trying to get home after the death of her mother-in-law.

Others described running out of medication for health issues, while EasyJet were also criticised over a lack of support and communication.

EasyJet has said it is operating an additional direct flight to Belfast on Tuesday night, and that it was "very sorry" for the inconvenience.

BBC News NI understands more than 100 people were booked onto the cancelled flight that was due to leave Enfidha-Hamamet Airport for Belfast International three days ago.

Stuart McCartney, from Dromore, County Down, said he had spent thousands on accommodation and flights to get his family home via a flight to Brussels.

"I'm willing to pay Â£4,000 to get us home, if needs be, and then battle for reimbursement if I have to after that," he said.

"But we shouldn't have to pay. My holiday was a fraction of what I'm paying to get home right now."

McCartney said EasyJet provided two nights of accommodation but then told the family to find alternative accommodation for the rest of the delay.

He said his mother Katherine, who accompanied his wife and children on the trip, relies on heart medication and they have had to keep a close eye on her remaining supply as the delay continued.

An EasyJet spokesperson said that the company "have been doing everything we can to support Mr McCartney, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred".

Georgina Doherty, who is originally from Londonderry but now lives in County Donegal, told BBC News NI the last few days have been an "absolute nightmare" for her family.

Her husband returned home a day before they were due to fly back due to his mother taking ill. She has since died, with Doherty and her six children stranded in Tunisia.

News.title: Inspectors to assess police after Henry Nowak murder
News.content:
An inspection into how a police force responds to violent incidents has been launched in the wake of Henry Nowak's murder.

The 18-year-old student was stabbed in Southampton by Vickrum Digwa, who lied to police and insisted he had been the victim of a racist attack.

Hampshire Police officers initially arrested Nowak and placed him in handcuffs as he lay dying.

His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Service (HMICFRS) will assess the force's processes, training and how officers are supported to make sound and impartial judgements.

The inspection was requested by Hampshire Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones, who said the public "must have confidence" in the force.

"This inspection will provide an independent assessment of the force's training, processes and culture, including the handling of allegations of racially aggravated assault," she said.

"Henry's family deserve answers, and the public deserve reassurance that their police service is equipped to recognise victims and provide the highest standard of care when it matters most."

News.title: Man dies in crash after police pursuit
News.content:
A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.

Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.

A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's 19-year-old male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics.

The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.

Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.

A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said.

Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.

It later reopened.

The draw for the Carabao Cup third round takes place this week as more teams from the Premier League, including current cup winners Manchester City, enter the competition and learn who they will face.

Most top-flight clubs, such as Chelsea and Tottenham, entered the tournament in the second round with those who are competing in European competitions this season now involved as well.

Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United are among those to enter at this stage.

Their participation also means that the third round will be played across two midweeks in order for the teams involved in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League to juggle their match schedules.

Here’s everything you need to know about the draw:

When is the Carabao Cup third round draw?

The draw for the Carabao Cup third round will take place on Wednesday 26 August. It will follow the conclusion of the second round tie between Preston and Everton which kicks off at 8pm BST, meaning the draw could start at around 10.15pm BST.

How will the draw work?

Pre-draw

Before the main draw, there is a pre-draw to decide if the eight Champions League and Europa League clubs will be at home or away. This part is before Preston North End’s Round Two tie against Everton on Sky Sports.

Main draw

The main draw will take place following the conclusion of Round Two tie, the first eight ties will involve those Champions League and Europa League clubs. Their home or away position will have already having been decided. They will then be drawn against a team in a separate bowl with the remaining teams in the competition – so cannot meet one another at this stage.

Following the conclusion of those eight ties being drawn, the final eight ties will be drawn as normal.

From Round Three onwards, there is no longer a divide between the Northern and Southern sections.

How can I watch the Carabao Cup draw?

The Carabao Cup third-round draw will be shown live on Sky Sports Main Event and Sky Sports Football following the conclusion of Preston v Everton.

Sky Sports subscribers will also be able to watch the draw live online via the Sky Go app.

Which teams are involved?

32 teams are involved in the draw including 23 winners of second round ties and nine additional Premier League clubs who are also competing in European competitions this season.

Those teams in Europe and entering the competition for the first time this season are: Arsenal, Aston Villa, Bournemouth, Brighton & Hove Albion, Crystal Palace, Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and Sunderland.

Of those, Brighton can be in Europe through the Conference League, but that competition does not begin until October, so it does not affect the Round Three schedule.

Carabao Cup draw ball numbers

The ball numbers will be confirmed on this morning ahead of the draw.

When will the Carabao Cup third round be played?

The third round of the Carabao Cup is scheduled to take place across consecutive weeks, starting on 7 September and 14 September. The ties will be played midweek as single-leg fixtures with the winners progressing to the fourth round.

Alvarez kicks off a last week of big transfer sagas

Liverpool’s long-winded pursuit of Paris Saint-Germain’s Bradley Barcola has received its latest boost after more positive talks were held with the club over a transfer, with PSG insiders now expecting the winger to leave the club this summer. Across the city, Manchester United target Alejandro Balde reportedly wants to leave Barcelona with the Premier League club exploring a loan move for the left-back. Attention has now fully turned to bolstering that position after completing their £148m midfield rebuild with the signing of Carlos Baleba.

Ollie Watkins and Emi Martinez were also absent from Aston Villa’s matchday squad amid rumours that both players could be preparing for imminent exits with Watkins’ in particular looking very close to a move to Saudi Arabian side Al-Hilal.

Iran says the Strait of Hormuz remains closed despite Tehran agreeing a temporary transit route through the key waterway with Oman.

“We agreed with Oman that the entry route to the Strait of Hormuz will be through our territorial waters, and part of the exit route will also be through our territorial waters,” deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said.

Gatwick airport has revealed half-year profits fell by nearly a fifth as fewer passengers passed through its terminals due to the Iran war hit to international travel.

The West Sussex airport reported pre-tax profits of £136.5 million for the six months to June 30, down 18% from £166.2 million a year ago.

It said 19.1 million passengers travelled through the airport’s two terminals over the first half, down 4.7% compared with a year earlier.

Long-haul passengers suffered the steepest decline, down 9.2% due to the Middle East conflict, while short-haul passengers fell 3.9%.

The group said passenger demand was impacted by concerns over jet fuel supplies amid the war, but said there had been no shortages so far.

Travellers are also booking closer to departure because of uncertainty caused by the conflict, it added.

The results come after a Court of Appeal ruling at the start of August paved the way for development of Gatwick’s second runway.

The £2.2 billion expansion, approved by Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander in September, will see the airport move its emergency runway 12 metres north to accommodate around 100,000 more flights a year.

Pierre Hugues-Schmit, chief executive of London Gatwick, said: “Despite a challenging geopolitical and economic backdrop, London Gatwick has continued to perform well.”

“We are also excited about our longer-term growth opportunities and with the legal process for the Northern Runway Programme now complete, we can turn our focus from planning to detailed design work and delivery,” he added.
