Will Mellor is proud of his working-class roots.

But the Broadchurch actor, who was brought up on a Stockport council estate, is all-too-aware that growing up in less-affluent areas like he did can have long-term effects on health and life expectancy – and he’s grateful that he’s been successful enough to move out to the countryside to bring up his two children.

He lived in London during the early years of his career, and says: “It was very busy, and quite polluted.

“So as soon as my kids were born, I decided to move a bit further out to the country, just so they could have more of a healthy life, be a bit more free. It’s better for mental health, as well to be able to go out on bike rides and walks and go to a green park.

“I’m very fortunate to be in that situation – but it doesn’t mean I can’t have a voice in this sector and say ‘Listen, I’m one of the lucky ones’.”

open image in gallery Where you live affects how long your life might be: Will Mellor (Radski Photography/PA)

Mellor is lending his voice to the new Shelf Life campaign led by the coalition Health Equals, which has analysed national data to reveal a substantial life expectancy gap across the UK, with people from some areas expected to live up to 18 years less than others because they don’t have access to health basics such as decent homes, secure jobs and enough money to make ends meet.

“My childhood postcode in Stockport holds an 80-year-average life expectancy, eight years lower than the highest in the country, which is 88 in places like Marylebone and Berkhamsted,” says Mellor.

“Some people haven’t got the choice of where they live because of financial restraints – but where you live shouldn’t be detrimental to your health.

“We need the government to look at these areas and make their living healthier and easier. Everybody should at least be given a chance at a long and healthy life.”

The 50-year-old now lives in leafy Buckinghamshire with his wife Michelle and their two children Jayden, 22, and Renee, 18. But many of his wider family still live around the area where he grew up, and he says: “I lived on a working-class council estate, and I’m very proud of coming from there, but another reason I’m involved in this is because there’s a lot of my family – uncles, aunties, cousins, sisters – who live around the area.

“Those areas are the ones that come high on the list for quite a lot less life expectancy, because of polluted air or damp conditions or healthy food that’s not available to them.”

open image in gallery Will Mellor with dance pro partner Nancy Xu on Strictly (Alamy/PA)

Mellor, who has also appeared in popular shows including Coronation Street, Hollyoaks, Casualty, and Two Pints Of Lager And A Packet Of Crisps, as well as making it to the semi-finals of Strictly Come Dancing in 2022, stresses that “everybody should have a chance to live a healthy life, no matter where you live”.

He points out that he and his family try to eat as healthily as they can, largely because his wife is a “very good cook” and the couple brought the children up helping them to cook, and avoiding sugary drinks and snacks as much as possible.

“It’s not that we’re being tight as parents,” he insists, “But we’re trying to let them know there’s a cost to this. If you drink a can of whatever soda or anything with sugar in it, a) it’s not great for your health, or b) for your teeth.

“It doesn’t matter how much money you’ve got, education and bringing your kids up in that way, that’s free. You’ve got to know what you’re putting in your body – there are ways you can help yourself by looking at better ways to eat.”

As for exercise, Mellor says he’s always on the go.

“I’ve got ADHD, so I don’t stop – I exercise when I’m not supposed to be,” he says cheerily.

“Sitting still was a problem, that’s why I didn’t do very well at school. But I’m a performer, I’m an actor, I’m a creative, and that’s what my brain is. I work out quite a lot.”

He says he goes for walks and runs, and works out at home.

“If I haven’t done something and I go to bed at the end of the day, I ask myself ‘What did you do today? What did you do with yourself that was positive?’”

He says he likes to have a drink, pointing out: “I’m a normal person – it’s not like I don’t eat takeaways or I don’t go out for dinner or I don’t have a beer every now and then. That’s not the case.

“What I try to do is balance it with exercise and drinking lots of water. What you can’t do is burn the candle at both ends.”

open image in gallery Mellor is publishing his autobiography in November (Alamy/PA)

The actor, whose autobiography, Where There’s A Will, is published on November 5, is very candid about his past mental health struggles, explaining that he became depressed after his sister Joanne, who had mental and physical disabilities, died suddenly in 2012 at the age of just 44.

“I struggled in silence for quite a long time with depression after my sister passed away,” he says.

“The reason I didn’t reach out is because I’ve been in quite a lucky situation through my career and been quite successful, and I thought ‘Who do I speak to?’”

He continues: “Mental health doesn’t discriminate how much money you’ve got in the bank, how successful you are, or where you live.”

He says time and the love and support of his family got him through those dark days.

“My wife stuck by me,” he says. “I wasn’t a great person to be around. I turned to alcohol and gambling and other forms of looking for a way to find some sort of colour in my life. But it just made me worse.

open image in gallery Will Mellor with his family in 2023 (Ian West/PA)

“And the hardest thing for me was I loved my family. I’m an energetic, positive person, and I just couldn’t find positivity at that time in my life.”

He says his mental health struggles were more than 10 years ago when he was filming Broadchurch and his children were young.

“They don’t even remember it, but I do,” he says. “And I remember not being present enough for my wife and kids for a good few months. I didn’t want to get out of bed.

“Thankfully, I’m better now. And you probably wouldn’t have known if you’d have seen me, because I was very good at masking it.

“I’m a big advocate of looking after your mental health. Talking is key. I just didn’t do that, and I learned from my own mistakes.

“It’s OK not to be OK.”

Will Mellor is supporting the Health Equals Shelf Life campaign highlighting the dramatic life expectancy gap in the UK. Check the life expectancy in your postcode on the Health Equals website.

News.title: AI in everyday devices: tokenised intelligence at the edge
News.content:
MIPS is a Business Reporter client

Artificial intelligence is reshaping computing by moving intelligence from centralised cloud environments directly into everyday devices. Advances in edge AI, custom silicon and embedded computing are enabling a new generation of intelligent systems that are distributed, context-aware and increasingly autonomous.

At the heart of this transformation are AI agents operating locally within devices and tokens serving as the fundamental units of AI computation and communication. Together, these technologies are redefining how devices process information, interact with users and respond to the physical world, laying the foundation for a future where embedded AI becomes as ubiquitous as operating systems are today.

Agents and tokens are coming to a device near you

For decades, computing has been defined by a simple model: applications run on operating systems, data is processed in centralised clouds or relatively fixed-function endpoints and intelligence is delivered as a service. That model is now shifting, thanks to rapid advances in artificial intelligence, edge computing and heterogeneous silicon, all of which are driving a new paradigm where intelligence is distributed, contextual and increasingly autonomous.

At the centre of this shift are two concepts that will define the next generation of computing: agents and tokens.

Agents are rapidly evolving from cloud-based assistants into embedded, always-on systems that live directly inside devices. Tokens are becoming the new currency of computation, flowing not just through data centres but across endpoints, sensors and embedded systems.

Together, agents and tokens are transforming how devices operate, communicate and interact with the physical world. In the coming decade, they will become as common in edge devices as operating systems and microcontrollers are today.

From cloud-centric AI to edge-native intelligence

Today’s AI systems largely depend on centralised inference, where massive models are hosted in hyperscale data centres. But as applications expand into robotics, autonomous systems, industrial automation and consumer devices, this approach is encountering fundamental limitations: latency, bandwidth constraints, privacy concerns and energy inefficiency.

The next phase of AI demands intelligence at the edge, where decisions are made locally, in real time and in direct response to physical environments.

This is where agents come in. Instead of relying on constant cloud connectivity, edge-native agents can interpret sensor data, maintain local context and take immediate action. Whether it’s a robotic arm adjusting to a changing production line, a smart appliance optimising energy usage or an autonomous drone navigating unpredictable conditions, agents are becoming the software layer that bridges gap between perception and action.

But to enable this shift, devices need more than software innovation. They require a fundamentally new compute architecture.

Tokens: the new currency of edge computation

In large language models and modern AI systems, tokens represent discrete units of meaning, words, data points or symbolic elements processed during inference. As AI moves to the edge, tokens are no longer just abstract inputs to a model; they become a measure of real-time computational workload distributed across constrained devices.

In this new environment, every interaction including sensor readings, user inputs and environmental changes can be broken into tokenised streams that must be processed efficiently and securely. That means future edge devices must be capable of handling continuous token flows with deterministic performance, ultra-low latency and strict power budgets.

Unfortunately, this shift places unprecedented demands on today’s silicon architecture.

Why traditional architectures are not enough

Legacy processor architectures were not designed for continuous AI inference at the edge. General-purpose CPUs struggle with power efficiency at scale, while GPUs and accelerators are often too power-hungry or too centralised for embedded environments.

What’s emerging instead is a need for purpose-built, scalable compute platforms that can support heterogeneous workloads: real-time control, signal processing and AI inference all within the same system.

This is where the MIPS by GF’s vision becomes critical.

MIPS: enabling the physical AI era

As a modern, RISC-V-native compute IP provider, MIPS is focused on enabling what it calls the “Physical AI” era, where intelligence is embedded directly into machines that sense, think, act and communicate in the real time.

In this new paradigm, MIPS is not simply providing processor cores. It is delivering a foundation for deterministic, safety-critical and edge-optimised computing designed specifically for agent-driven systems.

Through its RISC-V-based architecture and scalable processor IP, MIPS enables developers to build systems where agents can operate reliably at the edge, managing tokenised AI workloads without dependency on centralised compute.

This is particularly important for applications such as robotics, autonomous machines, industrial automation and intelligent infrastructure, where timing, reliability and safety are non-negotiable.

Working in alignment with the broader semiconductor ecosystem, including advanced manufacturing capabilities from GlobalFoundries, MIPS is helping bridge the gap between software-defined intelligence and physically grounded systems.

Agents in everyday devices

As agent-based computing matures, its reach will extend far beyond enterprise or industrial systems. Everyday devices, from home appliances to personal electronics to connected vehicles, will increasingly behave as autonomous agents.

A thermostat will not just respond to temperature changes but anticipate occupancy patterns. A camera will not just capture images but interpret context and trigger actions. A wearable will not just track health metrics but proactively co-ordinate with other systems to optimise outcomes in real time.

In each case, agents will rely on continuous token processing to interpret the world, reason about state, and act accordingly.

The infrastructure challenge

To support this shift, the industry must solve three fundamental challenges:

Deterministic performance at the edge: ensuring real-time response under strict latency constraints

Energy efficiency at scale: enabling continuous AI inference without draining power budgets or resources

Security and reliability: maintaining trust in systems that operate autonomously in physical environments

MIPS’ approach addresses these challenges by focusing on modular, scalable RISC-V compute IP designed specifically for embedded AI workloads. This enables system designers to tailor compute architectures to specific agent behaviours and token processing requirements.

The future: distributed intelligence everywhere

The transition to agent-driven, tokenised computing is already underway. We are entering a world where intelligence is no longer centralised in the cloud but instead distributed across billions of devices. The question for developers, system architects and silicon designers is no longer if this shift will happen, but how fast they can adapt.

MIPS is helping lead this transformation by delivering the foundational compute IP required for the Physical AI era.

News.title: China clamped down on exotic wildlife farms – now they’ve moved to Southeast Asia
News.content:
We hear the bamboo rats before we see them. At the bottom of almost 200 concrete containers are hundreds of chunky rodents – some squealing as they scurry in circles, others loudly gnawing corn, sugar cane and bamboo with their sharp protruding teeth.

“They’re very easy to keep,” says Suriyan Wanpakwaen, as he peers into one of the pits at the DIY breeding facility beside his home in Nakhon Ratchasima, a province roughly 150 miles northeast of Bangkok. “My favourite thing is how clean they are, there are no bad smells.”

For almost seven years, Mr Suriyan has been farming bamboo rats – and now, the business is booming. A single rodent can sell for as much as 4,000 baht (roughly £90), and there’s so much demand that Mr Suriyan and his wife can’t keep up.

They’re not the only ones cashing in. Since the coronavirus pandemic, backyard wildlife farms like this have proliferated across Southeast Asia.

While this industry long existed in the region, the mounting new additions are filling a vacuum created when, in the wake of Covid-19, China closed thousands of similar farms over bio-security concerns.

“There was a coordinated effort to set up these wildlife farms, led by people who could consolidate stock and move that stock illegally across multiple international borders,” he added.

News.title: Ten years after Brazil’s Zika epidemic, its children are still paying the price
News.content:
In the heated pool, ten-year-old Stephany Vitória Silva Costa is weightless. The water soothes her convulsing muscles, providing brief respite from constant pain, and she coos with delight, igniting smiles among everyone in the room.

Stephany is a “Zika baby”; one of more than 3,080 children born with Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS) following a devastating outbreak of the mosquito borne virus that swept Brazil in 2015-16. At least 444 of those children have died, mainly from respiratory and infectious diseases.

Like most of the surviving children from the cohort, she has suffered from an array of symptoms including microcephaly, severe cognitive and motor impairment, vision and hearing loss and seizures – which can occur up to ten times a day.

But a decade after the outbreak, a second wave of complications are emerging in children like Stephany.

Stephany’s exposed back, showing the pronounced 120-degree curvature caused by rapid, severe scoliosis Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

As her therapist gently turns her in the pool, a pronounced bulge shows through the back of her pink and blue swim top. Over the last two years, her growing spine has been pulled 120-degrees into an S-shaped curve that is now crushing her lungs.

While many of the children born with microcephaly after the outbreak died in early infancy, a much-loved group including Stephany lived on. Now, however, mortality rates are again climbing as the children near adolescence.

An x-ray image showing a severe s-shaped spinal deformity threatening to compress a young patient’s lungs Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“It weighs heavily on my heart. After so many years of following these children, it is inevitable to form bonds – not only with them, but with their families,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti, one of just 11 paediatric neurologists in the state.

“Every loss affects me deeply. It is very hard to say goodbye to them”.

At the Altino Ventura Foundation’s (FAV) hydrotherapy centre, steam clings to murals depicting ocean scenes – a smiling pink octopus swims around a silver painted shipwreck.

As Stephany coos, another girl in a brown swimsuit and rainbow coloured shorts smiles as her mother fills a cup with water and pours it over her black curls.

Originally an ophthalmology institute, FAV expanded into neuro-rehabilitation as the Zika crisis unfolded. It provides free therapy to children with CZS twice a week, with treatment plans reassessed every six months.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation and 84 are currently being treated. Its clinicians are tracking the cohort's long-term development.

Physiotherapist Gustav Wagner assists a young patient in the hydrotherapy pool Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

None of the Zika children present can walk or hold themselves up, and the majority have already had at least one major surgery.

Nevertheless, Gustav Wagner, a physiotherapist, says installing the hydrotherapy pool – which increases blood flow and loosens muscles – was a major breakthrough.

The children can’t express pain verbally. Mr Wagner and his team instead use a visual scale from one to ten, based on reading their posture and expressions. The mothers, above all, learn to spot the smallest changes and the pool, they say, makes a huge difference.

“It’s a very peculiar disease,” says Amanda Rodrigues, a physiotherapist. “We have to learn with them how to get better – we have never treated something like this before”.

A silent invasion

First discovered in 1947 in Uganda’s Zika forest, the Zika virus is thought to have quietly reached Brazil in 2014.

Experts attribute its arrival to increased air travel; either carried by visitors landing for the 2014 FIFA World Cup or brought from active outbreaks in the South Pacific islands.

Either way, the virus spread unnoticed and unchecked in Brazil for over a year.

Most Zika infections are asymptomatic or easily mistaken for dengue, both cause a similar red rash and flu-like symptoms.

The alarm was finally raised in August 2015 when neuropaediatrician Dr Vanessa van der Linden identified an unprecedented surge in infants born with microcephaly across Pernambuco state.

“It was very chaotic at the beginning,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti. She added that doctors frantically coordinated emergency responses over WhatsApp as the crisis unfolded.

“The physical toll on the children was devastating,” she said.

Paediatric neurologist Dr Milena Cavalcanti Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Infections early in pregnancy inflicted the worst damage. And in one of the side rooms of the hydrotherapy centre, it's evident that the disabilities are profound.

Five children sit motionless in their wheelchairs with blankets pulled up to their necks. One of them, Emily Sophia dos Santos Luna, weighed just six kilograms at age two before being given a feeding tube to enable her to survive.

The children are unable to swallow, causing mucus to pool in the back of their throats. To prevent choking, their wheelchairs are permanently tilted at a 45 degree angle.

Maria José da Silva wheels her granddaughter to specialist transport Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“In the beginning, we thought they would discover a treatment,” says Emily’s grandmother, Maria José da Silva, 43. “But now we understand she will always be this way”.

She added: “It’s a very difficult life, but God gave us the power to keep going. I will take care of her until the day God wants”.

In the therapeutic gym, a large room filled with foam mats, standing frames and slings hung from the ceiling, Allana Kauane perches on a large silver balance ball.

She wears a green skirt, shin-high pink socks, and a white T-shirt that has “be happy” printed in shimmery lettering.

Ms Rodrigues, her physiotherapist, supports her torso and bounces her gently to build core strength. With every movement, she patiently lifts Allana’s head back up as it falls onto her chest.

Thailene Maria uses a bright gold pompom to draw her daughter’s focus Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Thailene Maria, the child’s 28-year-old mother, waves a bright gold pompom in front of her eyes in an effort to draw her focus.

Down the corridor in a consultation room, Dr Cavalcanti examines another patient.

It’s a girl who has not had a seizure in six years, but her last one lasted thirty minutes – six times the length that defines a medical emergency in Brazil.

Manuelle does not like to be touched, her grandmother says. She used to bite herself, now she pulls at her own hair instead.

As Dr Cavalcanti taps gently at her knee with a reflex hammer, the girl tenses and struggles to lie flat. Fine dark hair has started to grow along the girl’s shins – a side effect, says Dr Cavalcanti, of the anticonvulsant medication she relies on to control her seizures.

It is one of several changes the clinic still cannot fully explain. Many patients entered puberty years earlier than expected, one as young as three. Most are treated with hormone-blocking injections.

Dr Cavalcanti gently tests the reflexes of a young patient’s knee Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“We don’t know,” says Dr Cavalcanti, when asked about the cause. “We are just following the cases”.

On the ground floor, past the therapy rooms, sits the Capela Santissima Trinidade, a small wood-pannelled chapel. Inside, there are rows of pews, and in the centre is a large stained glass window.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Dr Epitácio Rolim, the top orthopaedic surgeon in the state, has tracked a cohort of 152 children since the outbreak.

By age 10, 98 per cent developed orthopaedic deformities – 70 per cent suffer hip deformities, and 64 per cent from spinal curvature.

Previously, the public health system did not offer corrective surgeries or have a structured waiting list.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation Credit : Lucas Landau

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco state, told The Telegraph: “We know we have a lot to do yet. The needs are giant and the funds are not”.

The root problem is neurological, says Dr Rolim. Damaged brain pathways create severe muscle imbalances around major joints. Unable to reposition themselves, the children’s relentless muscle tightness pulls their hips out of their socket and twists their spines.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

“I am not talking about surgery to make most of these children walk,” says Dr Rolim. “The realistic goal is quality of life… hope does not mean promising a cure that we do not have… it means living with as little pain as possible”.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Only five to seven per cent of pregnant women exposed to Zika had babies with visible symptoms like microcephaly. For the rest, timing of the infection in pregnancy determined how destructive the virus was.

“The children you saw with microcephaly were at the extreme end of the spectrum,” says Dr Ernesto Marques, a senior researcher at Fiocruz in Recife. “As the others become teens, developmental delays are showing up more clearly”.

Dr Patricia Garcez, a neuroscientist at King’s College London who helped establish the link between Zika and brain defects in 2016, said that many of the “milder” CZS cases are now displaying severe autism and neurodevelopmental delay, or motor deficits caused by prenatal Zika exposure without severe microcephaly.

The perfect breeding ground

The night we arrive in Recife, known as the “Brazilian Venice”, heavy rains transform the city’s roads into rivers. Gesturing to the rising water outside, our taxi driver chuckles: “Here we say: When someone sneezes, the whole city floods”.

Centuries ago, the city was a low-lying landscape of tidal sandbanks, estuaries and mangroves. When Dutch colonisers arrived in the 1600s, they engineered canals, bridges and dikes to prevent flooding and make the swamplands habitable.

It is this geography that made Recife, the capital of Pernambuco, the epicentre of the 2015-16 Zika outbreak, its pools of still water proving the perfect breeding ground for mosquitoes.

The state recorded around 742 confirmed CZS cases – 24 per cent of cases nationwide, and 39 per cent of cases in the northeast.

In Recife’s hillside favelas – densely populated, self-built communities largely lacking basic public services – residents were forced to store tap water in open buckets and barrels due to intermittent water flow making the mosquito problem worse.

Joane da Silva Sena pushes her son Heytor up a steep hill to their home in Favela do Monte Credit : Lucas Landau

Halfway up a steep hill in Favela do Monte, Joane da Silva Sena lives in deep poverty, caring alone for her 10-year-son, Heytor, who was born with microcephaly in November 2015.

Ms Sena, 36, a thin, weary-looking woman with a kind face, is entirely on her own.

The father abandoned them at birth, and the neighbours refuse to even watch Heytor while she goes to the shop, instead watching her struggle up the hill from their homes.

Ms Sena rarely receives any help with her son Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“My family doesn’t help me, nobody cares,” she says. “People are afraid of Heytor, they say he’s ‘special’.”

Inside the house, only secured with metal bars on gaping door and window frames, Ms Sena frequently skips meals so Heytor can eat. There’s a shadow on the wall of the pink-painted kitchen where the fridge should be. She had to throw it out because it kept giving her electric shocks and was too expensive to repair.

Heytor’s specialised wheelchair broke months ago, leaving him only with an ill-fitting wicker chair that he constantly slumps on.

Ms Sena lifts her son roughly 10 times a day Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Ms Sena lifts his 54 kg frame roughly 10 times a day between the chair and the bed to soothe him when he gets agitated. She also carries him up the steep hill twice a week to reach physiotherapy classes.

“I will not abandon him,” Ms Sena says through tears. “I just ask God for health, because if I get sick, no one will look after him”.

In August 2025, Brazil’s Congress passed a bill – first floated in 2015 – to compensate the families of children born with microcephaly and other disabilities caused by Zika.

The package includes a one-off payment of 50,000 BRL (£7,150), and a tax-free monthly support payment of 8,150 BRL (£1,165), five times the previous allowance.

But despite the national law, Ms Sena receives very little support.

The hospital Heytor was born in did not provide official documentation linking Heytor’s condition to Zika, even though multiple experts say that it is the cause.

Ms Sena said she dreams about having access to the funds, adding that she would love to “buy a beautiful armchair that will be so comfortable for him”.

Ms Sena prays for her own robust health so that her son is not without a carer Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

After The Telegraph raised her case with the Pernambuco Health Department, state officials launched an investigation into Heytor’s birth records and admitted him to the hospital for a complete evaluation.

They also dropped off medication and nappies at the house and have arranged for a vehicle to transport them to therapy classes.

Acknowledging that Ms Sena’s struggles span housing, transportation, social support and caregiver mental health, the state told The Telegraph it would assemble a multi-agency task force to assist her.

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

It took a decade of campaigning for these women – a movement known as the Mothers of Angels – to finally secure the social security breakthrough last year.

They proved that the state failed families twice over: by not containing the virus, and by under-compensating the children for years.

A new generation at risk

It remains unclear whether Brazil is vulnerable to another Zika outbreak.

In 2016, amid the original epidemic, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

A few months later, cases began to drop and today the population is thought to be protected by herd immunity.

However, that immunity is unlikely to last forever.

A study in Salvador, the capital of nearby Bahia state, found antibody protection dropped from 59 per cent to under 39 per cent within two years of the first outbreak.

Dr Marques estimates Brazil could see another outbreak resulting in children born with CZS within 15 to 20 years.

Originally focused on eye care, the Altino Ventura Foundation expanded its operations during the 2015 outbreak Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A new generation has grown up without having been exposed to the virus, creating a growing population vulnerable to infection, he says.

The root cause of poor water infrastructure and mosquito infestation also hasn’t been resolved.

“Almost everybody born after 2016 has not been exposed to Zika at all... they are naive, and that piles up with the older people who did not get infected,” he told The Telegraph.

“Once the population vulnerable to Zika reaches a critical threshold, the risk of another outbreak grows”.

The research that could prepare Brazil for that eventuality has stalled.

There is still no approved Zika vaccine or antibody treatment. The most advanced candidate has only just completed early-stage safety trials, and experts say a larger trial is nearly impossible without an active outbreak to test it.

Basic diagnostic tools also have major limitations. Standard antibody tests still cannot reliably distinguish Zika from dengue, and PCR testing – the only definitive testing method – is only effective for around five days at the peak of infections.

For Erika Silva Costa and her ten-year-old daughter Stephany, the child with severe scoliosis, the struggle to secure that necessary care has reached a standstill.

Ms Costa contracted Zika five months into her pregnancy. When doctors recommended that she terminate, she refused.

Erika Silva Costa, Stephany’s mother and full-time caregiver, is also a fierce campaigner Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A former MRI technician, Ms Costa is now a full-time caregiver and a prominent campaigner for Zika children.

“My dedication to her is total, 24 hours a day… my brain is always awake,” she says, adding that she sleeps in the same bed facing Stephany in case she chokes during the night. “I feel like the umbilical cord was never cut”.

Despite the urgent need, Stephany’s position remains perilous.

Her doctors say she needs an operation costing 150,000 BRL (£21,400) on her spine but so far she has been refused coverage by medical insurers. Ms Costa is now mounting a legal battle to fight the decision in court.

“The authorities together with the health services aren’t tackling this properly,” said Dr Rolim.

“It’s so frustrating. The professionals know what needs to be done, but can’t do it because the system doesn’t provide the right conditions”.

With the public health system crippled by long waiting lists and a lack of specialised equipment, families like Ms Costa are waiting in limbo.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

For Erika Silva Costa and her ten-year-old daughter Stephany, the child with severe scoliosis, the struggle to secure that necessary care has reached a standstill.

Ms Costa contracted Zika five months into her pregnancy. When doctors recommended that she terminate, she refused.

Erika Silva Costa, Stephany’s mother and full-time caregiver, is also a fierce campaigner Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A former MRI technician, Ms Costa is now a full-time caregiver and a prominent campaigner for Zika children.

“My dedication to her is total, 24 hours a day… my brain is always awake,” she says, adding that she sleeps in the same bed facing Stephany in case she chokes during the night. “I feel like the umbilical cord was never cut”.

Despite the urgent need, Stephany’s position remains perilous.

Her doctors say she needs an operation costing 150,000 BRL (£21,400) on her spine but so far she has been refused coverage by medical insurers. Ms Costa is now mounting a legal battle to fight the decision in court.

“The authorities together with the health services aren’t tackling this properly,” said Dr Rolim.

“It’s so frustrating. The professionals know what needs to be done, but can’t do it because the system doesn’t provide the right conditions”.

With the public health system crippled by long waiting lists and a lack of specialised equipment, families like Ms Costa are waiting in limbo.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.

News.title: Glasner made to wait for first win as Trafford thwarts Forest
News.content:
Leeds manager Daniel Farke said: “He has the potential to be one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League and that is why Thomas Tuchel has picked him for England.

“I like his natural confidence and aura, he knows that he’s good and he will be outstanding one day.

“He has major chances to be under the spotlight and we are very pleased with him so far.”

Forest manager Oliver Glasner will be pleased to see the back of Leeds.

He was appointed by Forest for the primary reason of winning trophies after successful tenures with Crystal Palace and Eintracht Frankfurt, but this particular avenue is now closed for this season.

Four-time League Cup winners, Forest endured a difficult evening following the pre-match news that they have agreed a £45m deal with Chelsea for striker Liam Delap.

Forest have established a reputation for noisy transfer windows but are determined to focus on quality over quantity this year.

With Delap to undergo a medical on Wednesday, Forest will then focus on signing a new right wing-back before the deadline.

Newcastle’s Jacob Murphy has been discussed though a move is now regarded as unlikely, but there are understood to be other targets under consideration.

Glasner has insisted he does not want Forest to panic, and it remains to be seen whether they do spring into life on the final day.

He said: “I am not a magician or the Messiah and we cannot ignore the reality that Leeds are ahead of us at the moment.

News.title: Palmer and Rogers show promise of star double act for Chelsea
News.content:
“I am very happy for Cole,” Alonso said. “I have really enjoyed seeing him play with the dynamism and the freedom and the responsibility... when Cole feels this way we have a better team and a better Cole.”

Palmer makes it look very easy in this form, capable of switching the direction of play a beat before anyone else spots the opportunity. He and his old Manchester City academy friend Rogers came off before the end, Palmer having demonstrated some discomfort chasing a ball. Asked afterwards how ready he felt, Palmer responded in kind. “Did you not watch the game? I’m only joking, I’m ready... it was a difficult season with injuries and whatnot, but through the summer and since I’ve been back I’ve worked extra hard.”

If there was an attacker to compare with him on the other side it was King, who looks even better. The 19-year-old was way ahead of Arbeloa’s two young Real Madrid imports. García toiled away and took his chance, but César Palacios struggled for any impact in a position tucked in on the left. Oscar Bobb and King gave Fulham some edge but the concern, as ever, will be where Fulham get their goals.

Arbeloa pushed his full-backs high and encouraged Sander Berge to drop deep to get on the ball in the first passing phase. The Norwegian delayed too long in challenging João Pedro for Chelsea’s third – backing off and allowing Palmer to overlap to receive the pass.

Sánchez had not been the only concern for Chelsea. Back in the team, Levi Colwill misjudged a challenge on King in the first half and was relieved that the card was only yellow. Roméo Lavia took a wild swing at Calvin Bassey and was also booked. Moisés Caicedo was not fit to play. Enzo Fernández was on the bench and would come on in the second half to the kind of reception from opposition fans to which he will quickly become familiar.

There was a grin from the Argentine at those who berated him from the home stands when he returned at half-time. Fernández worked hard to transmit a general sense that the abuse did not land, although he will be relieved that the Chelsea fans were supportive. His future still feels very much in play.

It was Palmer’s subtle ball through that gave João Pedro the chance with 32 seconds of the game played. The ball came forward immediately from Lacroix’s firm header from defence. The Frenchman delivered a very accomplished assist for Rogers’s first-half goal. Before that King had equalised. There was an exchange with Timothy Castagne, and King looked up just inside the box and decided to have a swing at it. Sánchez was close enough to grasp the ball and somehow failed to do so.

Sánchez would later push a Castagne shot in the direction of García, who stooped and nodded the ball over the goalkeeper after Palmer had scored Chelsea’s third. This second error was unfortunate, but it is the kind of thing that happens to a goalkeeper as erratic as the one for whom Chelsea’s hierarchy seem to have such patience.

Sports.title: Carlos Baleba is final piece of Man Utd’s midfield jigsaw – now he needs to ‘do a Carrick’ and guide them to the title
Sports.content:
CARLOS BALEBA need look no further than his new manager for the inspiration to be a title winner at Manchester United.

It is 20 years since Michael Carrick joined the Red Devils from Tottenham in an £18.6million deal.



And current boss Carrick’s most consequential signing this summer is another deep-lying midfielder.

Baleba, 22, has arrived from Brighton for an initial £65million — a year since United first enquired about the Cameroonian.



It begs the question why United waited until the final week of the transfer window to sign him.

But their midfield overhaul is now complete — with Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos also arriving at Old Trafford this summer.

Towards the end of last season United also tied down England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo, 21, on a contract until 2031.

No player in Baleba’s position has proved such a game-changer in terms of helping United to fulfil their ambitions since Carrick’s arrival in 2006.

Sir Alex Ferguson needed to strengthen his midfield at the time with United having been unable to win the Premier League title in three successive seasons.

Carrick proved the final piece in the jigsaw as United were crowned champions in his first season.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

And along with Owen Hargreaves who arrived the following summer, Carrick was pivotal in the Red Devils finishing top of the pile in five of Fergie’s final seven seasons in charge — as well as winning the Champions League in 2008 — before his retirement in 2013.

United have made headline signings for their engine room since those two – Marouane Fellaini, Paul Pogba, Fred, Casemiro and Manuel Ugarte among them.

But none have them have been able to help United to their former Premier League heights. Pogba was Baleba’s idol.

But hopefully there will be none of the constant problems Pogba caused in trying to force an exit during his second six-year stint at United.

Baleba’s arrival is perhaps recognition that Santos — signed from Chelsea for £50m — does not offer all of the solutions to the Red Devils’ problem No 6 position,



Santos does not have Baleba’s physicality and United’s need for a specialist defensive midfielder saw them make a fresh enquiry to Real Madrid for Frenchman Aurelien Tchouameni last month.

Baleba commanded a cheaper fee and salary than Tchouameni would have done — and has the benefit of three years of Prem experience.

Director of football Jason Wilcox said: “Carlos’ determination to join Manchester United and his confidence we will achieve our shared ambitions mean he’s the perfect signing.”



Baleba was impressed by United’s vision for his development and was made to feel wanted.

He had briefly spoken with Carrick and been deep in conversation with Matheus Cunha after United’s 3-0 win at Brighton on the final day of last season.

Even though Brighton had just qualified for the Conference League, Baleba had set his sights higher.

He will get Champions League football at United and believes he is an ideal fit having adapted to the Prem’s speed and physicality over the past three season.

Baleba completed United’s rebuild for the new season.



Bruno Fernandes’ future has been a point of discussion for months and was this week crowed United’s first PFA Player of the Year since Wayne Rooney in 2010.

While the Portuguese midfielder has enough individual accolades to fill a skip, he has found team medals harder to come by.

He was won just two trophies in nearly seven years with United — although they have also lost two European finals in that time.

He can no longer complain that the squad is lacking.



United may be unconvincing in defence but they have nine fit senior defenders and Baleba’s arrival gives the squad greater balance.

Fernandes was close to Casemiro, the predecessor in Baleba’s position before his departure in the summer.

While Baleba does not quite have the presence of five-time Champions League winner Casemiro, he is more athletic and dynamic.

Fernandes turns 32 in September and his contract expires next year.



United will almost certainly trigger a one-year extension until 2028 — unless they furnish Fernandes with a new deal before then.

United have targeted 2028 — the 150th anniversary of the club — to end their long wait for a title.

Sealing a 21st United title would not only be the perfect send-off for Fernandes, it would seal his status as a legendary figure at the club.

Even before Saturday’s horror show at Hull — that saw them start the season with a shock 2-0 defeat — this season has felt too soon for United to be crowned champions.



But they should have little trouble in convincing Fernandes to agree to new terms.

He will have some leverage in terms of his salary however — particularly with the return of Marcus Rashford, the club’s highest wage earner despite having made his last start for United in December 2024.

But he is another man who can be inspired by Carrick in his quest for a Prem title.

Sports.title: Chelsea files: Sanchez’s woeful form laid bare after Fulham horror show and ‘frightening’ Cobham talent coming through
Sports.content:
SOME Chelsea fans had had enough of Robert Sanchez even before his performance at Fulham.

Now the calls for the Spaniard to be replaced, by a new top-class signing or by No 2 Mike Penders, are even louder.



Sky Sports pundits Jamie Carragher and Gary Neville agree. They have repeatedly said Chelsea will never win the Premier League with Sanchez in goal and his errors at Craven Cottage, especially for Josh King’s equaliser, were further ammunition.

And the statistics back up what they and many Chelsea supporters have felt for some time.



The current owners have spent more than £1.5billion on players in the last four years – including five goalkeepers.

At one point they had NINE senior stoppers on their books.



Sanchez, signed three years ago from Brighton for £25m, remains their No 1, despite the numbers suggesting he is not among the top PL goalkeepers..

No ‘keeper has made more mistakes leading to shots since the start of the 2024/5 season than the Spaniard’s 15.

And only Brighton’s Bart Verbruggen has been responsible for more gaffes leading to goals in the same period, with nine to Sanchez’s seven.

On Monday night, some Chelsea fans noted King’s equaliser had the lowest xG of any goal scored in the opening round of PL fixtures.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

His poor positioning and his lacklustre attempt to stop the shot were obvious.

But xG is designed to be used to identify long-term trends rather than deliver verdicts on one-off shots.

A better indication of how a ‘keeper is performing long term, in the basic business of stopping the ball going into the net, is the difference between the xG of on-target shots they face and the actual number of goals conceded, excluding own goals.

Among ‘keepers who have made 30 or more appearances since the start of last season, Sanchez’s “goals prevented” figure of 1.8 ranks ninth out of 15.

Three of those to finish above him play for clubs who, unlike Chelsea, qualified for this season’s Champions League.



Manchester United’s Senne Lammens and Manchester City’s Gianluigi Donnarumma were the top two, with Aston Villa’s Emi Martinez in sixth.

The outlier is Raya. The Arsenal ‘keeper has let in more goals than the algorithm says he should have done since the start of last season.

Since 2024/25, Raya is second to Sanchez in mistakes leading to shots. Arsenal’s defenders seem to be better at clearing up their ‘keeper’s messes than Chelsea’s.



Of course there is more to goalkeeping than can be measured by raw data.

Yet Sanchez on Monday night showed other signs of weakness. He rarely looks comfortable playing the ball short with his feet and as Fulham tried a high press, he allowed a backpass to go out for a corner.

Chelsea have insisted all summer they are happy with their goalkeepers.

Whether the Blues were linked yet again to AC Milan’s Mike Maignan, or more recently to Porto’s Diogo Costa, the message remained the same.

Chelsea have made a panic buy of a goalkeeper before and it turned out well for a while.



After error-prone Kepa Arrizabalaga made one too many mistakes, the Blues signed Edouard Mendy in September 2020.

Mendy was in goal when Thomas Tuchel led the club to its second Champions League crown the following May.

But if the current owners and recruitment team stick to their guns, there will be no new goalkeeper arriving before the window closes

In which case, Thursday’s Carabao Cup clash against Luton looks even more like the right time to give Penders a chance to stake his claim.

New manager Xabi Alonso has insisted “the pitch will decide” whether the Belgian or Sanchez is his No 1.



But if Penders did well, it would still be a big call to drop the Spaniard for the visit of former club Brighton on Sunday.

DO THE SIMPLE THINGS WELL

XABI ALONSO’s Chelsea revolution is full steam ahead, and it’s simplicity is what makes it beautiful.

After season upon season of inverted fullbacks, touchline wingers and players out of position, the most noticeable thing about Chelsea’s game vs Fulham was how everyone knew their role and stuck to it.

Fans grew sick of Enzo Maresca‘s floaty positional nonsense at times, and it feels as though those people will be in awe of Alonso’s positional excellence.

In fact, you’d be forgiven for looking at Chelsea’s average position map and confusing it just for their formation.



Below, if you compare it to Ruben Amorim‘s Manchester United side, it shows just how clear the difference is.

His plan to play a 3-4-2-1 system, as he did at Bayer Leverkusen seems clear with the players that Chelsea have signed to play specific roles, such as Morgan Rogers and Marco Palestra.

Although he did still maintain a fairly fluid shape towards the end of the game when the Blues were trying to see the game out and hold onto all three points with five substitutes on the pitch.



It’s quite a staggering difference to when Maresca, Liam Rosenior or Callum MacFarlane were in charge last season, and that clarity upon who goes where might just be the simplicity that Chelsea need to become a serious team once more.

CNG the next best thing!

CHELSEA have taken a fair bit of flak for their decision to rebrand their academy as ‘Cobham Next Gen’.

And that is to be expected – it sounds daft.

Despite that, however, insiders in the world of academy football still rate the Blues ranks incredibly highly.

Even though the club have operated under an academy transfer embargo since March, which runs until after the January window, their talent pool was this week described to SunSport as “frightening”.



After the pain of losing Rio Ngumoha to Liverpool, a review of how the academy was run was undertaken, led by Joe Shields at sporting director level.

Chelsea are now working desperately hard to ensure figures such as the highly rated Reggie Watson, 16, or Reggie Walsh, 17, do not become the next Ngumoha to leave and find first-team success at another top English club.

Walsh has even followed in the footsteps of captain Reece James by joining Wigan on loan as a teenager.



Chelsea’s depth of talent was evident on their pre-season tour of Australia and Asia, where a lot of effort was placed on keeping the youngsters engaged, with day trips out and their family involved too.

Conversations with family are a significant part of Chelsea’s work with younger players, educating them on the pathways available to players and how to navigate them.

Mahdi Nicoll-Jazuli, Chelsea’s Sydney-born midfielder, even had his mum and brother on the trip Down Under with Chelsea.

So while the name might sound silly, the talent on display is real.

Sports.title: LASK 5 Celtic 1 (Agg: 5-4) – embarrassing Hoops crash out of Champions League in extraordinary exit
Sports.content:
HIS first Champions League experience as Celtic manager was extraordinary and absolutely shocking.

So too was his LASK.



Martin O’Neill couldn’t believe his eyes in an infamous defeat to Juventus 25 years ago which left him utterly disgusted.

But it was nothing to what he witnessed here in Austria last night in one of the most incredible European exists the game has ever seen.



Celtic were 4-0 up in this tie with 21 minutes the clock in this second-leg.

Callum McGregor scored a goal that should have ensured trips to places like the Nou Camp, the Bernabeu and Alliance Arena.

Instead, though, O’Neill’s side contrived to throw away that advantage to crash out of the competition in shame with one goal after another flying into their net.

It was embarrassing, pathetic, utterly astonishing how a team could end up losing a game they were in such control of.

O’Neill has never looked as physically and emotionally drained as he did when this was all over.

For 120-odd minutes he’d paced up and down the touchline, virtually kicking every ball.



OUR BEST FREE BETS & SIGN-UP OFFERS

If the fourth official spoke to him once about stepping out of his designated area, he did it a hundred times.

But the Polish official was wasting his breath.

O’Neill couldn’t have sat down in the dugout had his life depended on it.



But the way his own team put him through the wringer was just incredible.

He’d said all the right things in the build-up.

From the second last week’s first-leg was over, he was telling anyone who’d listen that the tie wasn’t over.

That there was no way in the world his team would be taking anything for granted against a very good Austrian outfit.

But deep down he knew that his team could only throw this away.



Celtic were cruising.

They were so far ahead of LASK st one stage, they were virtually out of sight.

It should have been a stroll in the park after skipper Callum McGregor fired them ahead after 21 minutes.

They had to keep it tight for the first 20 minutes. And they did. Just.

LASK bombarded O’Neill’s defence early on.



They had shots blocked. Defender Andres Andrade hit the post.

But worse was to come for him because just seconds later he was turning the ball into the back of his own net as he attempted to block McGregor’s shot.

That was the moment Celtic took another huge step towards the big time.

Or so it seemed.

Celtic’s players thought it was done. It just felt utterly unthinkable that they could waste a 4-0 aggregate lead.



But LASK were then given hope again when it seemed there was none.

Benjamin Nygren? What the hell was he thinking.

The blind pass-back he played to goalkeeper Viljami Sinisalo was just awful. Inexplicable.

In fact, it was unforgivable.

Moses Usor couldn’t believe his luck as he ran through to score.



Suddenly Celtic had work to do.

They still had a three-goal lead and yet LASK were back believing again.

The odds were still stacked again them but you wouldn’t have known it going by the way their mad fans balked encouragement at their heroes from that moment on.

Shooting towards their vocal ultras in the second-half also seemed to them an extra yard.

O’Neill could have emphasised the importance of keeping it tight again immediately after the restart and making sure the home side weren’t given any more encouragement.



But that was easier said than done.

LASK’s second goal of the night came after 48 minutes and at that stage anything felt possible.

It was frantic football with Celtic unable to take the sting out of the game when they really needed to.

LASK just wouldn’t let up and when they scored their third the pressure on Scotland’s champions was extraordinary.

Samuel Adeniran is a big powerful centre forward who out himself about but his strike past Sinisalo from outside the box was sensational.



He just shouldn’t have been allowed the time and space to pick his spot and get his shot away.

It was backs to the wall now.

McGregor bawled at his team-mates to try and get them to waken up, Kasper Hogh also rallying everyone together.

High up in the stand, the 1500 away fans could barely watch.

LASK almost levelled the tie at 4-4 after 70 minutes with Adeniran firing off a shot which came back odd the crossbar. Next their skipper Sascha Horvath brought a vital save from Sinisalo.



O’Neill made changes to shore it up as best he could, centre-backs Liam Scales and Dane Murray taking over from Kieran Tierney and Colby Donovan.

But LASK couldn’t be stopped.

In the 90th minute, Florian Flecker scored their fourth of the night to level the tie to take it into extra-time.

There was even a dramatic VAR check before it was confirmed he was onside after he pounced on a sensational initial save from Sinisalo.

The roar from the home fans when 2022 World Cup final ref Szymon Marciniak pointed to the centre circle almost blew the roof off the place.



LASK had put so much into their comeback they looked shattered from then on – but with 109 minutes on the clock they scored yet again.

Luke McCowan was culpable this time.

The diehard Celtic supporter won the ball initially but took far too long on it and got robbed with Adeniran beating Sinisalo from distance again.

It was done. Celtic had blown it.

Sports.title: SPFL clash ABANDONED in second half after footballer suffers serious injury and rushed to hospital
Sports.content:
GAME OFF SPFL clash ABANDONED in second half after footballer suffers serious injury and rushed to hospital

THE KDM Evolution Trophy clash between Forfar Athletic and Formartine United was abandoned in the second half after a horror aerial collision left a player seriously injured.

Forfar left-back Adam Livingstone required extensive on-field treatment before being rushed to hospital following the sickening incident in the 50th minute.



The League Two outfit initially confirmed the match was halted shortly after the restart, with both sets of players taken off the pitch to allow medics to treat the defender.

Just 20 minutes later, official confirmation came through that the match had been called off.



A statement read: “The match has been abandoned. We’ll do our best to update you on the situation as soon as we can.”

Forfar soon provided an update on the 28-year-old’s condition, confirming he was awake and responsive.

Writing on social media, the club said: “Adam is awake and responsive after the aerial clash which has injured his neck/spine.

“He is being treated by medics on the pitch as we await an ambulance. This is likely the only update we’ll be able to provide for some time.”

The Loons had been leading the tie 1-0 thanks to Gus Mailer’s 18th-minute opener.

Jim Weir’s side were eager to bounce back following their opening-day defeat to Aberdeen B in the competition, but player safety rightly took priority.

The tie will now be replayed at a later date.

Livingstone came through the youth ranks at Motherwell and enjoyed loan spells with East Fife, Morton and Clyde before sealing a permanent move to Cove Rangers in 2020.

He later headed south in 2022, featuring for Stafford Rangers, Hednesford Town, Telford United and Buxton, before returning north to join East Kilbride in 2024.

Sports.title: James Maddison suffers fractured shoulder in Tottenham’s horror defeat to Brentford as injury update issued
Sports.content:
TOTTENHAM midfielder James Maddison has suffered a fractured shoulder.

Maddison, 29, missed almost all of last season after an ACL tear.



And the unlucky playmaker was crocked yet again in the horror opening day defeat to Brentford.

Maddison came on as a 68th-minute sub in the mauling at the Gtech.



But he was in the wars immediately and Spurs confirmed that an MRI scan has shown a slight fracture after an awkward fall during the game.

Maddison initially hurt his ACL at the end of the 24/25 season.

He attempted to come back during the following pre-season, but suffered a full rupture in the process.

He finally returned to action in May as he went on to make three appearances to help Tottenham avoid relegation.

The England international was also limited during pre-season due to a minor issue.

But there is hope that he will not spend too long on the sidelines as head coach Roberto De Zerbi labelled this latest setback as a “small injury.”



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Maddison was able to take part in limited training on Monday.

And it is hoped he will return before next month’s extended international break.

It is a relief for Tottenham as injuries continue to trouble the club after their 17th-placed finish last season.

Both Xavi Simons and Wilson Odobert are currently sidelined with long-term ACL injuries.

Dejan Kulusevski and Mohammed Kudus are also out of action with knee and quad injuries, respectively.



While new captain Micky van de Ven and Pape Matar Sarr also did not feature against Brentford.

But Spurs have been boosted by the £85million deal to sign Savinho from Manchester City – with Oumar Marmoush set to follow next.

De Zerbi’s side will next host Newcastle at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Saturday, August 29.

Sports.title: Epic Wolverhampton Wanderers-themed boozer wins Pub Shed of the Year award leaving owners ‘gobsmacked’
Sports.content:
A COUPLE have won Pub Shed of the Year for their Wolverhampton Wanderers- themed boozer.

Tina and Rich Hibbs have spent £25,000 over eight years crafting the backyard bolthole.



Packed with Wolves shirts and memorabilia, it boasts a bar with draught lager and cider, TV, Pac-Man machine and beer garden.

Baker Tina, 48, of Rugeley, Staffs, said: “We have a friend who runs a business making these, so he helped with the shell while the interior was all done by us.



“It has become a great space for entertaining.

“Every Easter we do an egg hunt and we decorate it all up for Halloween.



“We also have our Christmas dinner in there, I usually cater for about 15 people each year.

“Our friends love it.



“I’m not sure about our neighbours but we’ve not had any complaints!”

The couple were “gobsmacked” by the award and celebrated after retired skip firm boss Rich, 57, returned from Wolves’ 3-1 win at Preston.

Tina added: “It’s become a great space for entertaining.”

Award organisers Two Fat Blokes bar signs and Ngage Radio said: “Hibby’s Bar is a worthy winner.”

Sports.title: Raheem Sterling charged with dangerous driving and possessing laughing gas after crashing £270k Lambo
Sports.content:
FORMER Premier League ace Raheem Sterling could get two years’ jail if convicted of dangerous driving after his £270,000 Lamborghini M-way crash.

The ex-England winger, 31, has also been charged with possessing laughing gas and failing to provide a specimen following his arrest in May.



Motorists dialled 999 after seeing a black luxury 4×4 swerving across the M3 in Hampshire just before 9am.

The former Liverpool, Man City and Chelsea winger was arrested close to an interchange near Farnborough.



Sterling, who is currently without a club, had been due to answer bail on Friday.

He will now appear before magistrates in Basingstoke on September 15, police revealed yesterday.

A Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary spokesman said: “A driver will appear in court next month to face charges following a collision on the M3.

“Raheem Sterling, 31, from Berkshire, has been charged for the following offences: dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, failing to provide a specimen.

“The charges come following a single vehicle collision, involving a Lamborghini, on the M3 southbound, close to the Minley Interchange, on 28 May, 2026.

“No other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported.



“Mr Sterling is due to appear at Basingstoke magistrates court on 15 September.”

Nitrous oxide, also known as laughing gas and hippy crack, was made illegal when reclassified as a class C controlled substance in November 2023.

Usage is rife among footballers, despite its dangers including risk of heart attacks, stroke and brain damage.

It typically comes in supersized canisters used to fill balloons, which are then inhaled repeatedly to give a euphoric, short-lived high.

Sterling was just 15 when he was signed by Liverpool from the QPR academy in 2010.



He became a fans’ favourite at Anfield before a contract dispute saw him move to Manchester City in 2015.

There he enjoyed massive success — winning four Premier League titles, five Carabao Cups and an FA Cup.

However, sources close to Sterling told how his mental health suffered following his £50million transfer from Man City to Chelsea in July 2022.



He was eventually ordered to train separately to the first-team group after then-manager Enzo Maresca — now Man City boss — decided he was surplus to requirements.

A loan deal to Arsenal followed, but did not work out, so in February he joined Dutch club Feyenoord.

That deal ended in the summer and he is now without a club.



Sources also claimed he has been written off and made to feel “worthless” despite gaining 82 England caps.

One said: “He was a prolific international who steered the England squad to significant heights over the last decade and has been made to feel worthless.

“The psychological strain that has put on him is immeasurable.

“He feels isolated.

“The second he touches a ball, he’s told he’s a flop and he’s finished.



“He’s been mocked and heckled.

“He moved to the Netherlands to escape and rediscover his love for the game, but the negativity followed.

“It’s been extremely tough.”

Since the M3 incident, Sterling has kept a low profile and has rarely been pictured, apart from social media footage of him playing football with his children.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He is engaged to childhood sweetheart Paige Milian, 30, with whom he has two kids.



He also has a daughter from a previous relationship.

Sports.title: Mayer: I feel unbeatable - Cameron fight won't be close!

British WBO title holder Cameron (22-1, 8 KOs) faces American Mayer (22-2, 5 KOs) at the bp pulse LIVE arena on Saturday - live on Sky Sports - with every bout on the MVPW-06 main card pitting a UK fighter against a US opponent.

WBA and WBC champion Mayer has no shortage of respect for Cameron - who has won her last four fights since a rematch defeat to Katie Taylor in 2023 - but has backed her own ability to unify the titles in front of what is set to be a hostile Birmingham crowd.

"I feel better than ever," Mayer told Sky Sports. "I just know I just feel unbeatable right now. I feel in a great position and I can't wait to get out to the UK and do my thing.

"[Cameron] is good at what she does. She's an aggressive fighter. She lets her hands go.

"She fights at a fast pace and so do I. So that's going to make for a very exciting fight for the fans.

"But I just don't think it's going to be as close and as much of a war as everyone thinks.

"I'm fighting better than I've ever fought, smarter than I've ever been. And I just believe in myself.

"I feel like no matter where I go, I'm still going to kick butt. So it could be here. It could be there. I'm taking the win."

Mayer pointed to her "versatility" as a defining factor come Saturday, insisting nothing can prepare Cameron for the new and improved version of the 36-year-old that awaits.

"I'm really hard to train for because I've developed so much these last 10 months of being in the gym," Mayer told Sky Sports.

I'll definitely be using a little bit of everything I've got, but knowing mine and Chantelle's styles there will definitely be moments where it will be a dog fight."

The significance of the chance to become unified world champion by reclaiming the WBO crown is not lost on Mayer, with the American describing the prospect of victory as a career-defining moment.

Sports.title: Wolff 'not at all' disappointed by Verstappen's new Red Bull deal
Sports.content:
Mercedes chief Toto Wolff says he is "not at all" disappointed by Max Verstappen having committed to Red Bull with a new contract that runs until 2030.

Ahead of the Formula 1 season resuming with Verstappen's home Dutch Grand Prix over the weekend, Red Bull ended speculation over the four-time world champion's future by announcing the extension.

While Verstappen's previous deal was set to run until 2028, exit clauses in the agreement meant the 28-year-old would have been free to join another team in 2027, with possible switches to Mercedes and McLaren having been the subject of significant speculation.

Wolff made a very public pursuit of Verstappen after Lewis Hamilton announced in February 2024 that he was leaving Mercedes to join Ferrari in 2025, and the Mercedes boss appeared to still be interested in signing the Dutchman last season

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Verstappen admits that, with V8 engines' potential return in 2030, there may be another opportunity for him to reassess his future in F1

However, Wolff has insisted in recent months that he is happy with his driver pairing of Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, who sit first and second, respectively, at the top of the Drivers' Championship after Sunday's race in Zandvoort.

Asked about Verstappen's new contract in an interview with Sky Sports F1 on Saturday in Zandvoort, Wolff said: "Most important was that we had the clarity in the team since a long time.

"We're committed to George and Kimi, and in a way, that was just a logical consequence what happened now.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff had previously downplayed suggestions Verstappen could join his team

"Silly season is officially cancelled now, and everybody can concentrate on the racing."

Pushed on whether he felt any disappointment about the length of Verstappen's commitment to Red Bull, Wolff added: "No, not at all.

"We know each other well. With Kimi and George, it's the perfect set-up we have and the perfect line-up, so there is no disappointment."

Rosberg: I don't think Max had any options

The cooling of Wolff's interest in Verstappen appears as though it may have been influenced by the hugely impressive form that has put Antonelli in control of the championship.

The Italian, who turned 20 on Tuesday, has unexpectedly outperformed the far more experienced Russell to build a 59-point advantage over his team-mate at the top of the standings.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Dutch Grand Prix

While Mercedes showed huge faith in Antonelli by fast-tracking him in as Hamilton's replacement as a teenager, an inconsistent rookie campaign left doubt over whether he would be able to live up to expectations.

However, his 2026 form, which saw him break countless records by winning five successive races after finishing second in the season opener, could potentially have made Wolff reconsider whether bringing Verstappen to Mercedes remained necessary.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A 360-degree look at Verstappen’s race-ending crash at the Dutch Grand Prix on Sunday

McLaren appeared to be similarly content with their current driver line-up of reigning world champion Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri, who have combined to lead the Woking squad to successive constructors' titles.

Sky Sports F1 pundit Nico Rosberg, who won the 2016 world championship with Mercedes, said: "It's fantastic news for Formula 1 because Max Verstappen is the greatest driver at the moment, and we want him to stay here. He's a phenomenal driver!

"He was thinking about taking some time off, or stopping F1 for a while, so that's great.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Nico Rosberg discusses Verstappen's contract extension with Red Bull, saying it's a 'super important message' for the team

"I don't think he had any options. He was in talks with McLaren, but I think that was just to strengthen his position at Red Bull.

"Red Bull need stability so you offer him a bit more money, and the range is from £70-90m a year, so let's land on £80m - which is a lot of money!"

Sports.title: Williams and Alcaraz reach mixed doubles quarters before exit
Sports.content:
Star pairing Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz reached the quarter-finals of the US Open mixed doubles before being beaten by fourth seeds Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli.

Williams - a 23-time Grand Slam singles champion - returned to tennis in June at the age of 44 and secured her first professional win since 2022 as she and Alcaraz beat Britain's Lloyd Glasspool and partner Erin Routliffe in their opening match.

It was also seven-time major winner Alcaraz's first match back on tour after a wrist injury sidelined the reigning men's singles champion since April. The 22-year-old was born five years after Williams won the 1998 mixed doubles title at Flushing Meadows.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the US Open Mixed Doubles match between Serena Williams & Carlos Alcaraz vs Erin Routliffe & LLoyd Glasspool

The dynamic pairing bounced back from a slow start to claim a 5-3 4-1 opening victory over Routliffe and Glasspool, much to the delight of fans inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.

"I never expected to be back on this court," Williams said. "I never thought this would happen."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Carlos Alcaraz and Serena Williams react to Mixed Doubles US Open victory

With their quarter-final match scheduled immediately afterwards, Williams and Alcaraz ultimately ran out of puff as Bencic and Cobolli triumphed 5-4 4-1, the latter then having hailed their opponents pre-match as "the queen of tennis and the king of now."

The question now is whether Williams will seek an encore performance in women's doubles alongside older sister Venus, having already ruled out a repeat of her singles appearance at Wimbledon.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz won the first set of their Mixed Doubles match at the US Open

Djokovic and Sabalenka suffer early exit

Top seeds Novak Djokovic and Aryna Sabalenka were bounced out of the tournament in the opening match on Arthur Ashe, falling to a 1-4 4-2 10-2 ‌defeat to Britain's Henry Patten and Katerina Siniakova.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the US Open Mixed Doubles match between Aryna Sabalenka & Novak Djokovic vs Katerina Siniakova & Henry Patten

Djokovic, a ​24-time Grand Slam singles champion, and four-time major winner Sabalenka made a strong start by ​taking the opening set, but doubles specialists Patten and ‌Siniakova hit back to claim the second before dominating the tiebreak ​to secure a place in the quarter-finals.

Siniakova sealed the upset in style with an ace out wide on match ​point, ending the tournament hopes of the ⁠star-studded pairing.

"It wasn't looking very ⁠good for a while, in this format we play one bad game and all ‌of a sudden the first set's gone," Patten said.

"We knew the same could happen in the second, and we played ‌an amazing tiebreak. Kat acing Novak on match point was great."

The mixed doubles championship is once again being staged in the week before the singles main draw, after organisers revamped ⁠the format last year to attract more ​leading singles players by reducing the field and ​giving the event a standalone slot on the ​calendar.

The revamped format proved a commercial success in its ⁠debut year, drawing sell-out crowds and attracting many of the sport's biggest singles names despite criticism from some doubles specialists, ⁠who argued it marginalised established pairings.

Defending champions dumped out in first round

Italian ​duo Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori went on to ​retain the title by defeating Iga Swiatek and Casper Ruud in last year's final, but suffered a first-round exit this year.

Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev beat the defending champions 1-4 4-1 11-9 in the opening round, before clinching a semi-final spot with a 4-1 4-5 10-5 victory over Diana Shnaider and Casper Ruud.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gael Monfils hit an incredible shot during his mixed doubles match at the US Open

They next face Czech pair Karolína Muchova and Jakub Mensik in one of Wednesday's semi-finals, with Bencic and Cobolli facing husband and wife partnership Gael Monfils and Elina Svitolina in the other after they edged out Patten and Siniakova in the last eight.

The final two follow the two semis on Wednesday night will resemble a regular match, with traditional sets to six games.
