World.title: Inside China’s Shift From Short-Drama Sets to AI Factories
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018927/Inside China’s Shift From Short-Drama Sets to AI Factories
World.content:
China’s ultrashort-drama boom built a sprawling live-action industry of actors, directors, crews, and filming bases. Now, as AI drives down production costs, shoots are disappearing and companies are cutting staff. In Zhengzhou, filmmakers reckon with the slowdown; in Wuxi, former film and animation workers are building AI production systems that can turn scripts into finished videos with only a handful of people. Sixth Tone follows both sides of the shift to see how AI is changing not just how short dramas are made, but what filmmaking work itself is becoming.

Additional reporting: He Qitong; story editors: Apurva and Qi Ya; video editor: Lü Xiao

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018928/Chinese Mother Buys Daughters Extra Train Seat, Sparking Debate
World.title: Chinese Mother Buys Daughters Extra Train Seat, Sparking Debate
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018928/Chinese Mother Buys Daughters Extra Train Seat, Sparking Debate
World.content:
“We bought three tickets,” a teenager says to a woman asking to use the empty seat beside her — occupied by snacks — her sister sitting on the other side.

“We’re all in the same carriage,” the standing woman says. “Shouldn’t we help each other out?” She calls a train attendant for help.

“Places 5, 6, and 7 — those seats are theirs,” the attendant says after checking the teens’ tickets. “You need to talk to them about it. Telling me won’t help.”

This scene, which took place Aug. 18 on a slow train traveling from Shanghai to the southwestern city of Chengdu — a 27-hour journey — was captured in a video that went viral in China this past week.

Online, people heatedly discussed whether the girls should have shared the seat or whether they were entitled to keep it for themselves. The topic rose to the second-highest place on Chinese microblogging platform Weibo’s trending list, receiving over 37 million views and 12,000 discussions as of Monday.

Many were in support of the girls’ decision, arguing that giving up their seats would be a favor, not an obligation, as the teens themselves had paid for the three tickets. Others said that they were “wasting public resources.”

Still others contended that the train attendants should have been more proactive, pointing to railway ticketing rules that say customers can only buy one ticket for themselves per train and that if the ticket holder does not board, their seat should be reassigned by train attendants.

Despite these stipulations, passengers can buy tickets for others using their identification information on train ticket purchasing platforms.

The girls’ mother did just that, buying their tickets as well as entering her own information for the third seat, according to a now-deleted post she made on Aug. 20 on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok.

“My original intention was to keep them from taking up other people’s space because they had too much luggage, so I bought an extra ticket,” she wrote. “Since they’re both girls and didn’t want to sit with others, I bought three tickets together.”

In response to the issue, 12306 — China’s official train ticketing and service platform — told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper that in the event that a passenger does not board the train, their ticket remains classified as “sold” in the train’s online system. In addition, if a ticket is purchased for a passenger but they do not board, the person whose ID was used to buy the ticket retains the right to decide how the seat is used.

On Aug. 21, the Chengdu Bureau of China’s National Railway responded to the controversy, seemingly contradicting 12306: “If a passenger fails to board after purchasing a ticket due to personal reasons, the passenger is considered to have forfeited their right to use the seat … according to the rules, the seat cannot be occupied by a third party.” The bureau noted that such instances should be reported to the train staff.

But a day later, the case shifted from a dispute over passengers’ rights and entitlements to discussions on the lack of support for children traveling alone, as well as the difficulties faced by migrant families. The girls’ mother, speaking to domestic media on Aug. 22, explained that she works in Shanghai and was sending her two daughters back to their hometown. She added that she did not have enough time to escort them and wanted them to “develop their independence.” The extra seat, she said, could also serve as a place to lie down for the two, as she worried about male strangers sleeping beside them in sleeper cars.

She also noted that, under ticketing rules, minors cannot buy tickets themselves and their tickets must instead be purchased alongside an adult ticket.

In a commentary, The Paper wrote that “behind the purchase of the three tickets lies a harsh reality faced by millions of working families, leaving migrant families with no alternative.” It recommended that the railway system follow airlines — which allow parents to apply for service for unaccompanied minors in advance — as an example.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A video screenshot shows the empty seat that gave rise to a national debate. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018902/China’s Short-Drama Boom Was Built on Speed. Then AI Got Faster.
World.title: China’s Short-Drama Boom Was Built on Speed. Then AI Got Faster.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018902/China’s Short-Drama Boom Was Built on Speed. Then AI Got Faster.
World.content:
Editor’s note: This is the first of a two-part series on how AI is reshaping China’s ultrashort-drama industry. Read part 2.

HENAN, Central China — When a tow truck stopped beside three luxury cars at Zhoutu Culture’s compound in the central Chinese city of Zhengzhou in July, crew members assumed they were headed to another shoot.

Zhoutu was shooting so many ultrashort dramas that the company calculated owning the cars would eventually cost less than renting them as props, and bring some tax savings. Founder Wang Huan and his business partners had each chosen a model they had long wanted.

But the Mercedes-Benz G63, Aston Martin DB11, and Bentley Continental GT were leaving for good. Zhoutu sold all three for a combined 4.5 million yuan ($650,000).

Wang photographed the three cars before they left and posted the images on social media with the caption: “Selling cars and all in short dramas.”

“Of course it stirred up some emotions,” he later told Sixth Tone. “But it wasn’t anything like what people might imagine — like feeling we’d gone bankrupt or something.”

Within months of adding the cars to its fleet, Zhoutu’s output had plunged from as many as 200 ultrashort dramas a month to around 30. Its full-time workforce had fallen from more than 500 employees at its 2025 peak to around 200. More than 20,000 costumes had been moved to a nearby building as an AI studio took over their former space. Even the canteen was closed.

Beyond Zhoutu’s gates, shoots were disappearing across Zhengzhou, one of China’s largest ultrashort-drama production hubs, often dubbed the country’s “Vertical Hollywood.”

The smartphone-first dramas, typically told in episodes lasting only a minute or two, reached 851 million users across China by May, in an industry now worth more than 100 billion yuan. Major platforms fueled the boom with scripts, guaranteed funding, and incentives for producers that could deliver at scale.

But the production model underpinning the industry’s rise began to unravel in February. AI was rapidly reducing the cost of work that had previously required live-action crews, while major platforms began cutting the guaranteed funding that had helped sustain breakneck expansion.

Across the live-action industry, people began calling it a “winter.”

Shot clock

“Master Comes Down the Mountain, Tasks Me With Wooing His Daughter” is one of the few Zhoutu productions still shooting in July.

In one scene, four armed guards sent by two sisters from a powerful family rush the protagonist, played by Cai Zhongyuan. He waves one hand and sends them sprawling. One draws a gun and fires; Cai catches the bullet between two fingers.

Director Li Jun adds both flourishes on set, giving the hero two more moments of triumph typical of male-oriented ultrashort dramas.

Cai then turns his attention back to the sisters, whom he had earlier encountered while they were bathing, and continues flirting with them. When the elder sister finally loses her temper and slaps him, the two collide — and kiss.

Li steps away from the monitor before the kiss. “Don’t pull away too quickly. Three seconds. Separate only after I say so,” she tells the leads. She adjusts a side light, tells the camera operator to shoot in slow motion, then calls action.

“Perfect.” In just three takes, the drama’s most important romantic scene is finished.

“Master Comes Down the Mountain” will eventually run for around 100 minutes. Li has three days to shoot it, on a budget of roughly 200,000 yuan.

Barely 160 centimeters tall, with cropped hair and a voice that carries across the set, she keeps the production moving almost without pause.

When crew chatter continues as the cameras are about to roll, Li cuts across it: “Why don’t you chat in front of the camera instead?” A stalled fog machine, missing prop, or crew member drifting into frame brings another rebuke.

“For simple shots like this, don’t come back to me asking what to do,” she tells the assistant director, pushing the crew to keep routine shots moving without waiting for her.

A comparable production last year would have cost around 300,000 yuan and taken seven or eight days, Li says. The roughly 30-person core filming crew has remained largely intact, but around 10 jobs tied to stunt work and special effects have been cut after related scenes were removed or shifted to AI.

At her busiest, Li directed roughly four dramas a month. From preparation to release, she says, an ultrashort production could take less than a month, with crews routinely working 14 to 16 hours a day.

Wang Ruoyan, 24, who plays the elder sister in “Master Comes Down the Mountain,” remembers getting only around 10 hours of sleep during one five-day shoot as lunch breaks disappeared into costume and makeup changes.

“I even fell asleep in the shower once,” she says. “When I woke up, 30 minutes had passed.”

Wang also saw actors carrying quick-acting heart medication on set. Li says she did the same during especially intense periods, urging actors on her crews to keep some with them to “save their lives.”

Last summer, Li recalled ambulances arriving three times in a single afternoon.

“Some people had acute myocarditis, some suffered heatstroke, and some were simply exhausted from working too hard and staying up too late,” she says. “People would become mentally disoriented, and if they weren’t careful, they could easily fall and get injured.”

On more demanding productions, Li says, actors might finish at 3 or 4 a.m. and be back on set four hours later.

“No one has the energy or passion to create,” Li says. “They’re just thinking about finishing, getting off work, and going to sleep.”

Luo Haoyu, an actor who frequently worked with Li, was on set as many as 28 days a month at the height of the boom. Some nights, he filmed until 5 a.m., then rushed straight to another shoot without even removing his makeup.

“Deep down, everyone knew those crazy days wouldn’t last forever,” Luo says. “We were burning ourselves out because everyone understood that last year was an exceptional period for short dramas.”

Hard landing

Those “crazy days” lasted until February.

That month, TikTok owner ByteDance released Seedance 2.0, an AI video model capable of generating increasingly polished footage for around 1 yuan per second.

Soon after, Hongguo — ByteDance’s ultrashort-drama platform and a major source of scripts and financing — began withdrawing guaranteed funding from many small and midsize live-action projects.

The shift hit companies like Zhoutu particularly hard: three years earlier, a Hongguo-backed rebirth melodrama, “My Daughter Pulled the Plug on My Oxygen Tank,” had given the company its breakout hit, generating more than 10 million yuan in user spending on its first day.

“The landing was extremely hard,” says Zhoutu founder Wang Huan.

Zhoutu has since opened a 50-person AI studio, while about 20 live-action directors also work on AI productions. It makes six to eight AI dramas a month, largely, Wang says, to “maintain a presence” in the market.

At the same time, the company is using cheaper live-action projects to keep its remaining workforce employed. “With so much investment and so many employees, our strategy is still to operate on a model that keeps more people working,” Wang says. If that fails, he says, Zhoutu may shrink further.

The company had already spent nearly two months after the Spring Festival, in mid-February, with little work coming in. “When you don’t know what to do, the safest option is to stop,” Wang says. “At least you won’t lose more money.”

Productions booked before the downturn kept Li on set for a few weeks. Then new scripts dwindled to roughly one a month, and by April her team had nothing to shoot. Directors around her began moving into AI production, while actors suddenly found themselves waiting for work.

Luo says his monthly income fell from around 20,000 yuan during the boom to roughly 5,000 yuan. In the first three months after the Spring Festival, he worked just 20 days in total.

“I felt confused and lost,” he recalls. “What am I supposed to do in the future?”

He began binge eating, sometimes until he felt he might vomit. For an actor normally careful about his weight, the behavior unsettled him.

“At the time, I thought, things were already this bad. Eating at least made me feel a little better,” he says.

He considered leaving the industry altogether, but could not bring himself to do it. “I still want to see whether audiences can once again have higher expectations for live-action productions,” he says.

Yet producers kept pouring into AI. More than 95% of the 128,000 ultrashort dramas released in the first quarter of 2026 were AI-generated, according to the China Netcasting Services Association (CNSA).

By May, Bytedance pledged 1.5 billion yuan to support live-action short dramas, while six major platforms announced at least 6 billion yuan in planned investment. Regulators also allocated funding for higher-quality productions across 11 provinces.

Live-action output rebounded in the second quarter, partly due to shelved projects returning, though CNSA data shows AI still accounted for 64% of releases.

But Wang is reluctant to bet Zhoutu’s future on another round of platform money. “If Hongguo stopped giving you money tomorrow, what would you do?” he says.

For Shi, a 22-year-old background actor, the slowdown meant days spent waiting for work. During the boom, small speaking roles and regular extra work could bring him close to 10,000 yuan a month. By the time Sixth Tone met him, he had landed just one job in 10 days.

For 110 yuan, Shi spent the morning waiting to appear for a few seconds as a guard: charge at the hero, pretend to be hit, fall to the ground.

He was also still owed 800 yuan from a production the previous December. The company had disappeared, as had the person who recruited him. All Shi had left was their nickname on messaging app WeChat.

“We don’t even know who to ask for our money,” says Shi, who asked to be identified only by his surname. “Construction workers can at least find someone to demand their wages from. With film crews, they’re long gone.”

Shi barely watches live-action ultrashort dramas anymore. He prefers AI-generated comic dramas.

“AI is especially good at stories that rely heavily on visual effects,” he says. “It does those really well.”

Still rolling

For the opening scene of “Master Comes Down the Mountain,” the male lead falls from the sky. Last year, Li says, the crew would have used wire work and spent at least half a day filming it. This time, the actor simply lay face down on a round stone table in front of a small green screen.

“AI can generate all the surrounding scenery,” Li says. “It can make the male lead descend through the clouds, and even create a sweeping aerial shot following him all the way to the ground.”

The whole shot took less than 30 minutes, and Li estimates it saves around 10,000 yuan.

Months earlier, Zhoutu had offered many of its directors the option of switching to AI production. For Li, that meant planning shots and guiding a team through the video-generation process.

After a day or two learning the job, Li says she could already do the work. The pay was about 30% lower. Of roughly 10 directors around her who faced the same choice, eight switched to AI. Li refused.

“Live-action short dramas need a director more,” Li says. “With the right prompt, anyone can make AI videos. But with real filming, you have to work with the actors, camera, and lighting. The sense of achievement is different.”

Zhoutu now rarely makes premium live-action dramas with big budgets. Instead, it focuses on cheaper remakes of proven hits, particularly modern-day rural stories that can be filmed quickly.

“AI’s advantage is making two immortals arguing in the sky, not people arguing outside a village house,” Wang says. A family-conflict drama can cost less than 50,000 yuan to shoot with real actors. Internally, Zhoutu calls these “emotion-driven dramas for lower-tier markets.”

Many of Zhoutu’s remaining live-action productions are male-oriented stories and remakes of plots that have already yielded success. Wang says they can be shot faster than female-oriented dramas, which typically require more time for atmosphere and emotional development.

In one scene from “Master Comes Down the Mountain,” Wang Ruoyan and the second female lead enter the hero’s bedroom in lace and bunny-style nightdresses. Before filming, Li adjusts two strings of hanging round plastic discs. Placed close to the lens, the pieces blur into soft circles of light; she moves them farther apart until the effect sits where she wants it in the frame.

“This is the craftsmanship I only use in female-oriented dramas,” she jokes.

The extra effort does not always pay off. Some of her carefully polished dramas have performed poorly; others that she rushed through became hits.

“Those times make me wonder whether I really understand the market,” she says. “I started doubting myself.”

The final scene of “Master Comes Down the Mountain” has Cai seated at a dinner table as three women, including the two sisters, confess their love. The elder sister tells him to choose one.

“Can’t I have all three?” he replies.

The women rush him, pulling his ears and grabbing his arms as the camera pushes in. Freeze frame.

Although it’s the ending of the drama, it’s filmed on the first day of the three-day shoot. Li still has two days of scenes to get through.

At lunch, she makes the cast a promise: “I’ll do my best to get you back to the hotel by 7 p.m., so you can order takeout from bed.”

“That would be heaven,” Wang Ruoyan says.

Additional reporting: Lü Xiao; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Monitors show a scene being filmed by director Li Jun in Zhengzhou, Henan province, June 2026. Reedited by Ding Yining; photo by Lü Xiao/Sixth Tone)

World.title: China Before the Infinite Camera Roll
World.content:
Of the many consumer goods that entered China in the 1980s, one small item transformed how millions of families recorded their lives: 35mm color negative film.

In 1984, Fujifilm established its Beijing office, as Chinese photographers were beginning to embrace the company’s color film, known for its green packaging and the distinctive greenish cast of its prints. Kodak, Fujifilm’s main rival at the time, soon followed, expanding its presence and introducing a network of express color photo stores across China in the 1990s.

These developments, together with the arrival of point-and-shoot cameras that required little skill to achieve proper exposure and sharp focus, enabled ordinary Chinese people to record their lives in color. The film was developed to produce negatives, which were then printed as photographs for family albums.

Not everyone kept the negatives. Many ended up at recycling plants, which is where French artist Thomas Sauvin’s work began. In 2009, Sauvin met Xiaoma, a Beijinger who recovered silver nitrate from X-rays, CDs, and negatives. The two struck a deal, and Sauvin received his first batch of negatives to digitize. Their partnership would eventually help create one of China’s largest private archives of photographic negatives: the Beijing Silvermine.

The project gives broader significance in banal, amateur images. As patterns emerge across dozens, sometimes hundreds, of photographs, personal moments become part of a collective record. One example is a series of portraits taken beside refrigerators, an appliance many Chinese households were acquiring for the first time in the 1990s. Together, such images document the transformation of everyday life as a rapidly changing China became wealthier and more urban.

Much has changed since then. Film gave way to digital cameras, and then to smartphones. People can now easily take thousands of photos a year, a number unthinkable to most families in the 1990s, when a roll of film contained just 36 exposures.

More recently, however, analog photography has enjoyed a revival on social media, where users are drawn to its vintage tones and textures. In 2025, Lucky Film, a Chinese manufacturer that once competed with Kodak and Fujifilm, announced the return of its color negative film amid growing demand from nostalgic millennials and curious Gen Z consumers. Yet a roll of film and lab processing now cost more than 100 yuan (US$14.80) for just 36 photos, leaving analog photography a niche hobby.

The intention behind analog photography has also changed, according to Sauvin. “Now, when people take analog photos, what’s in their mind is that they will scan the negative, and they will post it on Xiaohongshu or Instagram,” said Sauvin, who does not shoot film himself.

What has been lost? Humor, perhaps. Looking through the Beijing Silvermine images, it is hard not to be struck by the ease with which people posed and smiled, gazing into the camera with little of the self-consciousness or affectation common in photography today. Before social media, people seemed simply to be enjoying the moments they were living.

In June, Sixth Tone sat down with Sauvin to discuss what analog photography reveals about the lives of ordinary Chinese people in the 1990s and today, his own relationship with the archive, and the challenges posed by artificial intelligence. The interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Sixth Tone: What was your first impression of the earliest batches of recycled negatives, and how did you begin to interpret their meaning?

Sauvin: They were very banal. Quite boring, sometimes very repetitive. It took maybe two or three years before I started to understand what I could do with them. At some point, because of the quantity, you leave the universe of personal stories and enter the universe of collective memory.

A simple example is that, at the beginning of the project, I came across a photo of a woman posing next to a fridge. And I thought, “Oh, having your portrait taken with a fridge is an unusual thing to do.” Then I saw another one, then another one, and now I probably have a series of 25 pictures like this. In the early 1990s, households in Beijing began acquiring refrigerators. They would decorate them and take photos with them. And that’s something no one else would really record. A photojournalist would never make a series about this, nor would a historian or an artist. It’s too close to daily life. It’s too simple. Yet ordinary people, accidentally and unconsciously, capture the bigger picture in these negatives.

Sixth Tone: Is there a single frame or series that interests you most?

Sauvin: So many. I like the photos taken at Beijing World Park. It opened in 1993, and people went there to get a sense of travel, to experience the outside world and its monuments. In the archive, I have thousands of photos taken there in 1993, 1994, and 1995. It was the perfect playground for taking photos. You could have your picture taken with the Twin Towers, the Statue of Liberty, the Eiffel Tower, and so on.

Then, when I went through photos taken in the early 2000s, these Chinese tourists weren’t at the World Park anymore. They were in the actual countries. And when I look at these negatives, as a French person, I always wonder: Is it the real one or the World Park one?

Sixth Tone: Besides the Eiffel Tower series, were there any photos that connected the collection to your own life?

Sauvin: A lot. I was born and raised in Paris, so I’m attentive to photos taken there. I found photos taken on Rue Fabert in the 7th arrondissement, where I learned to walk when I was 1 year old. It’s my home. Seeing someone posing right where I learned to walk was a strange feeling.

I also remember going to the Louvre Museum as a kid and seeing tourists taking photos: flash, flash, flash! Two or three decades later, I started the Silvermine project and found those kinds of photos. Because they were photographing oil paintings with a flash, you always get this big white dot in the image. I made a series about them called “Dazzling Old Masters.”

But the entire archive also has a very strong connection with me. The first time I went to Beijing was in 1999, on a family exchange. In 2009, exactly 10 years later, I started this project, which allowed me to discover the Beijing that existed before I arrived. I wouldn’t have done that with any other city in the world.

Sixth Tone: Have you been able to contact the people in these images?

Sauvin: There’s a photo I found in 2010 that I absolutely love: a young girl posing on a red motorcycle on a street in Dashilar, Beijing. One day, she got in touch with me on Weibo and said, “That girl on the bike, it’s me.” She sent me the printed photo from her family album.

I immediately sent her the other 35 photos from the same roll, and she discovered many that she’d probably never seen because people didn’t always print every photo. Looking through them, she realized that the roll contained four consecutive birthdays, meaning the film had been in the family camera for more than four years. They had to wait that long to finish the roll, have it developed, and finally see the images.

That says a lot about how our relationship with photography has changed and how analog photography captures who we are as human beings in a very pure way. Because it costs money and takes time, you make sure to record the moments that matter. I really like the idea of these latent images sitting in a film canister for four years, then one day being put into chemicals and revealing all these moments. And I find it crazy that, after waiting four years, the negatives could be thrown away the very next day.

Sixth Tone: There is a fine line between the privacy of these images and the public nature of your collection and exhibitions. How do you navigate that tension?

Sauvin: Of course, I’m dealing with very private, intimate photos that were never meant to be used in a book or shown in an exhibition. People are vulnerable because they are themselves. That’s something I always try to keep in mind.

I always make sure not to make fun of people. That’s not easy, because a very important part of the Beijing Silvermine’s visual universe is its sense of humor. There’s something very light, funny, and fresh about it. So you need to preserve that sense of humor because it’s the soul of the project, while never crossing the line into making fun of people.

Another rule I’ve given myself almost since the beginning is that I generally avoid using two images of the same person. That way, I make sure never to delve too deeply into one person’s life. What brings the photos together are more anthropological themes. The photos come together and contribute to a theme. But I would not be comfortable showing many photos taken by the same person.

In 2015, a very good friend of mine in Beijing came to me with a big cardboard box containing all the negatives and photos of her late father. He took a lot of photos and organized everything very neatly, with handwritten information everywhere: Here are the 120 films; there are the 35mm films. It was absolutely beautiful.

She gave it to me and said, “I think you’re doing great things with negatives, so this is yours, and just do what you want with it.” I was never able to open the box a second time because it was not my place to deal with this material. It all comes from one person. I know who this person is, so I can do absolutely nothing with it.

Sixth Tone: How do your curatorial decisions reflect the way you view analog photographs within their historical context?

Sauvin: In this exhibition, curated by Holly Russell at Fotografiska Shanghai, we present one room with 1,300 prints. That’s the selection I’ve been working on for 16 years. The selection was organized around themes, topics, and angles that emerged organically from the archive.

But when we brought the archive to Shanghai, we decided not to present each series together. Everything is mixed, so it’s up to the viewer to look at the photos and, just like I did, start seeing connections between them. I also didn’t decide which photo would go where. They were hung quite randomly by the workers who installed the show, and some amazing connections happened simply because of that.

We also decided to present everything as 10-by-15-centimeter prints, which is probably the size of the prints that would have been made from these negatives for family albums. No photo is bigger than another, so we’re not claiming that one is more important. What makes them powerful is their coming together.

There’s something about found photography, about vernacular photography, that is completely crazy: Quantity is more important than quality. You need quantity to make the switch from personal memory to collective memory. That’s how you end up with a gigantic photo album. It’s not the album of a family. It’s the album of a city, a generation, a place, and a time.

Sixth Tone: We have seen a resurgence of analog photography recently, globally but especially in China. Lucky Film is producing color negative film again. What do you make of this renewed interest? Why do you think it appeals to young Chinese people?

Sauvin: I suppose it’s about our relationship with the medium. We’re always drawn to technologies from the past. We’ve seen this with music. We had vinyl records, then CDs, MiniDiscs, and MP3s, and now we are going back to vinyl. There is a worldwide trend of people going back to analog photography. I’m not sure I’m very interested in that. Now we’re at a stage where we’re mass-producing images, and I’d rather live in my time and do that than go back to an earlier, previous tool.

And there’s something very different. People 30 years ago were shooting analog, but there was no artistic intention or intention to share these photos online. There wasn’t this element of staging or representation.

Now, when people take analog photos, what’s in their mind is that they will scan the negative and post it on Xiaohongshu or Instagram. So the intention is not pure. In the end, what does it mean? It means it’s a filter, like a vintage filter of some kind. That’s why I’m not very interested in the trend. I love analog photography, but it died about 20 years ago.

Sixth Tone: Artificial intelligence is being used to restore and recreate faded or damaged negatives. Do you see it primarily as a boon or a bane?

Sauvin: I find it completely fascinating, and I’m sure that, combined with the right idea, it could be an amazing tool. I’m really open to it.

That being said, I need to be very careful because I have this Silvermine archive of 1 million photos, all made of flesh and blood, that come from ordinary people. They are physical objects, and for so many years, when I scanned a photo and shared it, people trusted that the photo existed. There was no question about that.

Then suddenly, about a year ago, we had this explosion of AI-generated images, and it changed people’s minds, mine as well. Now when you see a photo, the first question you ask yourself is: Is it real, or is it AI?

I really don’t want that confusion to happen with the Silvermine. I want to make it very clear: I deal only with analog photography, and I do not modify the photos in any way.

World.title: Experts: Kurultai Results Put Political Parties’ Ability to Deliver to Test
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s first Kurultai election has shifted the focus from winning votes to how effectively political parties can represent voters, develop clear political agendas and deliver results in parliament, experts said following the Aug. 23 vote.

The Central Election Commission (СEC) confirmed final results on Aug. 25. Five parties entered the 145-seat Kurultai after clearing the 5% threshold, with Adilet securing three-quarters of the seats. The People’s Party of Kazakhstan received 3.11% and Baytaq 1.07%, while 2.51% of voters selected “against all.”

Dominant majority, higher responsibility

Political scientist Gaziz Abishev said the scale of Adilet’s majority places greater responsibility on the party to deliver results in Kurultai’s inaugural term.

“In other words, everything that will be done by the Kurultai and the institutions stemming from it during its first convocation will rest fully with the Adilet party and its leadership, given the vertical nature of management in Parliament,” Abishev wrote in his Telegram channel.

In his remarks to Kazakhstanskaya Pravda newspaper, Kazakh statesman Yerlan Koshanov said the campaign showed voters increasingly assessing parties by the substance of their programs and proposals rather than slogans alone. He said the first Kurultai’s lawmakers would be responsible for translating the new Constitution’s principles into legislation.

“Party programs became a subject of comparison and analysis, rather than simply a backdrop to the election campaign. People began to understand more deeply the role and place of such an important political institution as a party and to view it as a pillar of civil society,” said Koshanov.

Turnout rises, voter preferences consolidate

Participation was one of the clearest differences from the previous parliamentary election. Turnout in 2023 stood at 54.19%, compared with 74.08% in the first Kurultai election. Turnout was also close to the 73.12% recorded during the March referendum on the new Constitution.

Marian Abisheva, deputy director of the Presidential Center of Kazakhstan, said pre-election polling consistently pointed to high participation, with different surveys generally placing potential turnout between 70% and 76%.

“The March referendum and the August elections form a single political sequence. First, citizens participated in determining the state’s new constitutional architecture. Then, several months later, they came to the polling stations to form the first representative institution that will operate within that architecture,” Abisheva said at an expert meeting on Aug. 25.

She also pointed to a sharp decline in the share of undecided voters during the campaign. One early survey put the figure at 23.6%, while a later poll showed 3.9%.

“The reduction in uncertainty did not occur through growth in the protest electorate. The ‘against all’ option remained stable throughout the pre-election polling, with sociological studies showing it at between 1.5% and 2.6%. According to the final results, 2.51% of voters chose ‘against all,’” said Abisheva.

Political scientist Daniyar Ashimbayev contrasted the strong turnout with earlier expectations of voter fatigue after repeated nationwide votes in recent years.

“There is no clear algorithm in voter behavior. At the end of last year, some expressed the view that voters were tired of voting. But this year, according to the CEC, turnout reached 73-74%, and it seems no one was tired after all,” Ashimbayev wrote in his Telegram channel on Aug. 24.

Why Adilet converted recognition into votes

Serik Zhusupov, head of the Department of Comparative Studies and Scientific-Theoretical Analysis at the Eurasian Integration Institute, said party recognition alone was not enough if voters could not identify what a party stood for.

He said surveys in late 2025 and early 2026 had registered broad demand for political and institutional change, with the new Constitution and Kurultai election forming successive stages of that process.

“When we talk about party recognition, most people say that they have heard of the parties, but they do not understand their ideological positions. Adilet adopted a fairly simple and clear construct for everyone – the concept of justice. In all opinion polls, the theme of justice has always been one of society’s demands,” said Zhusupov.

He said Adilet built practical proposals around that concept and competed across several electoral groups rather than relying on a narrow base. By contrast, he said Respublica and Aq Zhol competed for overlapping business-oriented voters, while left-wing parties struggled to consolidate their potential electorate.

“As for Baytaq, I understand that the environmental agenda is quite relevant, but this ideology itself is vague, not clearly oriented and it is unclear which electoral niches it targets,” said Zhusupov.

Parties become central to representation

Zhandos Aktayev, a member of the Youth Policy Council, said the move to a fully proportional system places political parties at the center of parliamentary representation.

“People who want to engage in political activity and participate in politics, that is, to represent the country in the Kurultai, need to join parties and represent their interests through those parties. If we, as citizens, want to see ourselves represented in one party or another, or more precisely in the Kurultai, we need to go into that party. Most likely, we will also need to change its political discourse and its program from within in order to form the agenda that matters to citizens,” Aktayev told the press on Aug. 25.

Zhusupov said polling also showed expectations about deputies’ professional backgrounds. In one survey, approximately 30% of respondents favored a legal background, while others emphasized public-service experience, communication skills and strong professional and social reputations.

Election ends, inter-election competition begins

For political parties, experts said the more challenging phase begins after the campaign. According to Zhusupov, their performance would depend largely on what they do between elections.

“The parties that are working now and will continue working should not operate from one campaign to another. The inter-election cycle is very important,” said the expert.

“This is when they can promote not simply their recognition, but their ideology. Taking into account the mistakes that were made, many parties simply need to reconsider their ideology. If you are trying to build a more or less sizable faction in Parliament, you need to work with much broader electoral niches and expand them in order to receive more votes,” he said.

Abishev said the focus would now shift from electoral competition to legislative work.

“After the distribution of mandates and the annual address, the real work will begin. Inside the chamber, party division is no longer felt as strongly. Laws need to be adopted, and the best ideas from all programs need to be put into practice. It is important that new faces have the opportunity to make their contribution,” he wrote.

EU notes election process, urges further reforms

Anouar El Anouni, spokesperson for EU foreign affairs and security policy, said the European Union acknowledged Kazakhstan’s efforts to organize the election in a “well-prepared and orderly manner” despite the short period between calling and holding the vote.

“The EU strongly encourages Kazakhstan to continue its work on democratic reforms, and reaffirms its commitment to supporting Kazakhstan’s reform agenda, including in the areas of human rights, rule of law, and democratic governance. We stand ready to continue our cooperation with Kazakhstan to further strengthen our strategic partnership, based on shared values and mutual respect,” said El Anouni.

World.title: Tokayev to Convene First Session of Kazakhstan’s Kurultai on Aug. 28
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has signed a decree convening the first session of Kazakhstan’s elected Kurultai, the country’s new unicameral legislature, for Aug. 28 at 11 a.m., according to the Akorda press service.

The session will mark the start of work for the 145-member Kurultai, established under Kazakhstan’s new Constitution, which took effect on July 1.

The first parliamentary election under the new constitutional system was held on Aug. 23. According to the final results, five political parties cleared the statutory 5% threshold required to secure seats in the Kurultai.

The Adilet Party secured the largest share of the vote and will hold 110 seats. The Auyl People’s Democratic Patriotic Party will have 10 seats, while Respublica will hold nine seats. The Aq Zhol Democratic Party and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party will each have eight seats.

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan received 285,395 votes, or 3.11%, while the Baytaq Green Party received 97,751 votes, or 1.07%, falling below the 5% threshold. A total of 2.51% of voters selected the “against all” option.

The Aug. 23 election was the first parliamentary election conducted under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional framework. The Kurultai replaced the country’s former bicameral Parliament and consists of 145 deputies elected through proportional representation from party lists in a single nationwide constituency.

The opening of the first session will formally launch the new legislature’s work and mark the next stage in implementing the institutional changes introduced by the new Constitution.

World.title: Payment Without Plastic: How Smartphones Are Reshaping Kazakhstan’s Cashless Economy
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s cashless economy is entering a new stage as virtual cards become more common among active users and QR payments overtake bank cards at point-of-sale terminals. The shift suggests that digitalization is no longer simply about replacing cash with cards, but increasingly about replacing the physical card itself with a smartphone-based payment interface.

According to payment card statistics updated by the National Bank on July 31, Kazakhstan had 83.6 million payment cards in circulation as of July 1. However, only 41.9 million cards were actively used, or about half of the total. Among active cards, virtual cards accounted for 53%, compared with 47% for physical cards. That means that, among cards that are actually being used, digital versions have already overtaken plastic.

The way consumers pay at retail outlets is changing at the same time. During the first half of 2026, QR payments accounted for 58% of transactions conducted through point-of-sale infrastructure, compared with 42% for bank cards. QR payments also accounted for 53% of transaction value, compared with 47% for card payments. The number of QR transactions was 38% higher than card transactions through POS terminals, while their total value was 13% higher.

On average, Kazakh citizens made around 11 million QR payments worth 57.3 billion tenge (US$122 million) every day during the first half of the year. Card payments through POS terminals averaged about eight million transactions worth 50.8 billion tenge (US$108 million) per day. The difference is particularly visible in the average transaction size. A QR payment averaged 5,200 tenge (US$11), compared with 6,400 tenge (US$14) for a card payment through a POS terminal, suggesting QR is becoming especially prominent for routine, lower-value purchases.

From cashless to cardless

The broader trend is visible in the National Bank’s payment statistics. In June 2026, internet and mobile banking accounted for 79.5% of non-cash transactions by number and 90.2% by value. In the first half of 2026, Kazakhstan recorded around 7.1 billion cashless transactions worth 92.1 trillion tenge — data that points to the growing role of digital channels in everyday payments.

According to Ruslan Sultanov, author of Tengenomika, an analytical channel covering Kazakhstan’s macroeconomy, the tenge exchange rate and broader economic issues, the figures mark a new stage in the country’s payment digitalization.

“Earlier, the key change was the shift from cash to bank cards. Now the cashless payment itself is changing, as the physical payment instrument increasingly gives way to a digital interface,” Sultanov said.

For banks, this also changes the logic of competition. Kazakhstan has 83.6 million cards in circulation, but only about half are actively used. As Sultanov notes, the number of cards issued therefore says less about a bank’s relationship with its customers than which banking product becomes a customer’s primary one, which application they use for everyday transactions and where their payment activity is concentrated. Virtual cards can further lower the barrier to competition. Customers no longer necessarily need a physical card to use a banking product. This makes it easier to hold products from several banks, while competition increasingly moves from the physical wallet into the smartphone.

Competition moves to the smartphone

The shift also changes the infrastructure businesses use to accept cashless payments. The traditional combination of a plastic card and POS terminal is no longer the only familiar interface for a digital payment. For consumers, the change is even more visible: the bank account remains, and the card can still exist as a payment instrument, but the physical card is increasingly unnecessary at the moment of purchase.

The trend is also consistent with Kazakhstan’s broader push to build a more interoperable digital financial system. In July 2026, the country launched the nationwide Interbank Mobile Payment System, allowing customers of participating banks to make transfers by phone number and pay through a single interoperable QR code regardless of which bank they and the merchant use.

What QR means for everyday payments

The growth of QR payments does not mean bank cards are disappearing. Instead, it shows that the payment process is becoming increasingly detached from the physical card. For consumers, the change may be barely noticeable: the money remains in a bank account, while the smartphone becomes the interface through which they access and spend it. For merchants, meanwhile, QR payments provide an alternative to the traditional card-and-POS model.

Sultanov also cautions that the latest figures should not be interpreted as a complete replacement of card payments by QR. Rather, they point to a broader structural shift in which the payment itself is becoming less dependent on a physical carrier.

For banks, the main asset is increasingly the digital contact with the customer, the application through which people access their money, choose how to pay and conduct everyday transactions. Kazakhstan’s payment market is therefore moving beyond the familiar idea of a “cashless economy.” The more significant transformation may be toward a cardless economy, where the payment instrument remains digital, and the physical card becomes optional.

World.title: Why Kazakhstan’s Aviation Hub Ambitions Could Generate More Than Transit Revenue
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is investing heavily in airports, cargo infrastructure and international connectivity. But the bigger economic question is whether a growing aviation network can generate more than transit income – and become a platform for logistics, exports and higher-value economic activity.

Building the infrastructure for a regional hub

The government is upgrading aviation infrastructure as part of efforts to strengthen Kazakhstan’s role in the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or the Middle Corridor, and as a major Eurasian transit hub. From January to July, the country’s airports handled 102,500 tons of cargo, up 10% year on year. Almaty accounted for 66,100 tons, or more than 64% of the total.

Passenger traffic is also growing. In January-June, Kazakhstan’s airlines carried 7.4 million passengers, up 2.6% compared with the same period last year.

The country is also expanding passenger infrastructure. New terminals in Almaty, Kyzylorda and Shymkent have increased combined annual capacity from 3.5 million to 23 million passengers. Three new airports are being built in the resort areas of Katon-Karagay, Zaisan and Kenderli, with completion planned by the end of this year.

International connectivity is expanding alongside this infrastructure. Under the open skies regime, Kazakhstan now has 135 international routes connecting it with 30 countries. Cargo operators including Cargolux and Cathay Pacific Cargo have expanded operations through Astana, strengthening the country’s position in international freight networks.

Infrastructure alone is not enough

But infrastructure and rising traffic alone do not automatically create a successful aviation hub.

As Civil Aviation Committee Chair Saltanat Tompiyeva told The Astana Times in March, “the long-term sustainability of a hub depends on trust in the system: trust in safety, regulation and predictable rules.” She identified Kazakhstan’s high level of flight safety as a key competitive advantage.

International audits cited by the committee show 82% effective implementation of aviation safety oversight standards and 95.7% compliance with aviation security standards. These institutional conditions matter because airlines and cargo operators need more than runways and terminals. They need predictable regulation, reliable operations and confidence that a transit point can function consistently over time.

From transit flows to domestic value creation

The economic opportunity, however, extends beyond aviation itself.

Financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov notes that an aviation hub should be understood as a broader economic system, linking airports with roads, railways, warehouses and industries that can add value to goods before they reach export markets.

“The aviation hub is not simply the transportation of someone else’s cargo through Kazakhstan with refueling,” he told The Astana Times, stressing that the main goal should be to create additional value domestically.

For example, agricultural and food products could be processed, packaged or prepared for export near airports, allowing Kazakhstan to capture more of the value generated along the supply chain rather than simply moving foreign goods through the country.

The next test: economic integration

The next stage, therefore, is integration. New terminals, runways and cargo facilities provide the physical foundation, while safety and predictable regulation provide the institutional one. The larger economic payoff will depend on whether these assets attract logistics companies, processors, exporters and related services.

The key indicator will not only be how many passengers and tons of cargo Kazakhstan handles, but how much additional value that traffic creates.

If aviation can be integrated with rail, roads, logistics and domestic production, Kazakhstan’s emerging hubs could evolve from transit facilities into engines of export growth and broader economic development.

World.title: Kazakhstan Aims for 5% Growth, Expert Says Productive Capacity Is Key
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s government has approved the Forecast of Socio-Economic Development and draft national budget for 2027-2029, targeting annual economic growth of more than 5% through 2029 while reducing the budget deficit to 0.4% of GDP. Financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov says the targets are achievable, but only if Kazakhstan expands its productive capacity through greater electricity generation, industrial development and deeper processing.

Under the baseline scenario, real GDP growth is projected to average more than 5% annually, while the national budget deficit is expected to decline from 2.3% of GDP in 2027 to 0.4% in 2029. Inflation is projected at 7.5-9.5% in 2027, before moderating to 6-8% in 2028-2029.

Kazakhstan’s economy grew by 4.1% in January-July, while the government expects full-year GDP growth of at least 5%. The framework focuses on expanding non-oil sectors, improving public spending efficiency and maintaining macroeconomic stability.

Non-oil sectors to drive growth

The government expects manufacturing, agriculture, construction and services to provide the main contribution to growth.

Nominal GDP is projected to increase from 199.3 trillion tenge (US$436.2 billion) in 2027 to 245 trillion tenge (US$536.3 billion) in 2029. Manufacturing is expected to outpace mining, led by metallurgy, machinery, construction materials, chemicals and food production.

Agriculture is forecast to grow by at least 5% annually, while construction growth is projected to rise from 16% in 2027 to 17.3% in 2029. Transport and warehousing and information and communications are expected to grow by 10.4% and 9.2%, respectively.

Inflation remains an important assumption

The projected inflation path is an important part of the macroeconomic framework. Inflation is expected to remain relatively high in 2027 before declining in the following two years.

Its trajectory will affect household purchasing power, business costs, investment decisions and the government’s fiscal position. Keeping inflation on the projected path will also affect the sustainability of planned economic growth.

Reducing the deficit while maintaining investment

The government projects budget revenues of 19.9 trillion tenge (US$43.5 billion) in 2027, rising to 23.4 trillion tenge (US$51.2 billion) in 2029. Expenditures are planned at 30.2 trillion tenge (US$66.1 billion) in 2027, 29.4 trillion tenge (US$64.3 billion) in 2028 and 29.6 trillion tenge (US$64.8 billion) in 2029.

The non-oil deficit is expected to decline from 5.3% of GDP to 2.5% over the same period.

At the same time, the 2027 budget allocates 10.5 trillion tenge (US$23 billion) to the social sector and 3.8 trillion tenge (US$8.3 billion) to the real economy. Targeted transfers from the National Fund will provide 2 trillion tenge (US$4.3 billion) in 2027 and 1.5 trillion tenge (US$3.2 billion) annually in 2028-2029 for critical infrastructure and nationwide projects.

Can Kazakhstan deliver growth while tightening its budget?

The government’s targets raise a broader question: can Kazakhstan sustain annual GDP growth of more than 5% while reducing the budget deficit to 0.4% of GDP by 2029?

According to financial analyst Rassul Rysmambetov, the target is realistic, but achieving it will require increasing the economy’s productive capacity.

“In general, it is realistic. I would say a range of 4.5-5.5% is achievable. By then, we need to increase our economy’s potential by around 1.5%, meaning our productive capacity. This would require somewhat greater electricity generation, more factories and better processing. These are the key factors: productive capacity.

Right now, for example, you could build all the roads in Kazakhstan and increase GDP by 15%, but that would cost $20 billion, and this is not sustainable. GDP should grow healthily in line with the economy’s potential, not at any cost, but gradually. So, overall, 5% growth in 2029 is quite realistic,” he told The Astana Times.

Rysmambetov’s assessment points to productive capacity as a key condition for sustaining growth. Additional electricity generation, industrial capacity and deeper processing could allow the economy to expand without relying excessively on higher government spending.

This makes the composition of investment as important as its volume. Infrastructure spending can support growth by removing constraints on businesses and improving connectivity, but its longer-term effect will depend on whether investment creates new productive capacity and supports private-sector activity.

Indicators to watch

The government expects goods exports to rise from $82.8 billion in 2027 to $88.5 billion in 2029, while the National Fund’s foreign-currency assets are projected to increase from $65.2 billion to $70.6 billion.

Progress will depend on whether economic growth, inflation, budget revenues and productivity develop in line with the forecast while infrastructure and social investment are maintained.

Non-oil sector growth, private investment, export performance, inflation, tax revenues and the pace of deficit reduction will provide key indicators of how closely actual outcomes follow the 2027-2029 framework.

World.title: State Visit of King Philippe to Kazakhstan: Historic First and Mirror of Strategic Partnership between Brussels and Astana
World.content:
This fall, King Philippe of Belgium will pay his first-ever state visit to Kazakhstan, at the invitation of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. It will be the first time in history that a Belgian sovereign travels on an official visit to the Central Asian country since diplomatic relations were established in 1992.

An unprecedented state visit

The upcoming state visit of King Philippe is set to be a landmark in relations between the two countries. According to the Kazakh authorities, it will be the first state visit by a Belgian monarch to Kazakhstan since diplomatic relations were established in 1992. The visit was announced during the meeting between President Tokayev and Prime Minister Bart De Wever in Brussels in June 2026, where the Kazakh head of state stressed that he attached “exceptional importance” to the King’s forthcoming visit.

On Aug. 8, King Philippe confirmed his intention in a message to President Tokayev, replying to the latter’s greetings on the occasion of Belgium’s National Day (July 21). The sovereign expressed his gratitude and said he was “looking forward” to his state visit to Astana later in the year.

Long before ascending the throne, King Philippe already knew Kazakhstan well. As Crown Prince, he visited the country on three occasions — in 2002, 2009 and 2010 — leading economic missions. When Kazakhstan’s Ambassador Roman Vassilenko presented his credentials at Laeken Palace in September 2025, the King warmly recalled “the most memorable impressions” he retained of the country, its culture and its development potential. This personal experience lends a special dimension to the visit: more than a protocol event, it reflects a shared will to deepen an already solid partnership and give it fresh momentum.

Thirty-four years of diplomatic relations

Belgium recognized Kazakhstan’s independence on Dec. 31, 1991, and diplomatic relations were formally established on Aug. 25, 1992. Kazakhstan opened its embassy in Brussels in 1993, while Belgium established its embassy in Astana in 2006, further structuring bilateral relations and facilitating political and economic dialogue at all levels.

Under President Nursultan Nazarbayev, high-level contacts multiplied: the first president paid nine official and working visits to Belgium between 1993 and 2018. In December 2006, he received Belgium’s highest distinction, the Grand Cordon of the Order of Leopold, from King Albert II. In 2010, a monument dedicated to the victims of nuclear testing — inspired by the “Stronger than Death” memorial in Semei — was inaugurated in Ypres, a city emblematic of the memory of both World Wars.

The dialogue has deepened further in recent years. In June 2026, President Tokayev’s visit to Brussels marked a new milestone: beyond his meeting with Prime Minister De Wever, a business forum produced around 30 commercial agreements worth roughly 10 billion euros with European companies. Belgium’s Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot separately received his Kazakh counterpart at the Egmont Palace, marking 20 years of the Belgian embassy in Astana.

Kazakhstan: Belgium’s key partner in Central Asia

Kazakhstan stands as Belgium’s primary economic and commercial partner in Central Asia. Historically, it hosted Belgium’s first embassy in the region, reflecting its strategic importance. Today it accounts for the majority of Belgian trade in the region and plays a pivotal role in regional logistics, especially through the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, also known as the Middle Corridor.

A growing trade relationship

According to Kazinform, bilateral trade turnover reached approximately $523.7 million in 2023 — a 1.7% increase from 2022. Kazakhstan exported goods worth $220.7 million to Belgium, while imports from Belgium stood at $303 million. In the same year, Belgian foreign direct investment in Kazakhstan exceeded $1 billion, underscoring strong investor confidence. Belgium’s Foreign Ministry reported that trade subsequently surpassed 750 million euros in 2025.

Investment and business framework

Belgium ranks among the top ten European investors in Kazakhstan, with around 110 Belgian companies operating in the country across logistics, agri-food, renewable energy, green technologies, infrastructure and engineering, as well as metallurgy, petrochemicals, agri-tech and the processing of critical raw materials — an area of increasing importance for Europe’s strategic autonomy. The Benelux Chamber of Commerce in Kazakhstan plays a crucial role in facilitating business ties and promoting two-way investment.

“More than 110 companies with Belgian capital are operating successfully in Kazakhstan, reflecting our shared commitment to strengthening mutually beneficial cooperation,” Tokayev said.

On March 14, 2025, the Belgian Ministry of Foreign Affairs hosted the Team Belgium Global Gateway roundtable, highlighting investment opportunities in Central Asia with a strong focus on Kazakhstan. Organised with AWEX, Flanders Investment & Trade (FIT) and hub.brussels, it gathered more than 20 major Belgian companies. Then Belgium’s Ambassador to Kazakhstan Henri Vantieghem highlighted opportunities in transport, logistics and telecommunications infrastructure.

Kazakhstan actively promotes foreign investment through tax benefits, administrative facilitation and support from the national agency Kazakh Invest. The Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), which hosts over 3,500 registered companies, offers an advanced legal and financial framework based on international standards. Belgian companies have been invited to take part in large-scale projects such as the development of Alatau city, the expansion of the Middle Corridor, and renewable-energy production aimed at export to the European Union.

The Middle Corridor: a shared strategic stake

Kazakhstan’s position along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route enhances its attractiveness as a crucial partner for Europe–Asia connectivity. Over six years, freight volumes on the corridor increased fivefold, from 0.8 to 4.1 million tons per year, with a stated target of 10 million tons. For Belgium and its ports, the corridor offers a major logistics alternative towards Asia; for Kazakhstan, it cements its status as a hub between China, Türkiye, the Middle East and Europe.

Belgium: Kazakhstan’s gateway to Europe

Reciprocally, Belgium holds particular importance for Astana. As host of the EU institutions and NATO, Brussels is an indispensable political gateway for a country seeking to diversify its partnerships and strengthen ties with the West. President Tokayev has described Belgium as “one of Kazakhstan’s key partners within the European Union.”

This European dimension is reinforced by the EU’s growing strategic interest in Central Asia, illustrated by the Samarkand summit of April 2025 and a 12 billion euro Global Gateway investment plan for the region. Belgium is fully part of this dynamic: it is preparing to open its second embassy in the region, in Tashkent, confirming a long-term commitment to Central Asia.

Technology, academia and culture

Beyond trade, relations are expanding into technological, academic and cultural domains. Belgium’s advanced aerospace industry — including companies such as Aerospacelab — has attracted growing interest from Kazakhstan, particularly in satellite production and space cooperation. Academic collaboration is also gaining momentum: discussions between Ambassador Vassilenko and Ghent University have focused on joint research, PhD co-supervision and cooperation in biotechnology, agricultural sciences, artificial intelligence and digitalization.

Cultural diplomacy continues to strengthen people-to-people ties. Events such as the Shanyraq Fest in Brussels have showcased Kazakhstan’s cultural heritage, while tourism initiatives have connected Kazakh operators with Belgian travel companies, boosting the country’s visibility in the Benelux market.

Sport, too, is a common language: each spring the Astana cycling team is part of the Belgian sporting landscape, and in August 2026, the Kazakh embassy marked 34 years of relations with a bicycle ride starting from the Atomium. In September 2025, a football match in Brussels between the Kazakh and Belgian national teams had already exemplified this “sports diplomacy” that brings the two peoples closer together. The players and staff of Sporting Anderlecht had to endure a nine-and-a-half-hour flight to reach Almaty and play against the Kazakh team Kairat. Not to mention that last year, Belgium also hosted the Belgium-Kazakhstan match at the Anderlecht stadium.

Strategic alignment on global issues

Belgium and Kazakhstan also cooperate on key global challenges, including nuclear non-proliferation and resource security. Kazakhstan plays a vital role as a major supplier of uranium and critical raw materials to the European Union, reinforcing its strategic relevance. Both countries share a growing interest in international security, regional stability and multilateral cooperation, notably within the United Nations framework.

Outlook: from a symbolic visit to a lasting partnership

Recent discussions between officials have identified several priority sectors for the future: transport and connectivity, critical raw materials, petrochemicals, agriculture, manufacturing, digital transformation, artificial intelligence and financial services — alongside academic and scientific cooperation between universities, research centres and technology companies.

Through this state visit, Astana and Brussels send a clear message: Belgian–Kazakh relations are entering a new phase. Belgium’s role as host of the EU institutions gives it unique importance in Kazakhstan’s European strategy, while Kazakhstan leverages Brussels as a platform to deepen its ties with the Union. As high-level visits, economic cooperation and institutional partnerships intensify, the relationship is maturing into a forward-looking strategic partnership — one that mirrors broader shifts in Europe’s engagement with Central Asia and the growing importance of connectivity, sustainability and geopolitical balance. King Philippe’s first state visit could become a defining milestone, opening the way to even more ambitious cooperation in the years ahead.

Derya Soysal is a journalist & researcher specialising in Central Asia.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Reintroduced Tigress Umit Hunts Her First Prey in Kazakhstan’s Ile-Balkhash Reserve
World.content:
ASTANA – Tigress Umit, released into Kazakhstan’s Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve on July 31 as part of the country’s tiger reintroduction program, is showing positive signs of adapting to the wild, Anuarbek Bermagambetov, head of the Department of Hunting Management and Wildlife, said on the Jibek Joly TV channel on Aug. 24.

More than 70 years after tigers disappeared from Kazakhstan, the predator has returned as part of a long-term reintroduction effort.

Umit’s first recorded prey was a wolf, followed several days later by a wild boar. According to Bermagambetov, her hunting behavior in the first 10 days suggests she is adapting well to her new environment.

Her movements are monitored around the clock with a GPS tracker that transmits her location and direction of travel every 12 hours. Specialists still need to conduct field visits to identify the prey species she catches, as GPS data alone cannot determine this.

Strict monitoring and safety measures

The tigress is currently staying within the reserve’s designated green zone, which covers her main habitat and hunting grounds and poses no immediate threat to nearby settlements.

The reserve covers more than 450,000 hectares, and unauthorized access is prohibited.

The area around Umit has been divided into green, yellow and red zones. If she moves towards the yellow zone, a specially formed conflict-management team will begin monitoring the situation. The team is equipped with three vehicles, a snowmobile, an ATV, night-vision devices, a satellite phone and Starlink.

If Umit enters the red zone, authorities will issue an alert and notify residents of nearby settlements through mobile warnings.

Specialists will initially attempt to drive the tiger back into the green zone using sound and, if necessary, pyrotechnic devices. Temporary sedation is also available as a last resort.

Reintroduction program underway since 2010

Kazakhstan’s tiger reintroduction program has been underway since 2010. The project has included establishing the Ile-Balkhash reserve, restoring its wildlife population and developing the infrastructure needed to support the species’ return.

Two tigers, Bogdan and Puma, were previously brought from the Netherlands in 2024, while Russia transferred four more tigers to Kazakhstan this year. Umit is one of the four animals Russia sent under a bilateral agreement.

Before her release, specialists assessed the reserve’s food base. The area is home to potential tiger prey, including kulan, wild boar, roe deer and Bukhara deer.

Authorities say Umit’s ability to hunt and feed independently is an encouraging early sign that the tigress is adapting to life in the wild.

Officials have also urged the public not to rely on unverified social media footage. Videos of Bogdan and Puma have previously been falsely circulated as footage of Umit, highlighting the growing problem of AI-generated and misleading wildlife content online.

World.title: Adilet Wins Kurultai Elections with 71.17% of Vote
World.content:
ASTANA – The Adilet party secured a landslide victory in Kazakhstan’s Kurultai elections, winning 71.17% of the vote and 110 seats, according to the final results announced by the Central Election Commission (CEC) on Aug. 25.

The electoral rolls included 12,623,289 voters, and 9,351,539 cast ballots. Voter turnout stood at 74.08%.

Adilet received 6,528,948 votes (71.17%) and secured 110 seats in the Kurultai. The Auyl People’s Democratic Patriotic Party won 574,621 votes (6.26%) and 10 seats, while Respublica received 509,631 votes (5.56%) and secured nine seats.

The Aq Zhol Democratic Party garnered 478,083 votes (5.21%) and eight seats. The Nationwide Social Democratic Party received 469,058 votes (5.11%) and also secured eight seats.

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan received 285,395 votes (3.11%), while the Baytaq Green Party garnered 97,751 votes (1.07%). Both parties failed to clear the statutory 5% electoral threshold.

A total of 2.51% of voters selected the “against all” option.

Under Kazakhstan’s election legislation, political parties must secure at least 5% of the vote to qualify for seats in the Kurultai. Five parties crossed the threshold based on the final results.

The Aug. 23 election was the first parliamentary election held under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional system. The 145-member Kurultai replaced the country’s former bicameral Parliament under the Constitution that took effect July 1.

World.title: Azerbaijan confiscates cryptocurrency in favour of state for first time
World.content:
Cryptocurrency confiscated in Azerbaijan

The Yasamal District Court in Baku has sentenced two people arrested by the State Security Service, B.H.R. and I.R.F., and ordered the confiscation by the state of virtual assets identified as the proceeds or subject of the crime.

Details of the case

The defendants were found guilty under Article 206-1.3 of the Criminal Code. The article provides for criminal liability for organising the illegal covert transfer of particularly large sums of money out of Azerbaijan or into the country using set-offs and other forms of settlement.

According to the court’s ruling:

B.H.R. received a two-year-and-five-month restriction of liberty and a fine of 3,623,568 manats (about $2.13 million);

received a two-year-and-five-month restriction of liberty and a fine of (about $2.13 million); I.R.F. received a three-year restriction of liberty and a fine of 31,399,709 manats (about $18.47 million).

The court also ordered the state to confiscate 830 units of cryptocurrency held in an account on the international virtual-asset platform Binance. Investigators had frozen the assets during the preliminary investigation.

Official reports do not specify which cryptocurrency was involved, whether Bitcoin, Ethereum or another asset.

Legal basis

Under Article 99-1 of the Criminal Code, special confiscation involves the compulsory and free transfer to the state of tools and means used to commit a crime, as well as property obtained through criminal activity.

The Law on Combating the Legalisation of Property Obtained through Crime and the Financing of Terrorism also classifies virtual assets as property obtained through criminal activity.

The court has therefore applied the same legal regime to digital assets as it does to physical property for the first time in practice.

Context and significance

In 2025, the State Security Service had already secured a court order to freeze cryptocurrency in a similar criminal case. At the time, Baku’s Sabail District Court ordered the assets to be frozen. On 24 August, the process moved to the next stage: the authorities confiscated the assets.

Azerbaijan does not yet have a separate law governing virtual assets. The Central Bank previously said it expected the relevant draft law to be adopted by the end of 2026. Against this backdrop, the court ruling shows how authorities are addressing the existing legal gap in practice and could set a precedent for future regulation.

Experts note that international exchanges generally comply with court orders promptly. However, the authorities have not yet disclosed what will happen to the confiscated assets, including whether they could be sold at auction, transferred to state reserves or used in another way.

The case marks a new stage in Azerbaijan’s fight against digital crime and expands law enforcement agencies’ ability to track and confiscate virtual assets. At the same time, it highlights the real risks faced by people operating in the unregulated cryptocurrency market.
