World.title: Uzbekneftegaz, China Eximbank deepen cooperation on energy financing
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. Uzbekistan’s state-owned oil and gas company Uzbekneftegaz and representatives of China Eximbank discussed financing opportunities for prospective energy projects as the sides seek to deepen financial and strategic cooperation.

This was reflected in the statement by the Uzbekneftgaz.

The meeting focused on financing promising projects, expanding strategic partnership and strengthening mutually beneficial cooperation in Uzbekistan’s energy sector, Uzbekneftegaz said.

China Eximbank is among the company’s key institutional partners in expanding ties with international financial institutions and export credit agencies, according to the statement.

During the talks, the sides reviewed potential financing mechanisms for prospective projects and discussed priority areas for financial cooperation. They also considered adapting commercial terms to current market conditions.

Uzbekneftegaz expressed its readiness to continue cooperation with China Eximbank on mutually acceptable terms.

“Uzbekneftegaz is ready to continue cooperation with China Eximbank on mutually acceptable terms,” the company said.

The parties also exchanged views on improving financing mechanisms, expanding investment cooperation and supporting practical projects in the energy sector.

The discussions underscore the role of export-credit financing in supporting Uzbekistan’s energy development as the country seeks to attract additional investment and strengthen cooperation with international financial institutions.

For Uzbekneftegaz, deeper cooperation with China Eximbank could provide additional financing opportunities for projects while helping diversify the company’s sources of external funding.

The latest talks are part of Uzbekistan’s broader efforts to expand economic and financial ties with China and mobilize financing for strategic sectors, including energy and infrastructure.

World.title: More than 140 investors showed interest in Ziraat Bank Azerbaijan bonds – PASHA Capital
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. The successful placement of bonds issued by Ziraat Bank Azerbaijan is an important event for the bank, the country’s capital market, its participants and investment companies, Trend’s correspondent reports.

PASHA Capital Chief Executive Officer Isi Mustafayev said this at the “Opening Bell” ceremony marking the admission of Ziraat Bank Azerbaijan bonds to trading on the Baku Stock Exchange.

According to him, projects of this kind not only create new financial instruments in the market but also make them available to a broader range of investors.

“This is Ziraat Bank Azerbaijan’s first experience in the capital markets. I congratulate the Ziraat Bank team on this occasion. I hope that, alongside traditional financing channels, the bank will also choose capital markets as one of its key sources of financing,” Mustafayev said.

He noted that PASHA Capital’s main goal is to create more financial instruments in the market and increase investors’ interest in and confidence in the capital market.

“More than 140 investors have already participated in the placement of these bonds. One of the main reasons is that, in addition to traditional channels, the bond placement was also carried out through an electronic platform. Conducting the process through an electronic platform enabled a broader range of investors and members of the public to participate,” the CEO said.

Mustafayev said the same approach had previously been used in the placement of PASHA Bank shares and bonds.

“This approach provided access to a broader audience and ensured more active participation by investors. In our upcoming projects, we also aim to ensure more active participation by the public in these processes,” he added.

The PASHA Capital CEO thanked the teams of Ziraat Bank, PASHA Capital and the Baku Stock Exchange, as well as everyone involved in the process.

“Although this process is a beginning for Ziraat Bank, I hope it will continue and that the bank will issue new bonds in the future,” Mustafayev said.

World.title: Man convicted for $15k spend on stolen credit cards 'likely' from dark web
World.content:
A man in South Australia's Riverland has been convicted and jailed after purchasing almost $16,000 worth of Bunnings gift cards and merchandise, using stolen credit cards "likely" obtained from the dark web.

Aijaypal Tim Sanghera, 38, appeared via video link at the Berri Magistrates Court and pleaded guilty to 12 counts of dishonest dealing with property, one count of possession of a prohibited weapon and one count of possession of a prescription drug.

The court heard Sanghera used stolen credit card information to make 11 click and collect orders at several Bunnings stores for 98 items.

Police prosecutors told the court the orders, placed over a five-week period between April and May 2026, were purchased from stores in Berri, Parafield Gardens and Edwardstown.

Of the 98 items purchased, 20 were $500 Bunnings gift cards, which were all linked to Sanghera's Bunnings PowerPass account.

"As a result, it's not the individual card holders that are at a loss because those credit card companies have reversed the transaction," police prosecutors told the court.

"The total loss to Bunnings on those 11 transactions [was] $15,899.65."

The court heard Sanghera had endured a difficult upbringing and may suffer from borderline personality disorder. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

The court heard the police investigation suggested Sanghera had obtained "a bulk of personal data likely from the dark web of stolen credit cards".

Police prosecutors said some of the items purchased with the cards were found during a search of Sanghera's residence in Bookpurnong on June 10 this year, making the total uncompensated loss for Bunnings $14,592.

They told the court less than a gram of methamphetamine, three ice pipes and a dagger were also found.

Defence lawyer Craig Caldicott told the court Sanghera had a difficult upbringing, witnessing his father's suicide by poisoning and was the victim of sexual abuse as a teenager, which had fuelled a drug addiction.

Mr Caldicott also told the court a lengthy prison sentence would not be beneficial, arguing it did not address the root of the problem.

"The problem with incarceration, it doesn't address the issues of drug addiction," he said.

Senghara was sentenced to four months prison and a two month good behaviour bond for his offending.

'Protecting the community is paramount'

Magistrate Jay Pandya described Sanghera's offending as "deliberate and relentless", and "fuelled and motivated to raise funds to continue to be able to obtain drugs and use drugs".

She said sentencing had to reflect the seriousness of the offending.

"The most important part of sentencing is protection of the community," Magistrate Pandya told the court.

"These are ordinary people in the community, who are impacted by people like yourself, who are fuelled and motivated to commit crimes for their own advantage and to fund illegal habits.

" Your offending was not simple — it involved a number of steps. "

Magistrate Pandya accepted Sanghera's guilty plea.

"You have been clear about taking responsibility and you have been clear about your remorse," she said.

World.title: Division erupts within NT government as MLAs clash in parliament over VAD
World.content:
Division within the Northern Territory government has erupted in parliament, with politicians clashing during debate over long-awaited voluntary assisted dying (VAD) legislation.

The Country Liberal Party's (CLP) VAD bill was being debated into the night on Tuesday, when NT government backbencher Tanzil Rahman accused his colleagues of being inauthentic and of deliberately mischaracterising the VAD debate.

Dr Rahman said the claimed behaviour "genuinely upsets me", describing the bill put forward by the CLP as "a very narrow VAD act, that will take us 10 years back in standard".

The first-term MLA, who chaired a parliamentary inquiry into VAD, singled out NT Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby, who introduced the bill.

Marie-Clare Boothby introduced the VAD bill. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Ms Boothby has strongly defended the bill's "safeguards", which include a clause that will restrict VAD access to people with 12 months or less to live.

A controversial so-called doctor gag clause is also included, meaning medical professionals will not be able to initiate VAD discussions with terminally ill patients.

Dr Rahman has flagged that on Thursday he will move amendments to remove both clauses, which go against the recommendations made by the inquiry he chaired.

Another proposed amendment from Dr Rahman would prevent care facilities from refusing to provide information about VAD in residential settings.

Last night, he told NT parliament an individual's "terminality" — how sick they are, and therefore how likely they are to qualify for the 12-month window — was not always clear.

Tanzil Rahman plans to move amendments to the NT government's VAD bill. (Supplied: Department of Legislative Assembly)

"Today, the attorney-general said, 'I make no apologies for the safeguards I put in place and similarly, the 12-month prognosis period … is so important. Without it, terminality is subjective and we just can't have that'," Dr Rahman said.

"Respectfully, I also can't make any apologies for the fact that I have to challenge that.

" Because the fact is, terminality is completely subjective and everybody knows it. "

Deputy Chief Minister Gerard Maley immediately criticised Dr Rahman's contribution to the debate, backing in the 12-month timeframe.

CLP fielding VAD amendments A week out from a conscience vote on voluntary assisted dying in the NT, several CLP backbenchers have proposed amendments to the bill.

"I think [Dr Rahman] unfairly attacked the attorney-general, saying that he couldn't support [the 12-month timeframe], because I think his words were it was 'subjective', '12 months'," he said.

"He put a proposal in his amendments, which I'll just read one of the lines: 'The person is approaching the end of the person's life' — that's subjective!

"So he's replacing, in his view, a 'subjective' sentence with another subjective [sentence].

" So it really shoots his own argument in the foot. "

Mr Maley said Dr Rahman's "approach has gone all wrong".

"I wasn't going to speak about his amendments because I'm not going to support them, but I think his argument was just clearly wrong," he said.

"And having a go at the attorney-general using that word' subjective' and he's replaced it with three times that."

During his speech, Mr Maley criticised MLAs who had spoken to media publicly on the topic, saying the VAD issues were "above media hits".

Member for Fannie Bay, Laurie Zio, is among the NT politicians who have spoken to the media about VAD. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

It came after Dr Rahman and fellow government backbencher Laurie Zio — who is supportive of the amendments — both did interviews about VAD before the bill returned to parliament for debate.

"I know some people in the parliament have gone out in the media and done all sorts of things about it, but my view is above that," Mr Maley said.

"This is about a very delicate subject that needs to be treated with dignity.

"This is not about personal profiles or legacies … this is about getting things right for Territorians."

Debate on VAD has played out inside NT Parliament House this week. (ABC News: Michael Parfitt)

The amendments are unlikely to pass when a conscience vote is held on Thursday, with just six MLAs in the 25-seat parliament saying on Tuesday they would definitely support changes to the bill.

Opposition Leader Selena Uibo is also planning to move similar amendments to Dr Rahman, but it is currently unclear how many Labor MLAs will support them.

The NT was the first Australian jurisdiction to legalise voluntary assisted dying in 1995, but the laws were overturned by the Commonwealth in 1997.

The Territory did not regain the power to legislate its own VAD laws until 2022.

World.title: Potential insolvent trading probe after modular builder's closure
World.content:
The WA Consumer Protection Commissioner is calling on clients of a modular home building company which abruptly closed last week to lodge formal complaints so it can investigate further.

Bella Modular, a Perth-based manufacturer of transportable granny flats and home office buildings, wrote to all its customers on August 19 to say it would not be able to complete their outstanding projects.

In an email sent to clients last week, the company said, "Due to unforeseen and significant financial difficulties, Bella Modular is unable to complete your project directly."

The letter said a new manufacturer had agreed to take over existing contracts and complete the projects but did not provide the new firm's details.

Bella Modular has already closed its premises in Hopeland on Perth's southern fringe.

Builder's sudden closure A Perth modular home manufacturer has blindsided its customers by announcing its sudden closure and takeover by a new firm.

WA Consumer Protection Commissioner Trish Blake told 102.5 ABC Perth she wanted anyone affected to lodge a formal complaint with the department.

"I will be asking the team to investigate further and to look into it," she said.

"I'm also keen to link in with ASIC, because my concern is there may have been some trading whilst insolvent, questions that need to be answered."

Consumer rights apply

Dozens of customers have paid deposits, some more than $100,000, but have not received their buildings which are months, and in some cases, years overdue.

"Often with these companies, particularly if you've got a letter that says 'we're in financial hardship, we can't deliver your product', that tells me that something very wrong potentially has gone on in the background, which is why I want to refer things to ASIC as well," Ms Blake said.

Trish Blake says she has asked her team to investigate the company. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

Because the homes are manufactured off-site and clients independently arrange for them to be transported and place on sites, the contracts are not covered under building indemnity insurance which covers losses when a building company goes out of business.

However, Ms Blake said customers still had rights under Australian Consumer Law.

"There is an offence for wrongly accepting payment and not delivering," she said.

"Particularly … taking payment when they know they don't really have a reasonable chance of delivering.

" We want to look into all of this, which is why we need as many complaints as we can get, so that we can get across the entire fact scenario of this one and see what action we can take. "

At this stage, Ms Blake said it was unclear whether the agency would be able to get customers' deposits refunded.

A Credit Watch report shows the company has a debt to the Australian Taxation Office of $576,614.68.

It is also facing three court actions for other payments totalling just over $170,000.

Customers in limbo

Peter Elliot, who ordered a granny flat intended for his parents in May 2025, and which is now months overdue, said he was shocked to receive the letter.

Mr Elliot paid a $90,000 deposit, which was 50 per cent of the cost of building, to guarantee a three-month completion time and had been hoping to have his parents living in his backyard by Christmas 2025.

"This was a disability-ready home for them to move into as they progress further in their lives," Mr Elliot said.

He said he was uncertain how another company would complete the build.

"I can't envisage another company taking on, effectively, the 50 per cent debt against the buildings that are either underway or promised to be underway," he said.

Fellow concerned customer Steve Evans has paid almost $160,000 towards a customised home from Bella Modular.

He initially paid a deposit of $28,000, then was contacted by the company four weeks ago to ask for a further $130,000, which he paid.

"I feel like a bit of a patsy … and I've got a horrible pit in my stomach that I've lost the money," Mr Evans said.

World.title: Five of Dolly Parton's best songs explained
World.content:
When Dolly Parton received the 2026 Academy of Country Music Poet's Award a week ago, she accepted the honour virtually due to recent health issues including dizziness and dehydration.

The award was the latest Parton had received in recognition of her songwriting.

The American musician, actor, author and philanthropist, died after a brief battle with cancer. She was 80.

In a video message posted to Instagram upon accepting the ACM award, Parton said songwriting was always "the most important part" of who she was creatively.

"Songwriting has been my therapy," she said.

"Songwriting has been my release, my joy.

" Songwriting has been a gift from God that has allowed me to touch people with words and music. "

Parton was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2001, and in 2007, she received its highest honour — the Johnny Mercer Award.

Here are the stories behind some of Parton's best songs.

Jolene (1973)

The single Jolene was released in October 1973 and appeared on the 1974 album of the same name.

In 2008 Parton told NPR's All Things Considered that the name Jolene belonged to a young girl of about eight who wanted an autograph at a show.

"And she had this beautiful red hair, this beautiful skin, these beautiful green eyes … I said, 'Well, you're the prettiest little thing I ever saw. So, what is your name?' And she said, 'Jolene.'

"And I said, 'Jolene. Jolene. Jolene. Jolene.' I said, 'That is pretty. That sounds like a song. I'm going to write a song about that.'"

The story for the song came from another redhead — an adult this time — who was working as a bank teller and was paying a lot of attention to Parton's new husband at the time Carl Dean, who died in 2025.

Dolly Parton's one-liners Dolly Parton was rarely lost for words, possessing a remarkable ability to impart wisdom wrapped in her signature southern wit.

"She got this terrible crush on my husband," Parton said.

"And he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention.

"It was kinda like a running joke between us, when I was saying, 'Hell, you're spending a lot of time at the bank. I don't believe we've got that kind of money.'"

The song went seven times platinum in Australia.

Cover versions have been recorded by Olivia Newton John, the White Stripes, and Beyoncé on Cowboy Carter, which won Album of the Year at the Grammys in 2025.

I Will Always Love You (1974)

I Will Always Love You was released on the Jolene album and reached number one on the Billboard Country Music Chart.

Whitney Houston's version for the 1992 film The Bodyguard, starring Houston and Kevin Costner, took the song to new heights.

It reached the number one spot on the Billboard Hot 100 on November 28 that year and remained there for what was then a record-breaking 14 weeks.

Parton wrote the song about Porter Wagoner before she departed the syndicated television program The Porter Wagoner Show in 1974.

She had collaborated with Wagoner since 1967.

Elvis Presley wanted to record the song after it reached number one on the country charts, but his manager told Parton she had to sign over half of the publishing rights to Presley on any song he recorded.

Parton stood her ground.

"I said, 'I'm really sorry,' and I cried all night. I mean, it was like, the worst thing," Parton told Country Music Television.

" Then when Whitney came out, I made enough money to buy Graceland. "

9 to 5 (1980)

Parton wrote 9 to 5 for the 1980 comedy of the same name in which she made her acting debut alongside Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin.

The song is on Parton's album 9 to 5 and Odd Jobs.

It's an anthem celebrating women in the workplace, as well as an appeal for pay equity.

In 1980 the song led to Parton's first Oscar nomination for Best Original Song.

9 to 5 reached number one on three Billboard charts — the Hot 100, the Hot Country Songs chart, and the Adult Contemporary Charts.

It went seven times platinum in Australia.

Here You Come Again (1977)

This was a rare example of a song Parton recorded that she did not write.

Written by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, Here You Come Again was nominated for Best Female Pop Vocal Performance at the Grammys in 1978.

Parton had been looking for a song to broaden her appeal but was determined for it not to sound like a pop record, begging for a steel guitar so that it would still have that country sound.

The song was, however, the centrepiece of her pop crossover in the late 1970s.

The track is about the frustration felt when an ex-partner suddenly reappears when you've started to move on.

Coat of Many Colors (1971)

Parton wrote Coat of Many Colors on the back of a dry-cleaning receipt while on a tour bus, she said in her 1994 memoir My Life and Other Unfinished Business.

The song is about how Parton's mother Avie Lee Owens, who died at 80 in 2003, stitched a coat together from rags given to the family.

While sewing, she shared the biblical story of Joseph and his coat of many colours.

But while she was proud of the coat, Parton writes about the other school children "laughing and making fun of me" for wearing a coat made out of rags.

She said the song was about bullying, love, acceptance and good parents.

Parton called the song her favourite out of the more than 3,000 she wrote.

Parton released a children's book called Coat of Many Colors in 1994, as well as two made-for-television movies bearing that title. The first was released in 2015 and its sequel, Dolly Parton's Christmas of Many Colours: Circle of Love, was released in 2016.

Parton had 11 siblings and reportedly wrote her first song when she was six years old. It was about a doll her mother made from a corncob.

Parton won 10 Grammys and was nominated 55 times.

World.title: Giants star Toby Greene opens up on his AFL future
World.content:
Expecting to make a call on his future in the next two weeks, Greater Western Sydney captain Toby Greene has detailed his plans to meet Geelong and Essendon.

Greene, the greatest player in the Giants' 15-year history, is closely considering finishing his career in Victoria so he has more support for his young family.

Admitting it will be the toughest decision of his career, the 32-year-old denied he had already made up his mind to leave GWS.

"I felt like a lot of people in Melbourne, or friends, maybe even some people at the club, feel like I'm definitely going, which is not true," Greene told the Ausmerican Aces podcast.

"If I was definitely going, I'd say that now. I'd be up front with the Giants and make it easy for them."

Giants not sweating on Greene's future The Giants are keen to retain Toby Greene, but they are happy to wait until the 32-year-old is ready to make a call on his future.

Greene's good friend and former GWS teammate, Jeremy Cameron, looms as a natural attraction at Geelong.

Wooden spooners Essendon are desperate for senior stars to help their young talent develop.

Former Giants assistant Mark McVeigh has just been appointed Bombers coach and wants to talk with Greene.

"I'll meet with Geelong probably this weekend, I'd say," he said.

"I couldn't give a f*** about the tour, to be honest. I couldn't care about what their footy club looks like. They're a bloody good club.

"I'd do weights at Anytime Fitness, if I have to.

"'Spike' (McVeigh) has reached out as well since he got the job and asked to catch up.

"I said I'd catch up with him, but it wasn't exactly what I was thinking all year at all."

GWS missed finals for the first time since 2022, with several experienced players already making an exit.

Coleman medallist in 2024 Jesse Hogan, enigmatic forward Jake Stringer and ruckman Kieren Briggs are confirmed departures.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"If I didn't think the Giants would finish top-four next year, I wouldn't stay," Greene said.

"One thing I want to do with them is win a flag and that's the best thing I could do ever in footy.

"I could win two or three (premierships) somewhere else [but] it wouldn't be as good as one at the Giants."

Greene has played 282 games for GWS, including the club's first AFL game in 2012.

World.title: Breaking: WA government to appeal $150m Andrew Forrest Fortescue native title payout
World.content:
Mining magnate Andrew Forrest's Fortescue faces a renewed legal battle over a record $150.3 million native title compensation payout, with the WA government confirming it would appeal a landmark Federal Court judgement.

It comes after the Yindjibarndi native title group announced they would also appeal the amount awarded, renewing a bitter dispute with Mr Forrest's company.

The Federal Court had found Fortescue liable for $150 million in cultural losses, and $150,000 in economic losses, plus interest.

At the core of the dispute was the construction of four Pilbara iron ore mines without permission from the Yindjibarndi Ngurra Aboriginal Corporation.

In a statement confirming its appeal, Attorney General Tony Buti said the state government supported "proper compensation" for the impact of mining on country.

WA Attorney-General Tony Buti (ABC News: Mya Kordic )

"As this is a matter which is currently before the court, it would not be appropriate to comment on the specifics of the case at this time."

It's unclear what grounds the WA government is appealing the judgement on.

Legal battle

The $150 million judgement was the culmination of an almost two-decades long legal battle between the Yindjibarndi people and Fortescue.

Some Elders had expressed disappointment at the amount awarded when compared to the billions the mining company had made from its lucrative Solomon Hub mines, built on Yindjibarndi land.

Yindjibarndi Elders are disappointed at the compensation, given the revenue Fortescue gains from the Solomon Hub mines. (Supplied: Phil Davies, Juluwarlu / Yindjibarndi Aboriginal Corporation)

Traditional Owners and Fortescue had attempted to negotiate land use agreements in the past, but never reached a consensus.

In a statement, Yindjibarndi Group CEO Michael Woodley said the Aboriginal corporation's decision to appeal came after a unanimous vote.

Michael Woodley speaks at a Yindjibarndi community meeting in Roebourne prior to the decision. (ABC Pilbara: Alistair Bates)

He said both Fortescue and the WA government had argued in court for lower compensation amounts.

"The state government has a responsibility to also provide support and protection to the Yindjibarndi community from miners," Mr Woodley had said.

World.title: Anger as Coles in home of the Big Banana to drop local bananas
World.content:
In the home of the Big Banana, local farmers say it is a "kick in the guts" to have supermarket giant Coles end an agreement to supply locally grown fresh produce to stores in the region.

Instead, the bananas on the shelves of the Coles supermarket in Coffs Harbour are now expected to largely come from North Queensland.

"The fruit is going to travel 1,600 kilometres compared to six," Coffs Harbour and District Banana Growers Association secretary-treasurer Mick Gentle said.

" [It] just doesn't make sense. "

Coles supermarkets in Coffs Harbour have always sourced some fruit and vegetables, including bananas, within a 10-kilometre radius of their stores. (ABC Coffs Coast: Claire Simmonds)

Until now, producers in the region have sent their fruit and vegetables directly to supermarkets through agreements involving wholesaler Golden Dawn.

Coles initially flagged its intention to exit from the agreement a year ago.

In correspondence seen by the ABC, Coles said the decision was "part of a broader strategic shift [to simplify their] supply chain and focus on a smaller number of strategic partnerships".

In a statement, a Coles spokesperson said: "We regularly review our supply chain to ensure we are delivering the best value, quality and availability for our customers."

Disappointing decision

Mr Gentle said the decision threatened the sustainability of the industry on the Coffs Coast.

"My mind struggles to think what Coffs Harbour might be without bananas one day," he said.

"It's really scary that Coffs might lose its iconic banana."

Mick Gentle is concerned about the industry's future. (Supplied: Mick Gentle)

Coffs Harbour banana grower Dominic Canale said it would take time to determine how much of an effect the exit of Coles would have on the industry in the region.

"We will know more come summer," he said.

"I'm hoping not too much needs to go down in the markets in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane because you always get a lot less of a return when they go [there]."

Dominic Canale wants to secure a path in the industry for his children. (Supplied: Dominic Canale)

The fourth-generation farmer said he was not planning on leaving the industry.

"I'd love for the kids to have the opportunity to take on the farm in the future too," Mr Canale said.

"If Woolies takes on a bit more for us of what Coles have stopped [taking], we should be fine, but I don't know; things change all the time."

Australia's banana industry is worth $1.3 billion. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Golden Dawn declined to comment.

Supplier crunch

NSW Farmers spokesperson and banana farmer Paul Shoker said the decision by Coles would affect up to 40 local families, despite the fact that Woolworths would continue to stock produce from the Coffs Coast.

"Those two supermarkets combined nationally sell 70 per cent of the fresh produce market, so if you haven't got access to half of that 70 per cent, it just means … businesses have uncertainty," he said.

"That's a big hit to our industry, and it's not something that we can create a new market [for] over 12 months."

Paul Shoker is calling on Coles to reconsider the move. (ABC News: Charles Rushforth)

Mr Shoker said bananas at Coles stores in the region would most likely come from north Queensland.

"It just means that we won't see locally grown bananas at Coles supermarkets," he said.

"There's plenty of local produce here to go around and … it's a shame to see we aren't utilising that."

World.title: Cricketer Will Pucovski sues Melbourne school over alleged concussion
World.content:
Former Australian test cricketer Will Pucovski is suing Brighton Grammar School over an alleged concussion incident he says ultimately ended his cricket career.

Pucovski's lawyers have filed a statement of claim against the Melbourne private school in the Victorian Supreme Court.

The claim alleges that a head knock during an "aggressively physical" football training session 12 years ago caused a brain injury from which he has never recovered.

Pucovski announced his retirement from cricket in April 2025, at the age of 27, after he sustained his 13th-known concussion.

The particulars contained in the writ are untested allegations only, and Brighton Grammar has not yet put forward its defence to the claim.

Pucovski leaves the field after being hit on the helmet by a ball while playing for the Australia A side in 2020. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Pucovski made his Test debut for Australia against India at the SCG in January 2021, scoring 62 in the first innings.

Two months earlier, the batting prodigy became the first player this century to score two consecutive double centuries in the Sheffield Shield.

He last played Sheffield Shield in March 2024, when he sustained the 13th known concussion of his career.

He finished with a first-class average of 45.19, including seven centuries and a highest score of 255 not out.

Head clash during training session following footy loss

Pucovski's lawyers allege Brighton Grammar School (BGS) "exhibited a high-handed, contumelious and callous disregard" for his safety.

According to the writ, Pucovski was part of BGS's second-18 football team that suffered a substantial loss to Scotch College in a round of the APS AFL school football competition in 2014.

It is alleged that after the loss, the team was told that the next training session would be "especially physical and demanding" and that they were instructed to be aggressive "due to the team's unacceptably weak performance" in the game.

"The plaintiff understood the intention … was that players would show aggression towards each other and that they deserved physical pain," the claim states.

"Requiring the plaintiff to participate in the training drill at the training session involved fault that concerned or related to an intentional act, namely the training drill, that was instructed to be undertaken, and was undertaken, with the intent that it would cause injury or harm to those participating."

Pucovski's lawyers allege Brighton Grammar School breached its duty of care to him when he was a student. (ABC News)

The claim states Pucovski was sling-tackled and his head collided with the knee of another student, knocking him unconscious.

His lawyers allege he was helped off the field, where he was left alone while the drill continued, after which he was asked to resume training, including tackling.

Over the following days, Pucovski said he suffered head pain and other symptoms and was taken to a doctor who advised he had a concussion.

The following weekend, Pucovski acted as a team runner, conveying messages to the players throughout the game.

His parents took him to Cabrini Hospital the next day after his headaches intensified and he developed nausea.

Medical staff advised him not to go to school and to cease physical activity.

"In the period of about six weeks following the plaintiff's attendance at Cabrini, the plaintiff frequently stayed at home, mostly alone, and often in a darkened room; continued to experience headaches; and developed for the first time persistent, looping and intrusive thoughts which would subsequently be diagnosed as a form of mental health disorder (Obsessive Compulsive Disorder)," the claim states.

Pucovski (right) trains with David Warner at the SCG in 2021. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

The claim alleges the head collision caused a sustained traumatic brain injury from which Pucovski has never recovered, vision impairment and was predisposed to worsening symptoms if he receives any further concussions.

It alleges BGS grossly breached its duty of care by failing to properly treat and manage his injury, failed to comply with its own first aid policy and did not follow the AFL's concussion protocol.

Brighton Grammar said it was unable to comment because the matter was before the courts.

World.title: ‘No need to hide it’: Accused CBD stabber launches tirade from custody
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime ‘No need to hide it’: Accused CBD stabber launches tirade from custody Eleanor Campbell and Carla Jaeger August 26, 2026 — 5:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The man accused of assaulting a 10-year-old boy and repeatedly stabbing his mother has launched an extraordinary tirade, telling a Melbourne court “at least they’re both still breathing” while appearing from custody. Jerry Sowood, 27, from Sunshine West, shouted at times during a Melbourne Magistrates’ Court hearing on Wednesday, where he refused to answer the magistrate’s questions and told the court that there was “no need to hide” his offending. “I punched the kid in the head, I took the scissors, I stabbed the woman in the head,” Sowood told the court. “There’s no need to hide it. At least they’re both still breathing so at least I kept my humanity.



“I’m telling you what I did. And I’m saying there’s no family that was torn apart. Even though I did what I did, the mum did not lose her child. A child was not taken away from her. It was outside the police station.” Sowood was arrested on Tuesday afternoon after he allegedly punched the 10-year-old boy outside Victoria Police’s Spencer Street headquarters, and then placed the child’s mother in a headlock and stabbed her with a pair of scissors before several passers-by intervened. Appearing via video link and dressed in a grey T-shirt with a large sailing boat motif, Sowood refused to speak to a lawyer before the Wednesday hearing, the court heard. The Sunshine West man told the court he would not see a nurse while in custody, and he also refused to tell the magistrate whether he had any medical conditions. “I was in a mental state of mind when I did what I did,” Sowood said. Police said the 46-year-old woman was visiting Melbourne from Phillip Island with her 10-year-old son and two other children when the completely random attack occurred, which ended only when several witnesses intervened.



The mother is at the Royal Melbourne Hospital recovering from injuries to her back and shoulders, while her son recovers at the Royal Children’s Hospital. Sowood has been charged with affray, intentionally causing injury, multiple counts of unlawful assault, conduct endangering life, and conduct endangering serious injury. Sowood’s next court date is set for November. ‘A bit frightening’ Barista Phoebe Maw, who works at a coffee shop near the Victoria Police Headquarters on Spencer Street, was shocked to hear about Tuesday’s attack.



Phoebe Maw (left) and Sue Yang. Jason South The 29-year-old recently moved to Melbourne from Sydney’s western suburbs and felt the city was less safe for young women compared with where she grew up. The cafe worker said it was common for people to come into the shop affected by drugs or mental illness and to behave erratically. “It’s honestly a bit frightening because we work so close,” she said. “There are days when it’s really crazy, but there are some days when it’s nothing.



“I feel like it’s getting worse.” Phoebe Maw and Sue Yang said they’ve noticed an increase in crime since last year. Jason South Maw and her colleague, Sue Yang, 28, both pointed to a rise in visible homelessness and drug addiction near and around Southern Cross Station. “Every morning when I go to the bathroom at Southern Cross, I always encounter a lot of them [drug-affected people] ... there’s a lot of police walking around, but I feel like people aren’t scared of them,” she said. Since the pandemic, retail workers have noted a sharp increase in antisocial behaviour around the Spencer Street strip from a small group of repeat offenders despite a strengthening of bail laws.



Security guard Ahmad Fawad Safi said he has witnessed hundreds of thefts and confrontations at the strip’s Coles supermarket, often involving the same person, since he started working there a month ago. The 35-year-old said he was assaulted by a man accused of stealing a two-pack of Red Bull after he chased him outside the shop last week. “He started attacking me and punching me in the face,” he said. 7-Eleven worker Mahipal said he was assaulted last month after confronting a man who walked out of the store without paying for a coffee, though he said he did not file a police complaint because he assumed the thief would be released quickly. “We feel like [calling police] is a waste of time,” Mahipal said, claiming he witnessed theft on average every 20 minutes at the store.



Commercial operations manager Ali, who lives in Craigieburn with his wife and two young children, said he thought crime was a bigger issue in the city’s west but noted the CBD had grown increasingly volatile. He said a lot has changed since his family moved to Clifton Hill to from Lebanon in the ’90s. “House prices, rental prices, cost of living – everything goes up and people’s wages never do. Mental health has increased because of the pandemic – there’s crime everywhere to be honest.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Loved on both sides of politics, Dolly Parton represented the best of America
World.content:
CultureCelebrityPop culture Editorial Loved on both sides of politics, Dolly Parton represented the best of America The Herald's View Editorial August 26, 2026 — 5:09pm

August 26, 2026 — 5:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The songs of Dolly Parton soundtrack the lives of generations but her public life also chronicled the extraordinary changes experienced by many around the world. Parton has died aged 80 and in a career spanning more than six decades, penned some 3000 songs and inspired a range of communities, from fans who simply loved her voice and lyrics to rednecks who could see she was one of them, and members of the LGBTQ community impressed by her rhinestones and chutzpah. Photo: AP The writer Chet Flippo’s August 1977 Rolling Stone magazine cover story escorted the country and western singer into the larger world of rock with the line “Big Rock Candy Mountain”, borrowed from the Depression-era song about a hobo’s vision of paradise that neatly encapsulated her dirt poor Appalachian childhood and the arrival of glittering stardom. Blond ambition, Daisy Mae, Steel Magnolia and toast of Dollywood were just some of the sobriquets that showered down as Parton moved from C&W and country radio to television, pop, film and business and philanthropy.



But, her enduring legacy came from more than celebrity: she was a songwriter and owner who turned her personal story into something that touched on the admired American trait of rugged individualism but remained fixed to the unselfish reality of helping others. Her philanthropy touched millions around the world. She funded research for a COVID vaccine and established the Imagination Library, a philanthropic book gifting program to inspire a love of reading among children, especially those from more disadvantaged communities. Every child in the program receives a book a month in the mail for free, until they turn five. The library stemmed from her father’s inability to read properly. Since 1995 more than 200 million books have been distributed around the world. Last year, the Imagination Library delivered its 2 millionth book in Australia. In NSW, the program is run by charity United Way and has targeted 15,000 children in vulnerable local government areas. To many, Parton also came to define feminism. She forged her own path with confidence, smarts, and humour and encouraged women to embrace who they wanted to be and stand up for their values. She starred in 9 to 5, the 1980 film regarded as a feminist landmark for its portrayal of equality in the workplace and satire of corporate gender dynamics. Anthony Albanese meets Dolly Parton in 2011. Facebook/Anthony Albanese



Parton’s popularity crossed geography and age groups. Older Australians watched her emerge from Nashville roots on mainstream US television programs with her 1974 hit Jolene. Younger fans met her courtesy of Whitney Houston’s 1992 version of Parton’s song I Will Always Love You. Throughout, Parton stayed away from politics. Despite blandishments, she refused Presidential Medal of Freedom offers and would not choose between Donald Trump and his Democrat opponents. Her reason was homespun common sense: “Because you’re going to lose half your audience.” Parton was one of the last public figures who was a hero to both ends of the political spectrum. In a polarised world that too often sees the worst in America, she was its best. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: WA government appeals landmark Yindjibarndi compensation ruling, seeking ‘clarity’ on law
World.content:
NationalWACourts WA government appeals landmark Yindjibarndi compensation ruling, seeking ‘clarity’ on law Michael Philipps August 26, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The West Australian government has filed an appeal of a Federal Court native title compensation decision following the Yinjibarndi Ngurra Aboriginal Corporation’s decision to appeal the same judgement. In May this year, Justice Stephen Burley awarded the Yindjibarndi people of WA’s Pilbara region about $150 million dollars for cultural loss following an 18-year battle for compensation with Andrew Forrest’s mining company Fortescue. Yinjibarndi Ngurra Aboriginal Corporation chief executive Michael Woodley. Carla Gottgens Yindjibarndi Ngurra Aboriginal Corporation this week lodged an appeal with the Federal Court over the amount of compensation awarded over mining that has occurred on the group’s traditional lands since 2012. The corporation’s appeal follows a large meeting of Yindjibarndi people last month, where attendees voted unanimously to proceed with the legal process.



YNAC chief executive Michael Woodley said the appeal related to the amounts awarded by the Court for both economic and cultural loss. “Broadly speaking, our appeal addresses the court’s rejection of a royalty-based measure of compensation for economic loss and its application of freehold value to our native title rights based on pastoral rather than mining use,” he said. “In addition, we address the decision that Yindjibarndi People are not entitled to compensation for cultural loss arising from the effects of social division in our community caused by the mine.” The Yindjibarndi people sought substantial compensation of more than $1 billion for their cultural and economic losses, while Fortescue aimed to limit compensation to no more than around $8.1 million. However, the state contended that compensation should be awarded in the vicinity of $5 million to $10 million.



In handing down his original decision, Burley said the claim was substantial, despite it falling well short of the $1 billion the group was seeking. Related Article WA courts WA government cleared of any liability in landmark native title case Woodley has previously described the landmark compensation figure as “unsatisfactory in the context of what has been lost”. The final figure handed down included $150 million for cultural loss, but only $100,000 for economic loss. Woodley said the state government has a responsibility to also provide support and protection to the Yindjibarndi community from miners.



On Wednesday, WA Attorney-General Tony Buti said the government acknowledged the impact of mining on country and supported Yindjibarndi receiving proper compensation from mining proponents for these activities. “Western Australia has led the country in native title determinations, with many determinations reached by agreement,” he said. “Native title compensation is a complex and emerging area, and it is important that we have clarity on the law to support future negotiations and native title settlements across the state.” Buti added that the government is committed to maintaining respectful and constructive engagement with YNAC as the proceedings continue, as has been the case for the previous four years. “This includes our existing and significant partnerships with the Yindjibarndi people, such as through negotiations to support Yindjibarndi Water’s acquisition of the Dampier Seawater Desalination Plant,” he said.



“As this is a matter which is currently before the court, it would not be appropriate to comment on the specifics of the case at this time.”

World.title: Tips and previews for racing at Wagga on Thursday
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Tips and previews for racing at Wagga on Thursday Neil Evans August 26, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Track heavy 8 and rail true RACE 1 4. The Buncha is a four-year-old on debut behind three trials. Bolted in the latest, cruising clear late after crossing to the front from wide out on a heavy surface. Had plenty in hand, and looks ready to go in what is a moderate lineup. 6. Reds Express is fit and handles rain-affected ground. Has placed in his last three when working home from midfield. Expect home track filly 8. Ultrasonic to improve at her second start, with blinkers added, after dropping out in a deeper maiden five weeks back. 2. Phenomenon is a market watch second-up after an even effort into a place at huge odds over the border on soft ground. Drawn inside and bred to handle heavy going.

How to play it: The Buncha to win. RACE 2 1. Mr Tadashi won three straight up to BM 66 level when relishing the wet before a flat performance over the same trip and grade five weeks back. Freshened to recapture his best, and while rising to 59kg deep into the campaign, finds a thin lineup for this level, and in his pet conditions with all six wins from 30 starts coming on rain-affected ground. 2. Winning Point will appreciate getting back up to this distance after doing his best work late over the mile in a lesser grade. Include Goulburn-based stablemates 4. Devine Outcast rising in distance fifth-up, and 5. It Is To Be having dropped in weight for a tougher race, in all trifecta and first fours.

How to play it: Mr Tadashi to win.



RACE 3 8. Nikita Zou is a lightly raced and progressive Canberra filly in a position to open her account in her first full preparation. Was ridden much quieter at Nowra 17 days ago when charging home to beat all. 11. El Cool Gee comes through that same race as the top selection when also making up late ground at her second start. Showing promise. 3. Hellfighter has been up for a long time, and after running a place in consecutive provincial maidens, put in a howler as a heavily backed favourite at the Sapphire Coast. Given a month between runs, with winkers replacing blinkers. 7. Brilliant Bull Ant is chasing a breakthrough win at his 13th start, but gets an overdue drop in weight.

How to play it: Nikita Zou to win. RACE 4 1. Time For Snow is still a maiden after beating all but the winner seven times from 14 starts. Found one better in five consecutive starts last time out before failing at the provincials and spelling. Looks well weighted against country opposition. No official trials, but reportedly been working well, and is the one to beat. 6. Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer, SC, has asked Anita Perrottet why she charged a $30,000 sign-on fee to Beckington for her services, and what work she did to justify her monthly retainer when there was no record of any work for Beckington’s client, Greyhound Racing NSW.

World.title: ‘No need to hide it’: Accused CBD stabber launches tirade from custody
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime ‘No need to hide it’: Accused CBD stabber launches tirade from custody Eleanor Campbell and Carla Jaeger August 26, 2026 — 5:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The man accused of assaulting a 10-year-old boy and repeatedly stabbing his mother has launched an extraordinary tirade, telling a Melbourne court “at least they’re both still breathing” while appearing from custody. Jerry Sowood, 27, from Sunshine West, shouted at times during a Melbourne Magistrates’ Court hearing on Wednesday, where he refused to answer the magistrate’s questions and told the court that there was “no need to hide” his offending. “I punched the kid in the head, I took the scissors, I stabbed the woman in the head,” Sowood told the court. “There’s no need to hide it. At least they’re both still breathing so at least I kept my humanity.



“I’m telling you what I did. And I’m saying there’s no family that was torn apart. Even though I did what I did, the mum did not lose her child. A child was not taken away from her. It was outside the police station.” Sowood was arrested on Tuesday afternoon after he allegedly punched the 10-year-old boy outside Victoria Police’s Spencer Street headquarters, and then placed the child’s mother in a headlock and stabbed her with a pair of scissors before several passers-by intervened. Appearing via video link and dressed in a grey T-shirt with a large sailing boat motif, Sowood refused to speak to a lawyer before the Wednesday hearing, the court heard. The Sunshine West man told the court he would not see a nurse while in custody, and he also refused to tell the magistrate whether he had any medical conditions. “I was in a mental state of mind when I did what I did,” Sowood said. Police said the 46-year-old woman was visiting Melbourne from Phillip Island with her 10-year-old son and two other children when the completely random attack occurred, which ended only when several witnesses intervened.



The mother is at the Royal Melbourne Hospital recovering from injuries to her back and shoulders, while her son recovers at the Royal Children’s Hospital. Sowood has been charged with affray, intentionally causing injury, multiple counts of unlawful assault, conduct endangering life, and conduct endangering serious injury. Sowood’s next court date is set for November. ‘A bit frightening’ Barista Phoebe Maw, who works at a coffee shop near the Victoria Police Headquarters on Spencer Street, was shocked to hear about Tuesday’s attack.



Phoebe Maw (left) and Sue Yang. Jason South The 29-year-old recently moved to Melbourne from Sydney’s western suburbs and felt the city was less safe for young women compared with where she grew up. The cafe worker said it was common for people to come into the shop affected by drugs or mental illness and to behave erratically. “It’s honestly a bit frightening because we work so close,” she said. “There are days when it’s really crazy, but there are some days when it’s nothing.



“I feel like it’s getting worse.” Phoebe Maw and Sue Yang said they’ve noticed an increase in crime since last year. Jason South Maw and her colleague, Sue Yang, 28, both pointed to a rise in visible homelessness and drug addiction near and around Southern Cross Station. “Every morning when I go to the bathroom at Southern Cross, I always encounter a lot of them [drug-affected people] ... there’s a lot of police walking around, but I feel like people aren’t scared of them,” she said. Since the pandemic, retail workers have noted a sharp increase in antisocial behaviour around the Spencer Street strip from a small group of repeat offenders despite a strengthening of bail laws.



Security guard Ahmad Fawad Safi said he has witnessed hundreds of thefts and confrontations at the strip’s Coles supermarket, often involving the same person, since he started working there a month ago. The 35-year-old said he was assaulted by a man accused of stealing a two-pack of Red Bull after he chased him outside the shop last week. “He started attacking me and punching me in the face,” he said. 7-Eleven worker Mahipal said he was assaulted last month after confronting a man who walked out of the store without paying for a coffee, though he said he did not file a police complaint because he assumed the thief would be released quickly. “We feel like [calling police] is a waste of time,” Mahipal said, claiming he witnessed theft on average every 20 minutes at the store.



Commercial operations manager Ali, who lives in Craigieburn with his wife and two young children, said he thought crime was a bigger issue in the city’s west but noted the CBD had grown increasingly volatile. He said a lot has changed since his family moved to Clifton Hill to from Lebanon in the ’90s. “House prices, rental prices, cost of living – everything goes up and people’s wages never do. Mental health has increased because of the pandemic – there’s crime everywhere to be honest.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: WA government appeals landmark Yindjibarndi compensation ruling, seeking ‘clarity’ on law
World.content:
NationalWACourts WA government appeals landmark Yindjibarndi compensation ruling, seeking ‘clarity’ on law Michael Philipps August 26, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The West Australian government has filed an appeal of a Federal Court native title compensation decision following the Yinjibarndi Ngurra Aboriginal Corporation’s decision to appeal the same judgement. In May this year, Justice Stephen Burley awarded the Yindjibarndi people of WA’s Pilbara region about $150 million dollars for cultural loss following an 18-year battle for compensation with Andrew Forrest’s mining company Fortescue. Yinjibarndi Ngurra Aboriginal Corporation chief executive Michael Woodley. Carla Gottgens Yindjibarndi Ngurra Aboriginal Corporation this week lodged an appeal with the Federal Court over the amount of compensation awarded over mining that has occurred on the group’s traditional lands since 2012. The corporation’s appeal follows a large meeting of Yindjibarndi people last month, where attendees voted unanimously to proceed with the legal process.



YNAC chief executive Michael Woodley said the appeal related to the amounts awarded by the Court for both economic and cultural loss. “Broadly speaking, our appeal addresses the court’s rejection of a royalty-based measure of compensation for economic loss and its application of freehold value to our native title rights based on pastoral rather than mining use,” he said. “In addition, we address the decision that Yindjibarndi People are not entitled to compensation for cultural loss arising from the effects of social division in our community caused by the mine.” The Yindjibarndi people sought substantial compensation of more than $1 billion for their cultural and economic losses, while Fortescue aimed to limit compensation to no more than around $8.1 million. However, the state contended that compensation should be awarded in the vicinity of $5 million to $10 million.



In handing down his original decision, Burley said the claim was substantial, despite it falling well short of the $1 billion the group was seeking. Related Article WA courts WA government cleared of any liability in landmark native title case Woodley has previously described the landmark compensation figure as “unsatisfactory in the context of what has been lost”. The final figure handed down included $150 million for cultural loss, but only $100,000 for economic loss. Woodley said the state government has a responsibility to also provide support and protection to the Yindjibarndi community from miners.



On Wednesday, WA Attorney-General Tony Buti said the government acknowledged the impact of mining on country and supported Yindjibarndi receiving proper compensation from mining proponents for these activities. “Western Australia has led the country in native title determinations, with many determinations reached by agreement,” he said. “Native title compensation is a complex and emerging area, and it is important that we have clarity on the law to support future negotiations and native title settlements across the state.” Buti added that the government is committed to maintaining respectful and constructive engagement with YNAC as the proceedings continue, as has been the case for the previous four years. “This includes our existing and significant partnerships with the Yindjibarndi people, such as through negotiations to support Yindjibarndi Water’s acquisition of the Dampier Seawater Desalination Plant,” he said.



“As this is a matter which is currently before the court, it would not be appropriate to comment on the specifics of the case at this time.”

World.title: Rio2 gets green light for Peruvian copper expansion
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Rio2 gets green light for Peruvian copper expansion Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 26, 2026 — 4:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Diversified metals producer Rio2 Limited has been given the regulatory green light to expand its Condestable underground copper mine in Peru, clearing the path to a production boost and an extension of the mine’s environmentally approved life by another decade. After a 14-month process, Peruvian authorities have approved the company’s Modified Environmental Impact Study. The decision is a significant milestone, permitting an increase in throughput capacity to 10,000 tonnes per day from the current 8400 tonnes per day. Rio2 Limited’s Condestable copper mine in Peru has received a key environmental approval, paving the way for a significant expansion. The official nod also provides environmental authorisation for a new dry-stack tailings facility with an initial permitted capacity of 43 million tonnes. The company says the design allows for staged expansions up to a massive 170 million tonnes, providing plenty of room for future mine-life extensions while reinforcing its commitment to modern, low-risk tailings management and supporting the operation’s pathway to Copper Mark certification. Copper Mark is a leading assurance framework that promotes responsible production practices in the copper, molybdenum, nickel and zinc industries. Certification ensures a company’s mining and refining site meets environmental, social and governance standards, and lines up with the UN’s sustainable development goals.



‘The approval of the MEIA is a significant regulatory milestone for Rio2 and Minera Condestable and allows for several significant operational milestones.’ Rio2 Limited president,chief executive officer and director Andrew Cox The company expects the move will significantly improve total water recovery from its current 60 per cent to almost 90 per cent. This could provide further headroom for process growth without chasing additional water permits or increasing the draw on local water resources. Rio2 says it’s now progressing technical and economic evaluations, ahead of a final investment decision on the expansion during the second half of this year. Rio2 Limited president, chief executive officer and director Andrew Cox said: “The approval of the MEIA is a significant regulatory milestone for Rio2 and Minera Condestable and allows for several significant operational milestones. This decision extends our operating horizon, confirms our environmental approach with dry-stack tailings, and opens the regulatory path to expand operations to 10,000 tpd and beyond.” The confidence to push ahead with an expansion is backed by some serious numbers from a recently updated June mineral resource and reserve estimate for Condestable. The project now hosts proven and probable reserves of 36.5 million tonnes grading an impressive 0.73 per cent copper, 0.15 grams per tonne (g/t) gold and 4.28g/t silver.



The broader resource is even bigger, with the measured and indicated categories holding 82.1 million tonnes at 0.69 per cent copper, 0.13g/t gold and 4.12g/t silver. Contained within that is a significant metal inventory of 565,000 tonnes of copper, 355,000 ounces of gold and 10.87 million ounces of silver. That reserve underpins an operational mine life of 14 years and a post-tax net present value of a hefty US$710 million (A$988M). In the second quarter of this year, the mine processed over 700,000 tonnes of ore, producing 4218.5 tonnes of copper, 4451 ounces of gold, and 74,374 ounces of silver contained in concentrate. While the current resource provides a solid foundation, Rio2 is also exploring other ways to support an expanded operation. The company is set to kick off an ore sorting pilot program in the fourth quarter of this year, targeting existing low-grade stockpiles and waste dumps to unlock additional value. In parallel, Rio2’s exploration campaigns are continuing at both the surface and underground levels to expand the resource and replace mined reserves. A complete surface geophysical survey of the entire Condestable land package was recently completed, with management now analysing the results. The company is also continuing to produce gold at its Fenix Gold heap leach mine in Chile, clocking 9088 ounces in the second quarter this year as it ramps up production to a forecast 100,000 ounces a year.



With the MEIA now approved, Rio2 appears to have all its ducks in a row at Condestable. It has a significant resource, solid economics and now the crucial regulatory permit to grow. As engineering studies continue and the company barrels towards a final investment decision later this year, all eyes will be on how it plans to turbocharge this already productive Peruvian copper asset.
